div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

MIGHTY poor dogs sometimes make fine sausage meat. PIETY is like beans, it seems to do the best on poor sue. SECOND thoughts are always best. Woman was an afterthought of creation. THE daughter of the millionaire of the future will probably be a billion heiress. WHEN a man has the nature of a sheep he has an easy time of it curbing his impetuosity. GOING to law is like skinning a new milk cow for her hide and giving the beef tew the lawyers. THE scientist who says that a person could not live over five days without water is suspected of being a milkman. BE modest, but not too modest. Be just modest enoilgh. The violet is so modest that everybody tramples it under foot. • ' A WOMAN never sees a baby without wanting to run to it; a man never sees a baby without want- ing to run from it. THE Persians have a saying that "Ten measures of talk were sent down upon the earth, and the women took nine. .

"METALS are more active," wrote the market reporter whose wife had hastened his exit that morning with a flying flatiron. , WOMEN love admiration, approbation, self-immo- lation on the part of others; are often weak, vain, and frivolous. Ditto men. THE proof of the pudding is in the eating; the proof of a woman is in making a pudding; and the proof of a man is being able to dine without one. "IN Siam the cats have their tails banged." In this country the aim is to bang their heads, but the bootjack sometimes flies wide of the mark. AN indirect way of getting a drink of water at a cheap boarding-house is to ask for a third cup of tea.

A COLLEGE JOKE from the "Trinity Tablet."— Fresh.—" May I have the pleasure 7" Miss Society " Oui." Fresh.— "What does 'we' mean?' Miss S—" 0, 13. and I." A. LITTLE GIRL in school gave as a definition ol "bearing false witness against your neighbour,' that "it was when nobody did nothing and some- body went and told of it." _ .

A WOULD-BE WIT once said, speaking of the fail sex, "Ah 1 it's woman's mission to make fools oi men." "And how vexed we are," said a bright- eyed feminine present, "to find that nature has sc often forestalled us." _ _
IT is said that it is no longer the style for girls to learn to play on the banjo, from which a critic infers that they now play on that instrument with- out learning.
, WATER contains microbes, whiskey is frill ol snakes, and a bottle of milk exploded at Baltimore the other day. It looks as though we will have tc drink beer all witter. _ _
THE rage now in Paris is to be married at mid- night. This is a wise move. It accustoms the bride to waiting up until "the wee small hours" foi her husband's return. _ _ _

"He that taketh the sword shall perish by the sword," is a proverb that was written before the generals of an army witnessed battles through field-glasses and gave their orders through aides. STIE—" Indeed, Mr. Dawbin, yours were the only pictures I looked at in the Exhibition." Dawbin— "Ah, you flatter—" She—" No. The others, you know, were so surrounded by the crowds." " DOCTOR, don't you think the queer bonnets that the ladies wear now-a-days have a tendency to produce congestion of the brain 2" "No, madam. Where you see one of those bonnets there is no brain to congest." TusYcP—" Will the gentleman give a trifle to a poor man 2" Gentleman—" How do. I know you are a poor man 7" "How do I know you are a gentleman? It's only by the outside that either of us can judge the other." _ . .

LITTLE TOMMY had spent his first day at school. "What did you learn ?" asked his auntie on his return. Didn't learn apything," said Tommy. Well, what did Lou do 7" Didn't do anything. A woman waTted to know how to spell cat,' and I told her."

BOBBY (whispering)—" Didn't I hear Clara tell you, Mr. Featherly, that she, was sorry but she really couldn't give you a lock of her hair ?" Featherly—" Sh, Bobby !—er yes." Bobby— " Well you just wait a day or two, and I'll get some for you when she's out." "THE prettiest thing in bonnets," said Mrs Brom- ley the other day, "is—" "Your face, Mrs. Brom- ley," said the old gentleman, gallantly, and Mrs. Bromley carried around a nine-inch smile bra week afterward. "Do you love solitude, Miss Smith " "I do indeed,' she replied. After a few moments silence —" I think I'll be going." "Oh, don't go yet Mr. Brown 1" "But I thought you liked to be alone ? " "So I do, but that need not hurry you." IT rather disgusted a cute Yankee who went to a neighbour's barn t 3 steal a cow to find, when be got the animal home, that it was his own cow, which his neighbour had stolen earlier in the night. He says the neighbour is a confounded 11120(111 sneak- ing thief. LITTLE Miss Lily—" Mamma, will you let me go to the funeral of my playmate, Mary 8., to-morrow?" "No, Lily, you went to a party on Saturday, you attended a matinee yesterday; it seems to me that you are having enough distractions for the present." BROWN—I don't see how you can find time to go .to church every Sunday. I'm sure I can't, I've so much to do. Fegg—Yes, I suppose you do turn off good deal of work on Sundays. I wish I could do it; but fact is, I can't go without my sleep as well as you can. Wonder what be meant HE (solemnly)—You had a very narrow escape last night, Miss Julia. She—Why what do yon • mean? He—Well, you see, I had a dream about you. I thought I was about to kiss you when the housemaid rapped at the door and I woke up. She (after a short pause)—That girl must SO. LITTLE FEED—" Oh, mamma! Fido bit me." Mamma—" Not badly I notice." "Right in the finger, mamma. Do you know, I think he's mad?" "Nonsense, Fred." "I wanted him to bite me, mamma." "Why, what do you mean, you silly fel- low ? " "I want to go to Paris. They are sending lots of boys there, when dogs bite 'ern." THE last witticism attributed to Mr. Whistler is - as follows :—Being seated in the stalls of a theatre, and finding the text of the piece insipid, he indig- nantly inquired, "Who wrote this 'Pompadour?'" 'The answer was, "Mr. Grundy "—to which he re- joined, "Oh 1 Mr. Grundy was it I should have • thought it was Mrs. Grundy.' A GENTLEMAN, having occasion to call upon a • physician, stopped at the door and rang the bell. He was answered by an Irish servant girl, of whom he inquired if the doctor was in. " No. ' "Was his lady in ?" "Yes." "Was she engaged 2" The girl looked at him for a moment, and a curious expres- sion rested on her face as she replied, "'Dade, sir, -she's already married." COLONEL Fizznrror was under the painful necessity of administering a severe castigation to his eon Johnny. After he had completed his labours he said sternly to the suffering victim—" Now tell me why I punished you ?" "That's it," sobbed Johnny, "you nearly pounded the life out of me, and now you don't even know why you did it." SERVANT MAlD—Have you heard the news. ma'am? Last night thieves broke into a hen pen and cleared out all the poultry. Mistress—Serves them right, the stupid people. Why don't they take proper precautions; but where did this happen? Maid—At No. 12. Mistress—Why, that is our house! Maid—Certainly; I did not like telling yon for fear you might be startled. CRABB ROBINSON writes in his Diary :—I called on the Lambs. . . . Lamb said, "If you *ill quote any of my jokes, quote this, which is really a good one. Hume repeated the old saying, One fool makes many." Ay, Mr. Hume,' said I, Roint- ing to the company', 'you have a fine family.' 4Do you mean to call me a liar r asked one max of another during a dispute they had on business. "No, I don't mean to call you that. On the con- trary, I say you are the only man in town who tells the truth all the time; but I am offering a reward of £3 to any other man who says he believes me when I say you never lie," was the response. "Well, I'm glad you take it back," replied the other, man, as the tiger-like look of ferocity faded out of his features. A PRECOCIOUS boy accompanied his mother to the theatre. The number was marked K 9, and the boy refused to sit there, insisting that it was re- served for a dog.

Dom Pedro, late of the Brazils, is working hard upon a history of that country. He no longer reigns, he pores.

It is understood that Mr. Gladstone intends dur- ing part of the coming winter to repeat his very successful visit of three years ago to Naples, where he passed a portion ot the winter of 1889-90 as the guest of Mr. Stuart Rendel.

Mr. Gladstone continues to enjoy good health. He attends Hawarden parish church in the morning, and in the afternoon takes a drive and passes a few hours in the Iron Library. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone were on Wednesday entertaining a party, which in- cluded Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P., Mr. Stuart Rendel, M.P., and the Hon. Arthur Acton.

One custom, more creditable than common, pre- vails on Lord Walsingham's Norfolk estate. He allows a shilling for every patridge shot, and the whole sum thus realised is applied to the reduction of the cottager's rents. In this way each cottager has received near]) a sovereign on account of the birds killed in one season,

There is talk in musical circles of the establish- ment of a permanent orchestra for London on as grand a scale as Sir Charles Halle's famous Man- chester band. In the cultivation of these arts, which soften the manners (according to the Latin poet) and prevent men from becoming ferocious, London is far behind Manchester both in public taste and the generosity of public benefactors.

Dr. Emma Ryder, the founder of the Soroais Club, in Bombay, for native women, is about to publish a book entitled "The Little Wives of India.' As she has been amongst them professionally for many years, her revelations are looked forward to with a very great deal of interest. She cites many cases of the sufferings of young wires which have corue per- sonally under her .obs.eivation, and declares that their ill treatment is as bad as human ingenuity can devise.

There is generally a crowd of people lurking about the Queen's Hotel, Eastbourne, to catch a glimpse of Mr. Spurgeon going out for his daily drive. When the weather is fine the carriage is at the door of the hotel a little before elven o'clock. All hats are taken off, the ladies generally wave their pocket-handkerchiefs. Mr. Spurgeon looks much older and very worn. He wears a fur coat and a round soft felt wide-awake. The fine air of Eastbourne is doing him much good.

At Para, in Hungary,a vagrant was arrested some days ago,who called himself Arpad Spielman. Not- withstanding his German name, he did not know a word of German. When called upon to produce his documents, he drew from his pocket a paper, which he handed with much pride to the police officer. It contained the following :—" I hereby testify that Trpad Spielmann is a scamp, a scoundrel, and a thieving vagrant.—Leipsig, January 1, 1891." A veritable Bellerophon's letter.

One of the last M.P.'s who received paymen:-, for their services was Andrew Marvell, the incorrup- tible patriot, who represented Hull from 1660 to 678. He was a political satiristof much weight in his day, and Charles 11. made large bids to gain him to the Government party. These offers Mar- vell rejected with the remark that "he had pro- vided hi 9 dinner for that day." His wages as M.P. were two shillings a day, a sum which would not go far in providing a dinner for some M.P.'s now-a- days.

Mr. E. R. Philips, the new president of the Metropolitan Board Teacher's Association, has been a teacher under the London School Board since 1875. He is a well-known progressive member of Camber- well Vestry and is chairman of the Finance and Law Committee. He is a member of the Peckham Liberal and Radical Association and of the general committee of the Liberal and Radical Union. As a vestry-man he advocates plenty of free libraries, good baths, washhouses, open spaces, and well-paid workmen.

The Browning Society will not have long sur- vived the poet to whose greater glory it was devoted, for the present session will be its last. The society boasts that its appointed work, what- ever that was, is done. It must be allowed, to the credit of the societ,y, that if Robert Browning never showed much concern about its proceedings, he did not discountenance it. When a disputed passage in one of his poems was referred to him for an explanation, he replied that he did not know what he meant, but thought the Browning Society woultl be able to find out.

"I cannot understand why it has pleased Provid- ence to remove on the same day our rose and your thorn." Such was the sentiment uttered to a " Btar" man by a Conservative friend yesterday. The Con- servative friend is one of the most honourable and at the same time one of the most thoroughgoing men of the party, in which he at present occupies a conspicuous place, and will before long occupy a still more prominent one. There can be little doubt that his words express the real views of the Tories in relation to the death of Mr. Smith and Mr. Parnell.

That much travelled journalist and keen observer George Augustus Sala contributes a long article on "The Levant of To-day," to the " Spectator." It is 11 years since Mr. Sala visited Egypt and Syriabe- fore, and there has been revolutionary change since thew. The influence of British occupation of Egypt is seen in Syria in 'Various ways ; one is the notable increase of grogshops. "In Nazareth ,with a popu- lation of 6,500, there was only one drinkshop 11 years ago; there are now 17. On my former jour- ney I do not remember to have seen one drunken native, but this time I saw many." Mr. Sala, how- ever, thinks that our organisation of Egypt has been an undoubted success.

The result of the Bute election is good. It is not a gain, but it shows that the Liberal cause is gain- ing. It teaches the same lesson as North.LEast Manchester. No one expected that landlord-ridden Bute,where the popular feeling is swamped by fag- got votes, would return Mr. McCulloch. Mr. Graham Murray, the successful candidate, says that Bute "has erected another bulwark in front of the Union " ; but despite great advantages there are in- dications that the flowing tide of Liberalism is break- ing down that bulwark. The Tory vote has decreased by 29 as compared with the 1886 election, and is 39 less than it was in 1885. The Liberal candidate polled 171 more than in 1886, and 100 less than in 1885, which leaves 71 to the good. It is nothing to boast about, to be sure ;it is only a straw which shows how the political wind is blowing.

A case of misappropriation of public funds was brought before the Ameer of Afghanistan, ,last month for final disposal. The accused was one Mirza Ahmed Jan, and a correspondent gives" tilt) following curious account of the case :—" In the course of prosecution he was proved to be a poetaster and a great plagiarist, too. • I may not punish him for the thefts of public money, which are not proved, but I cannot pardon him for literary thefts from the work of saintly poets like Saadi and Haflz,' said the Ameer ; and so he ordered that the tongue of the accused should all through be perforated by thick long needles. No sooner was the sentence pronounced than the tongue of the unfortunate wretch was formed into a sieve."

41,Although he never paraded his religion in the face of the world, the late Mr. W. H. Smith was a man of sincere and unaffected piety. He was a prac- tical believer in the efficacy of prayer. Of this I have a touching illustration. I am assured by a well-known clergyman that amid all the worries of public business and the cares of State he never omitted to make a brief prayer before commencing his work in the House of Commons. From another quarter I learn that the absence of any disagree- ment between employers and employed in the firm of W. H. Smith and Son was greatly due to the good influence of the head. The employOs have always been satisfied that they have had fair treatment and good wages, and the worst strike mania has never dragged them into dispute with their employers.

Details are now furnished, under official author- ity, of the Naval Exhibition which is to be held in Liverpool in the Walker Art Gallery early next year. Like its forerunner, which has afforded so much pleasure to Londoners and visitors to London this year, it will comprise historical pictures and portraits, naval relics, models of warships, old and modern steamships, yachts, lighthouses, life-saving apparatus, engines, nautical appliances, relics of discovery,and a large variety of models illustrating naval construction and the valuable inventions connected with our mercantile marine. It is ex- pected that a large number of the pictures, relics and models now at the naval exhibition, Chelsea,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, OCTOBER 17, 1891. A DARING IMPOSTOR.
will be transferred to Liverpool, and that these will be supplemented by many contributions from great steamship companies and large shipbuilders and manufacturers.

A strong reaction against purely intellectual education and in favour of good old-fashioned housewifery is setting in just now. A novel board,. ing school just opened by a clergyman's daughter at Caterham, in Surrey, is one of the outcomes of the reaction. A lady established a farm-school where girls under twenty years of age can be trained in all the domestic duties of a country house. For three months the pupils are trained, not only to superintend, but to take an active part in the work of dairy, kitchen, and pantry, and are rendered independent of " servant-girlism." The clever and genial lady who has started the school makes the three months' course delightful to active girls. It has always seemed to me that such a course as this might very beneficially relieve the strain of hard, intellectual work for examinations which is often imposed on a growing girl during the most critical years of early life.

hoisted out of the stalls,their bodies being suspended in the air,while their heads lay on the floor. Then another man went the length of the room, and dealt the poor things another terrible blow,which knocked one nearest us quite sick. Their throats were next cut, and then a man very quickly removed their heads, and the carcasses were finally rolled over on their backs to be dealt with by the butchers, who swarmed in the place.

BLOOD FLOWED EVERYWHERE and it was one man's ghastly duty to keep the river of blood flowing. The dead and the dying were on all sides of us, and we fled from the scene. We passed through the great refrigerating rooms,verit- able chambers of death, in which you could not hear a sound, and under the guidance of a young Ameri- can, with a very knowing air, we soon reached our starting point. I, for one, was glad to get out of sight of the horrible butchery, and still more glad to think that none of the wholesale murder was being wrought to satisfy my appetite. But the smell ! Take the odour that emanates from the Bridge Inn Yard, Latchford, on a wet day, and mix with it newly shed blood, and you will have some idea of it. It stuck to me for two whole days. It was in every thing I touched, smelled, or tasted. I fancy 1 see the whole ghastly business now and the horrid sensation comes with the recollection. I want no more stock yard for a long time to come.

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
BY " TOWNSMAN?' XIV.-THE CITY OF DESTINY. THE WORLD'S MEAT MARRET.-THE 'UNION STOCK
YARDS.-WHOLESALE SLAUGHTER OF HOGS.-THEY
ARE DEAD BEFORE THEY KNOW IT !-TilE SUR-
PRISED HOG.-ITS FINAL JOURNEY.-ARMOUR & CO,
-BLOOD EVERYWHERE. -CONCLUSION.

Chicago is the world's meat market. Thither gravitate with slow but certain steps, the domes- ticated beasts of the American continent. The cattle from the prairie' the sheep from the meadows, and the hogs from the homesteads wind their way in a never-ending procession to the city's great stock yards. Day after day, year after year, the vast herds throng the roads leading to the world's great slaughter houses. As you approach the city for the first time, the miles of cars for the conveyance of both live and dead stock arrest your attention, and give you some indication of the extent of the meat trade. In the city itself are numerous exten- sive meat markets and curing establishments, that tend to increase your curiosity respecting the traffic, but it is only when you visit the south of the city that an adequate conception of the butcher- ing business is oltained. No visitor to Chicago with an hour to spare omits to make a pilgrimage to the Union stock yards, and see for himself how the business is done. It is a fearfully ghastly work, and brought home very forcibly the remark of my sleeping companion on the voyage out. He was a Belfast man, and he had heen engaged in the Pork ' trade, but he said it was "a soul-deadening busi- ness," and he was heartily glad to get out of it. Anyone who could witness the sights I saw—if only for one day—and not come to the same con- clusion, must be very bard to reach. By taking a southside car and making a suitable connection, you are soon deposited by

div.head: UNION STOCK YARDS,
div.p: THE UNION STOCK YARDS,

and crossing several railway lines the change in the atmosphere leaves you in no doubt as to your whereabouts. On the east are acres of fenced yards, some of which are reached by overhead roadways, and into which the stock are first driven; and on the west are the factories of the various firms en- gaged in the meat trade. The yards are well away from the city propelitnd form a small city in them- selves. They are intersected by streets which run direct to the city, and by rails connected with all the through railroads. It was Monday morning when, in company with Mr. James F. Bate, I visited the stock yards. A light persistent rain fell all the morning, adding to the gloom and melancholy of the surroundings. It also had the effect of in- crAasing the stench that emanated from the facto- ries. We first visited the premises of the Inter- national Packing Company, where the

div.head: WHOLESALE SLAUGHTER OF;HOGS
div.p: WHOLESALE SLAUGHTER OF;HOGS

is perpetrated. At this factory you can see the hogs enter alive, and take them home with you as sausages if you wait long enough. The hogs really seem to be killed like clockwork, and then the carcasses proceed on their travels along over- head railways, during which they are scraped, dressed, cut up,and converted into bacon,hams,and sausages. Oh, you should see the hogs slaughtered! The view would last you a lifetime. They don't go to work as I've seen them at the Norton Arms, with a man hold of each leg, another the snout, and the butcher to I.lunge in the knife; nor yet as they do at the pig stickery on Wilderspool Causeway, where the performance reminds you of the procession of a culprit to the gallows, and where you can tell by the tone of the pig's screams the very stage of the oper- ations. No, by neither of these means could they slaughter 4,000 hogs a day, as they do at the Inter- national Packing Co.'s place when in full work. The hogs, literally have not time to scream, and

div.head: THEY ARE DEAD BEFORE THEY JEMMY IT,
div.p: THEY ARE DEAD BEFORE THEY JEMMY IT,

as the Irishman would say. This is no exaggeration: it is a sober fact. If you are at all sceptical, just come along with me and see for yourself. Through rooms hunlming with machinery, and reeking with grease, on which you have to pick your way very carefully. the guide leads you to the death chamber right at the top of the building. It is a dull day, and the chamber rather dark, so it takes you a few min- utes to realise your surroundings. At length you can penetrate the gloom. On ycur right, suspended by the leg, are half-a-dozen dead or dying hogs; before you but eight ov ten feet below is a chamber about twelve yards by four yards, a foot or so deep in blood, and standing in the crimson pool is a man deep over the tops of his stockingless shoes. He is engaged in sharpening what proves to be the lethal weapon, so there is a lull in the proceedings. Mean- while you look for the hogs. It is so dark you positively cannot see them for they,.too, are black. In a minute you hear a squeal, and then, oh, horror! one of the pigs has jumped over into a huge trough of blood and is wandering all over it. Presently it is got out, and hearing another movement in the corner you look again, and this time see a swarm of very black hogs, cooped up like beetles in a box. Then a man jumps down amongst them, seizes one by the hind leg, secures a chain round it, fastens the chain to a.hoist, and up comes the hog. Swing- ing and plunging

div.head: SURPRISED HOG
div.p: THE SURPRISED HOG

is sent rolling down the railway to the pig sticker, who plunges his knife into its throat, and by a dexterous twist sends it on its travels again. A stream of blood rushes forth, and the suspended animal by its wriggling and plunging aids its own deltruction, for every kick jerks the life-blood from its body. Whilst you are watching the career of this hog, two others have followed it, and the slaughterer has not a minute to turn himself in, so quickly do the hogs come upon him. As I watched this ghastly scene Mr. Bate turned to me, and asked if I had had enough, and with a sicken- ing sensation I replied that I had. As we descended the stairs hot water splashed upon us from the trough into which the dead hogs are tossed five or six at a time to soften the bristles, and as the machine tosses them out, the carcasses are seized by another ingenious machine,which scrapes all the hair off them as they ascend it. Hogs as black as boots on going into the machine, come down the other side of it as white as sheets. Again the dead hog starts on

div.head: ITS FINAL JOI:TBDTEY.
div.p: ITS FINAL JOI:TBDTEY.

A man with one cut severs its head, another man disembowels it, a third man dresses it, and away it goes into the refrigerator for a couple of days, whence it emerges and is finally disposed of. We passed through the refrigerating rooms and saw thousands of hams upon shelves ; we passed small mountains of pork destined for the sausage room, and we saw until we were well nigh sick. Labour is so greatly subdivided that every man has just certain acts to perform, and he becomes very expert at them. We went down to the packing room, but we were glad to get into the air, strong as it was. We then proceeded to view the stock yards. As it was Monday and early in the day, little was doing. Still we saw a number of steers, with ranchmen on horseback amongst them. We saw the steers driven through the weighing house and out again; and then we went to a great factory of the well- known firm, where 5,000 men are employed, of

ARMOUR AND CO. It was nearly mid-day, but work was only just be- ginning. We asked for the cattle department, and on arrival, passing on our way the hog and sheep shambles, we noticed a large crowd of men standing idly about the room. These men turned out to be butchers, and in a few minutes all were at work. Down one side of the room were 24 pens into each of which two steers were driven. Over the stalls, from one end to the other, was a sort of gangway, along which walked a fine athletic fellow, who with "one fell swoop," knocked the creatures to the ground, 48 animals lying senseless as he reached the end of the path. The weapon the man used was like a stone breaker's hammer. As the poor beasts lay moaning on the ground, chains were secured to their hind quarters, and they were

div.head: CONCLUSION.
div.p: CONCLUSION.

Time fails me to tell of the glorious though tedi- ous ride through northern New York into Canada, past the canvas tents of pioneers and the log cabins of early settlers ; of the great bridge across the St. Lawrence at Montreal; of the city itself; of the sail down the noble river, with the Frenchified vil- lages along its banks ; of quaint Quebec, with its fort, its senate house, its hard snow in June, its intensely Gallic (!) fircns,such as John Flynn et Cie, menuesiers ; and the sail home. Suffice it to say that I arrived safely, and that 1 have thus been enabled to contribute to the Examiner these letters, which I trust have been the means of interesting and instructing its readers.

div.head: ADVENTURES OF A .45 NOTE.
div.p: ADVENTURES OF A .45 NOTE.

On day last week a woman residing in South Shields in passing along Kepple-st., near the South Shields police headquarters, tore up a £5 note, under the impression that it was an ordinary piece of paper. She did not discover the mistake until the evening, whereupon she informed Chief Con- stable Aloorhouse of the unfortunate circumstance. It being very dark, a number of police officers were set to work with lanterns, and after a good deal of labour succeeded in collecting in different parts of the street a number of pieces of the note. These were pasted on to a sheet of paper, and application was math) to a Newcastle bank, but the patched-up note being refused there, it, was' sent to London to the Bank of England, and by return of post a new £5 note was received by the woman, who showed her gratitude for the efforts of the police by send- ing a contribution, which has been placed to a private police fund.

div.head: REV. J. G. HUGHES.
div.p: THE REV. J. G. HUGHES.

An Earlestown correspondent writes ;—lt will not be generally known, that we have dwelling in our midst, a gentleman who, tor the last 14 years. has laboured in the Baptist ministry at the lrwell- Terrace, Baptist Chapel, Bacup, where he was be- loved and respected by all. His health having failed him, he has been obliged to resign his pastorate and seek other spheres of labour,altogether different to what he has been accustomed to. The " Bacup and Ilawtenstall Times," devoted four columns to a review of his labours. On the 21st ult., Rev. J. S. Hughes and his wife were invited to a gathering at Bacup of a few of their friends, and although the meet- ing was of a semi-private character, not having been publicly announced, over 200 persons attended the tea, and there was also a large attendance at the meeting held subsequently. After many references in high terms to the services rendered by Mr. Hughes as pastor of the church, the Chairman called upon one of the elders to make a presentation of a beautiful purse containing 25 sovereigns. This makes the third present of a similar nature given to Mr. Hughes by his congregation. Dur- ing the 14 years of his pastorate, he had won a place in their affections, he had filled the offices of president of the Band of Hope, secretary for the Blue Ribbon move- ment in the town, when over 6,000 persons signed the pledge in a few weeks, and teacher of the young men's Bible Class. There is not a chapel of any denomination in the whole of Rossendale in which he had not spoken or preached, and this goes to prove his catholicity. He has been one of the foremost in Bacup to further any social scheme, and was always glad to help in any, ob- ject for the well-being of the people. His work had been arduous, and the strain had told upon him. I think it ! will be, adds our correspondent, to the interests of our Christian and temperance workers, and especially our Baptist friends, to court Mr. Hughes's friendship. As a town and as a people we can do with more of Mr. Hughes's type.
INDEPENDENT ORDER OF GOOD TEMPLARS.
NO. 1 CONVENTION . SOUTII-IN EST LANCA- SHIRE.

The monthly session was held in the Congrega- tional School, Peasley Cross, on Saturday. Bro. Colour-Sergeant Mantle (Warrington), convention chief templar, presided, and there were present representatives and visitors, to the number of M, from Warrington, Widnes, St. Helens, Earlestown, Ashton-in-Makerfield, Ilindley, Wigan, Peasley Cross, and Lymm. The officer's report mentioned —Visit of Bro. Mantle to Portsmouth ; new juvenile branch being started at Sankey Bridges; publica- tion of a guide to lodges in the Convention, by Bro. Jameson, of Warrington ; starting of juvenile branch at Wigan; number of licenses refused by magistrates; action of Rev. R. J. Ward in recent prosecution at St. Helens ; and the balance in hand of the Treasurer as 17s. Regarding proposed new lodges, Bro. Clarke (Earles- town) stated he was waiting the sanction of Church members at Downall Green to hold a public meeting there; Bro. Kean (Warrington) reported that eight or nine persons had expressed their willingness to join in forming one at Penketh; and arrangements were being made for a meeting-room. Bro. Paymaster- Sergeant Roberts (Warrington), convention councillor, read a report of the Spacial Committee on temper- ance education, which recommended that one mem- ber in each lodge should write a paper on some phase of the temperance question, and send it to the Convention Secretary, who would send all the papers round each lodge in succession for discussion. This course was agreed to. It was decided to hold the next session at Hindley. Bro.G. Clarke, P.C.C.T.(Earlestown), read a paper on "Aggressive temperance work," in which he recommended that following the example of the Band of Hope Union in choosing the motto" one million more," we should adopt the words "one hundred more before February, 1892." This was not too great a task, and meant only an addition of 25 per cent. In carrying it out, he suggested more attention to absentees, special overhaul of roll books for names of lapsed members, and judicious tract distribution from house to house. A dis- cussion followed, in which Bros. Lindon (St. Helens), Taylor (Earlestown), Skaife (St. Helens), and Roberts (Warrington), took part. Bro. Clarke having replied, he was voted the thanks of the convention for his paper. A vote of congratulation to Bro. Mantle on his election as District Chief Templar of the Military District of Eng- land, and one of thanks to the Peasley Cross members for their arrangements brought the session to a close. Tea was then partaken of. At 730 p.m. a public meet- ing was held, under the chairmanship of Mr. R. Shaw, president of St. Helens Temperance Union.

div.head: DAMAGES FOR SINKING A. FLIT ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: DAMAGES FOR SINKING A. FLIT ON THE MERSEY.

At the Liverpool County Court, on Saturday, his Honour Judge Collier, assisted by Captains Ham- mill and Rudolph. national assessors, concluded the trial of an admiralty action, in which the owners of the fiat Argyle sued the owners of the coasting flat James for damages for the sinking of the Argyle by collision in August last. Mr. Pickford (instructed by Messrs. Hill. Dickinson, and Co.), appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Walton (instructed by Messrs. Bateson and Co.) for the defendants. Plaintiff's flat, in company with ten others in tow of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company's tug—Queen of the Mersey, was proceeding down the upper Mersey. There was a strong breeze blowing at the time. Near Hale Head, the defendants' flat, which was bound from Widnes for Llandulas, was sighted The wind was north-west, and the James was tack- ing across the river, and it was alleged that in com- ing across on the starboard tack the James ran into ' the Argyle, which was the hindermost flat of the !ten, and sank her. There were two men and a woman on board the Argyle. One of the men saved I himself by clambering on to the James. The other man and the woman were precipitated into the water. The man was hauled up by the James, but :the woman was sucked under the bows of the sink- ing fiat and drowned. The defence was that every- thing possible was done to avoid the collision. The master of the James intended to pass under the stern of the flat, and be put his helm up with that intention, but he was crowded in between the tug and the flats in tow, and had no time to effect the movement—The court held the James entirely to blame for the collision.

div.head: THE
div.p: THE
STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT
BY ALFRED It CALHOUN.
CHAPTER XVII. ALLEN GETS NEW QUARTET:S.

After Allen had secured a place with Mr. Lefferts he and Florence again took up the night-school work, but to their great surprise they found their fellow-tenants completely changed. The workers in the tenement house—ignorant but well-meaning enough people in their way—had read the charges against Allen in the papers, and believing what they read rather than what they knew, they not only refused to let their children return to the school, but they treated Allen and his sister with studied coldness, and more than once with open contempt. It is hard for even a rugged nature to have a well-meant action construed tqi la,' wicked in its intent. It is hard to be It/Aft by the cur one would save from the threstening wheels. And to a sensitive nature, it is doubly hard to be charged with evil designs by those he is unselfishly trying to save. _ . _

"Our usefulness is over here, dear sister," said Allen, as he and Florence sat by the window, one night, discussing the situation in whispers, for their mother was now so ill that she could not leave her bed, and so they tried to keep all their troubles from her. _ _

"And I am sorry for it, Allen, for I was becoming as deeply interested in the little ones in this place as if they were of our own flesh and blood. But we must not lose heart. We can get rooms, MOTE desirable, perhaps, in some other house, and, as we are used to changing, it will not be much trouble after we get mother safely out," said Florence, with the confidence and cheerfulness that made her life such a blessing to those who knew her. "I shall be sorry to leave my little friends, Victor Blane and his sister." Victor had been dffice boy, anclwwas still devoted to him. "But they can come to see us, no matter where we go." And so it was decided on, and Allen got off two days afterwards and secured rooms in another tene- ment hose some distance away. He began to move at once, and he sent on a bed and took his mother to the new quarters first thing, and remained there to set the furniture to rights, while Florence stayed back to send on tho things, which were being transported by a stout negro with a hand-cart.

Florence had just sent off the last load, and was putting on her hat and coat, preparatory to going to the new quarters, when Dr. Putnam entered. The doctor had been a frequent and an interested visitor from the time he secured Allen a place as collector, until the night when Reybold made his infamous charges. Since then he had kept away. And so great had been the doctor's interest in the night school, and so marked his attentions to Flor ence, that had he been far less favoured by nature she must have felt for him a deep gratitude if not profounder feeling. Without any thought of the consequences—km when did love ever stoop to reason 7—Florence, happy in this man's companionship, gave him hei love.
Neither her mother nor her brother knew he] secret, and so they were in ignorance of thE weight that pressed on her brave heart night and. day.

And she bore herself with so much discretion ant self-possz‘skon in the doctor's presence, that not even he, scientist and man of society though he was ever suspected the secret that for a brief time, at least, had thrown a golden light on the hithertc darkened path of her life.
The start, the flush on her cheeks, and thE momentary light in her gentle eyes, the doctoi accounted for by the suddenness of his appearance _ _

She took his hand as cordially as had her custom, and frankly told him why Allen had decided to change their quarters. "And so," said the doctor musingly, "the very peonle for whose elevation and comfort you sc generously worked have turned against you.' "We should not blame them," she replied. "They have seen or heard of the cruel charges against Allen, and believing them, as have more in- telligent people, they very naturally wished to keer their children away from the corrupting influence of two criminals; for, mark you, Dr. Putnam, the papers that call my brother an impostor spoke oi me with comments crueller and harder to refut4 than direct charges of infamy." _ _
Deeply moved by her own words and the though' for which she could not find words, Florence turned away her face to hide her tears.

"Miss Lee—yes, I shall call you by your owr name—a name that has been ennobled by you— will you—can you forgive me for my seeming in• difference, suspicion and neglect?" said the doctor, Seeing that he made as if he would take her hand, and then drew back, Florence extended it to him, saying, in her gentle but firm way: "Why should I blame you, Dr. Putnam Why should you endanger your high position by continu- ing to associate with people to whom your kind- ness was most generous till you discovered what you bad every reason to believe was crime and deception 1" "Florence, do not talk so lam to blame. I have played the part of a coward through my feat of what society might say. From the first I was convinced of the full truth of your brothel's story, and for years I have known something of the infamy of the man who accused him. Oh I I have been wretched and miserable, for I am not mean nor a coward by nature; and I ask you to forgive me." _ _

This time he reached out both hands, and Flor- ence did not hold back. Again there were tears in her eyes, but they were tears of joy—of a joy that filled every fibre of her exquisite being. "There is nothing to forgive, doctor," and she made a slight effort to release her hands; but he still clung to them. "Your words make me happy and Alien's heart will be lightened when I tell him what you say." "Florence, there is more I would say," continued the doctor, his hand.: trembling, and his eyes on the ground. "My thoughts, since last I saw you, have nearly driven me insane. lam alone in the world, and neither wealth nor standing give me the comfort they did before I knew Ton.' I can no longer hide my secret from TO:). Oh! Florence, I love you, loyally and tender), and I would stand in a position to protect you from the cruel world, and to defend the honour of him who is so dear to you, while using my every effort to prove his inno- cence, and to bring his enemies to justice. You understand me; will you trust me?" He looked pleadingly into her face; he could feel her hands. trembling, and an effort to withdraw them, which at length he yielded to. With downcast eyes she said: "Yes, I understand you, Doctor Putnam, and I will not try to conceal the joy your assurances give me. But in justice to yourself—in justice to all of us—let your words be as if they had not been said."
"Then you do not love me?" be cried. " I cannot reply to that—at least not now." _ _ _
"When then -7 "

"When 7 " she repeated, and now she did loot st him, and her strong, calm manner returned. "When the world knows what you now believo." "I do not clearly understand." he said. Yo . ir coilto believe in my brother IP . . - "You think him innocent? "Yes." "Then help me to convince the world, that luss so , cruelly wronged him, that he is as honourable as he is innocent—and then—" . "And then, what ?" asked the doctor, eagerly. "Then come for my answer." "And if I win, what will your answer be ?" "What in all love and honour should my answer be ?" she asked. "If you eln say ' yes ' with love—" "Dr. Putnam, I could not say ' yes ' without love." There was no need for another word. They understood each other as fully as if they had. dis- cussed the matter for hours. The doctor bent forward, pressed his lips to her. forehead, and her heart blood rose to meet them. The act sealed his devotion and pledged her con- sent "I will go with you to your new quarters," he said, when the last article of furniture was re- moved and Florence had handed the key to the agent of the tenement houso. Though Allen in his heart did liot blame the doctor for his seeming coldness, yet he was deeply pained, for he had conceived a strong liking for the young physician, and had come to look on him as , his most valued friend. -
"Allen, I have escorted your sister to her new home, but my real object in coming was to see you and ask you to forgive me," was the doctor's salutation when he and Allen came face to face.
"There is nothing to forgive, Dr. Putnam; my appreciation of your kindness to me is as strong as ever. _ You had good reason for believing that I
naa cteceiveu you in Keeping irom you my past life," said Allen, his voice husky with emotion, while he still held the doctor's hand.

"No, you told me nothing about your past life, therefore you did not deceive me. If I had been in your place, I should have done the same thing. Ah, my friend, if we used a little more of the sweet oil of charity in lubricating the complex machinery of society, it would run better. I see by your face, and I feel by the grip of your hand that you have no ill-feeling against me—" "No feeling but affection and gratitude, Doctor."

"Now, give me a chance to practice my pro- fession. Miss Florence tells me her mother is not at all well. Poor woman, the wonder to me is that she did not long since break down under the heavy burdens she has had to bear," said the doctor, his manner as open and as:generous as of old. He was conducted into Mrs. Lee's room, and found her very low. Although not yet forty-eight years of age, Mrs. Lee looked like a woman of seventy. Care carves more lines on the face, and blanches more heads than time.

"If I could only live," whispered Mrs. Lee, "to have Iny son's name freed of the stain so unjustly attached to it, then could I thank Heaven and pray to depart in peace. Ah, Doctor, the greatest human suffering is hidden from the world in the hearts of mothers like me."

Still pressing his fingers to her feeble pulse, the doctor said: "I am here as your friend as well as your doctor. Here I pledge you that, from this hour on, I shall devote whatever I have of time, money and talent to clearing your son's name. And in the work I have set myself, may Heaven help me." "Amen, amen!" she fervently replied
CHAPTER XVIII. DESPERATION.
Irene Lefferts never gave up the hope of reforming her brother and reconciling his father to him.

As has been shown, she shared her own money allowance with Frank ; and while taking every opportunity to show her dislike of his conduct, she never made her reproof so strong as to lead him to believe that her love for him was dead.

Whenever Frank was short of money, and this became every week more frequent, he would take advantage of his father's absence to visit his sister, and he never came away empty-handed. He had not been to see Irene for nearly two weeks, and she was wondering what had become of him, when one day she met him on the street, and his dress showed recent prosperity, while his face told he had not been drinking of late. Pleased at, the change, Irene asked him home with her; and when they reached there she kissed him for the first time in years, and said: "You are looking better, Frank, and it gladdens my heart to think you must be doing better." "Yes," he replied, and he looked as if he meant what he was saying; "I made some money not long since, and then I took an oath that I wouldn't drink or gamble, or do anything else to make you ashamed hereafter. I shall keep away from bad company, and I will try to get work with my pen— I mean, Irene, the right kind of work " • and his face grew crimson as he realised the delicate subject of his skill.
"And Mott Reybold—does he know of your reso- lution?"
"Oh, yes. I've told him." "And what does he say 7"
"He thinks lam on the right track. But I say, Irene, does he still come here 2" "Yes. But he should not persist in his visits." "Why not 1" "Because I have refused to see him."
"And yon_are.still interested in this Lee r

"I am still interested in Mr. Lee, and I shall be so long as I live and my heart is capable of grati- tude. But let us talk about you. She drew nearer to him, and laying her hand on his arm, she con- tinued: "Frank, if I could restore father's faith in you, and see you leading such a life as would reflect honour on you, I should feel as if I had ac- complished a great life work." "I'm not a strong character, Irene," said Frank, with his handkerchief to his eyes, for he could command tears as readily as he could forge a name or make a resolution—meaning to keep it, too— that he would never do so again so long as he lived. "I know my faults, and I never did a wrong that did not haunt me. Help me to keep straight, and I'll obey you as if I was your slave." Touched by his tears and evident penitence, she said, tremulously: "I must believe you, Frank. If I were to lose all faith in you, I think it would kill me. I shall help you with money, and I am sure I can get you a place. Meanwhile I shall gradually win father over. Your conduct has shortened his life, but if he saw you what he would have you, his heart would be glad again, and, oh, how happy we could all be—" She could not trust her veice further.

Frank rose, and, raising his hands, he cried: "I shall do as you say 1 From this day on lam changed 1" He may have meant this. Irene certainly be- lieved him. How could she know that his peni- tence was largely due to recent acts of infamy? How could she know that the new clothes on his back were purchased from the proceeds of a forgery. Fury would have been added to her horror, could she have known that this forgery, planned by Mott Reybold, had for its main object the ruin of Allen Lee.

Frank Lefferts parted from his sister fully resolved to merit her confidence. He was too weak to realise the enormity of his offences, and, like a great many other people in the world, he imagined good resolutions to be an offset against bad acts.

One strange thing about this weak young man's, character was his stubborn and criminal fidelity to, his partners in crime. He knew full well that Mott Reybold was in every way unfit for his sister's recognition ; and he further knew that it was in his power to rid himself of the tyrant master who had led bini astray, and to show his true character to the world, but that stranger fidelity to vile associates, that distinguishes even the weaker of the lawless classes, led him to. keep his secrets to himself.

Unstable as water, Frank Lefferts, after leaving his sister, went directly to Reybold's quarters. The partners had raised money, and the gambling establishment was in full blast again. Of late Reybold had been in high spirits, for the tide of chance had again set in his favour, and his dread of Allen Leo ceased, though his hatred in- creased, if that were possible. He let his partner "run the estnblishment," for he had other and more important ventures that kept him away a great deal at night. Disguised, and under the assumed name. of Farley," he was a frequent visitor at Mingo Petes house, for he knew that only by constant watch- fulness and urging, as well as by holding back a considerable part of the proposed reward, could he get the ex-convict to do his bidding.. The night of the day on which Frank Lefferts visited his sister found Reybold again in the thieves' , den. I He had come to fear Minnie, Mingo's wife, and so took good care never to visit the place except at night, and when he knew the master of the place was at home.

Mingo answered his knock to-night and let him in. "rm glad yer on hand early,'t'said Mingo, as he led his visitor up to the little room described before, "for I've got a lot of important things to tell you? Well, go on and tell me„ Mingo,. for I haven't got long to stay. But first let me give you some money to help things along,, for I made a little caise to-day," said Reybold„ handing the other a roll of crisp notes, when they were alone and the door closed.. _ _

Mingo, without counting the monsy, pushed it into his vest pocket, and said:, "I ain't a watchman no longer. "Then you've taken my advice and resigned?" "Yes." "When I" "Yesterday; but I got another man into my glace, and the firm gave me a good character." "Then they suspect nothing 7" "Not a thing; but the new man is a friend a 367_ "You mean of Lee?" "Yes; he lives, in the same house. He's beeaup fur burglary before, but neither the firm nor Lee know that, so you see, I've got things nicely flied;" and Mingo laughPd and smote his own knees and Reybold's shoulder to give expression to his feelings. "Well, when will this trap be sprung r asked Reybold, his voice trembling with anxiety "Not till the company take stock." "When will that be 2" "In about three days." - . -

"And you've left the goods at Lee's ?" "Well, I should say I had. Why, I got about fifteen hundred dollars' worth of jewellery in that valise. He carried it with him to his new quarters. Oh, he's in for it," And Mingo laughed again. But how will. thq fin:ll34 Eda_efield ad Phipps

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. W. H. SMIT.d.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. W. H. SMIT.d.

The funeral of Mr. W. H. Smith, M.P., took place ott Saturday at Hambleden cemetery, a short distance from Henley-on-Thames. The Queen sent a wreath, and both at Walmer in the morning and at Hambleden in the after- noon there were many visible signs of the respect enter- tained for the deceased statesman. A memorial szTvice, attended by several peers and a large number of members of the House of Commons, was held in Westminster Abbey.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. PARNELL.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. PARNELL.

The remains of Mr. Parnell were interred on Sunday evening in Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin, in the presence of an immense concourse of persons. The body was removed from Brighton on Saturday, and was landed in Dublin on Sunday morning. After a funeral service in St. Michan's Church, the body was taken to the City Hall, where the coffin, covered with an immense number of wreaths, remained until the afternoon. The funeral procession which included the Lord Mayor and other members of the municipal government of Dublin, as well as nearly all Mr. Parnell's Parliamentary supporters and many representatives vf trade and political. organisations passed through the streets filled with sympathetic spectators. The cemetery was not reached until nearly six o'clock, and night had fallen before the proceedings were concluded. None of the prominent men of the majority section of the Irish Parliamentary party attended, their absence being due to a desire to aroid any occasion being offered for an unseemly demonstra- tion.

div.head: ROUMANIAN ROMANCE.
div.p: THE ROUMANIAN ROMANCE.
lIAPPY AGAIN.

A correspondent of the " Gaulois," who is on in- timate terms with Mdlle. Vacaresco, states that the facts with regard to the reconciliation which has been effected between that young lady and her lover, Prince Ferdinand of Roumania, are perfectly true. The breaking off of their engagement? says the informant of the" Gaulois," was only brought about in consequence of false letters and telegrams sent to each of them,which made the believe that they had ceased to care for one another. When the Prince discovered this he was very much affected. It occurred while he was staying with a family who were great friends with Mdlle Vaceresco. It seems that they had received him very cooly. When he asked the reason of this, he was told that it was due to his conduct towards the young lady. On demanding further explanations, he learned that a telegram had been received by :Halle Vacaresco, which was supposed to emanate from him. The Prince was very indignant, but could not, of course. accuse anybody in particular. He therefore sent a mes- sage to Mdlle. Vacaresco asking whether she wonld believe him on his word. The result was that she came herself with an affirmative answer.. Now, says the informant, they will not be separated again.

div.head: IITTNCOTCS FOOTBALLEIL IN AUSTRALIA.
div.p: A IITTNCOTCS FOOTBALLEIL IN AUSTRALIA.

Judging from a report in the " Brisbane Courier," August 24th, Mr. H. C. Speakman, who, it will be remembered, was a prominent member of the Run- corn Football Team, has not allowed his talents to remain idle. It was in May, 1887, that Mr. Speakman joined the English Rugby team which was bound for the Antipodes, and regret was expressed at that time that Cheshire and Runcorn were losing so able a centre three-quarter. Although the Rugby game in Australia is played under different rules than those associated with the sport in this country, our subject has evidently become a master of the Australian game. Having been selected captain of the Queensland Colcny, this team entered into rivalry for the second time with New South Wales. The first engagement had resulted in a draw, but, on the second time of asking, the Queensland team proved far too clever for their opponents. The victory was, in a great measure, due to the brilliant play of Speakman, for, besides the inauguration of the first try, he succeeded in registering a couple of points, in the report to hand the old Runcornian is described as having made the grandest run of the day, clearing everybody by his feigning to pass, a tactic with which his play was associated when performing for his club or county when in England. The effort resulted in o':,hea, scoring, Turning to a criticism on the match, Speakman is described as having played a most brilliant game. The first try which he scored for his side was as grand a piece of play as the finest connoisseur in Rugby football could wish to see. The game was still hanging in the balance, and the play going on in the Queens- land half, when the captain came through with the ball at his feet, and picked up neatly. One of those feints at which he is a past master, took him by the New South Wales backs, and the effort was rewarded by O'Shea scoring a sub- stantial point. The excitement at the Queensland team's success was surprising, and after this the game was-never in doubt, Speakman's two sub- sequent tries serving to increase the excitement. Warbrick, who, it will be remembered, played full back for the Maories when they visited England,. is also described as having played a fine game. He was second to Speakman in the ovation the crowd gave as the players made their way to the pavilion.. The result of the game was that the Queenslanders received a handsome silver shie4 presented by Messrs. Wirth, and at a performance at the circus• on the evening of the match, during a short inter- val, the Mayor, on behalf of the donors, presented it. Mr.Speakman received the shield,and in thank- ing the Mayor and Messrs. Wirth, said he was sure the Northern Rugby Union would be very proud of the trophy.. Runcorn people, in fact, all English enthusiasts of the Rugby game, will hail with de- light the success of one of Runcorn's exponents of the winter's sport. We may add that Mr.Speakman. is a member of the Union Harrier Club.
