div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Forty years in a Moorland Parish" is the title of an important volume of reminiscences of and researches in Denby. in Clevelend, by the Rev. J. C. Atkinson, D.C.L., incumbent of the parish, and author of a " History of Cleveland," "Glossary of the Cleveland Dialect," &c. This is a work of unusual interest and excellence. Mr. Atkinson is a ' keen observer, quiet and contemplative in his habits of mind, and has shown himself exceedingly, industrious in making use of his opportunities dur- ing the long period in which he has resided in this part of North Yorkshire. He estimates that he utast have walked more than 7,000 miles in the prosecution of his clerical work only, and much more than As many again for exercise, relaxation, and recreation. He has journeyed alone, for the most part, and has noted every feature of the country and the habits of beast and bird. He has evidently had a faculty for getting along with the country people amongst whom he has resided, and has thus got to the very kerrel of their folk lore. 'The inhabitants amongst whom his lot has been cam are like others in having made progress during the last 40 years, especially in applying modern Improvements in farming, in advancing the stand- ard of education, and especially in the housing of farm labourers. It is satisfactory to learn that -there has been little or no ehange in their honesty of character, and 'their thriftiness and industry. 'There is no attempt in any part of the volume at -writing for effect, the author evidently feeling that " an honest tale speaks best being plainly told." The charm of the work is that it can be read by all classes, and in this and in many other respects it suggests comparison with White's "Selborne." We make the following extract, by way of showing that Dr. Atkinson has a keen ear for a good story, and is thoroughly master of the Denby dialect : " Another impromptu saying, in the nature of a retort, struck me much, especially taking all the circumstances into account, as really somewhat telling. ,Our local medico was visiting an old lady, an old acquaintance of mine, who always had a "agey gud dish" of " my Lady Tongue "ready for instant production. She was in peril of her life with htemorrage which the doctor had much .difficulty in staying, and Which might come on again at ;any moment, and was almost safe to recur if she began ,her usual voluble chatter. However, talk she would, and at last the doctor,out of patience with her,addressed her sharply in -her own tongue: " Ho'd thah noise, thee blethering ati'd fecal, or Ah'll tie thah tomigue ti thah teeath .;" the instantaneous rejoinder being "Thee caan't, doctor; fur Ah ha'e na teeath mah ' heead !" But much of this readiness seems a thing of the past now, and I think it is because the stiffness of the "New English" instilled in the Elementary School lends itself both less familiarly and less well to the ready ex- pression of quaint conceit or incisive repartee. As fur- ther illustrative in the same connection, I may perhaps mention the following. Making inquiry one day about , who, I had supposed, was no longer single, I was ans- wered as follows: "Neea, neea, he's nane married. He trails a leeght harrow : his hat covers his household." And from an old note book I extract the next: "He's ower mickle a fecal to ken how many beans mak's five." Of a miserly skinflint, "He wad skin tweea deevils for yah pelt." Of an emaciated man, "He's that thin, he's lahk a ha'porth o' soap efter a lang day's weshing.” Of a wowan newly but not wisely married, "Ay, she's tied a knot with her tongue she'll be matched to unloose wiv her teeath." And lastly this, of a man without brains or' gumption,' "Ay, there's t' heead an' t' hair; but there's nowght else." The students of antiquities, zoology, ornithology, and history will find the work a complete storehouse of reliable information. The volume, which is one of 458 pages, is provided with two maps and several illustra- tions, and is published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., at *e. 6d. We have had occasion at various times to notice and highly commend the publication by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., of "English Men of Letters," edited by Mr. John Morley. In order to ensure accuracy and thorough- ness, the various monographs have been placed in the hands of writers who are known to be well acquainted with the particular subjects to be dealt with, and the re cult is a series of is. works which must be regarded as un- surpassed in their way. Those who can afford the series cannot do better than make a wholesale purchase, if they wish to have a ready means of becoming ac- quainted with, England's greatest writers. Taking a few at random, by way of illustration, we have Hume, by T. H. Howley; Pope, by Leslie Stephens; De Foe, by W. Minto •, Sydney, by John A. Symonds; Dryden, by G. Saintsbury •' Spenser, by the Dean of St. Paul's; and Gibbon, by J.C. Morrison. It will be seen from such a list as this—and it is only a sample of the rest— that it is a case of men of eminence writing the lives:of eminent ;men. The "English Illustrated Magazine" leads off wi th a portrait of his Honour Judge Hughes, Q.C., author of "Tom Brown's school days," followed by an illustrated article on Rugby School. The next paper illustrated is "Broad Guage Engines," followed by a capital story, "The sheriff and his partner," "The Birds of London," and "Boston, the capital of the Fens." A new story, also illustrated, is commenced by W. Clarke Russell, with the title of" A strange elopement." Messrs. Macmillan and Co. have just published the first part (price is.) of "A short history of the English people," by John Richard Green. The frontispiece is a faithful reproduction in colours of St. Matthew from the "Book of Kells," A.D. 650-90. The number to hand is profusely and admirably illustrated, and is accompanied with various maps of Britain. The type and paper are alike excellent, and there is every promise that the work when complete will be all that one could wish. Messrs. F. Warne and Co., have ptgalished in the .Ohandos Classics, price 25., "The poetical works of John Greenleaf Whittier." There is a prefatory notice which gives a brief sketch of Whittier's career. He is still living; he has never married, and on his 70th birthday the publishers of the "Atlantic Monthly" gave him a hanquet, at which the best American writers were pre- sent. In the proem of his work he says :

I love the old melodious lays, Which softly melt the ages. through, "The songs of Spenser's golden days, Arcadian Sydney's silver phrase, Sprinkling OUT noon of time with precious morning dew. He goes on to say that in his quiet hours he vainly tries to breathe their marvellous notes, but, the reader who ,studies his verse will be of opinion that his trial has not been in vain, for he will everywhere find melody and felicity of expression, and a high moral tone. Whittier rendered a great service to his country by his " Voices of Freedom," written in opposition to slavery, and it is pleasing to reflect that he has lived to see the stain wiped from the banner of the stars and stripes. This ,oheap edition of his poems ought to have a large sale. It is rendered all the more valuable by numerous notes and a copious index. The" Westminster Review" for October is an excep- tionally able and interesting number. Mr. C. E. Plump- tre deals with the life and character of the late Mr. Bradlaugh, and makes an appeal on his behalf which we cannot but think will meet with a hearty response. Mr. 4, W. Crombie has a thoughtful paper on "The Ordeal or Trades Unionism"; and the subjects of other articles are :—Free Education in the United States; Ernest Renan ; Gothic Architecture; and The New Empire, fol- lowed by the usual review of contemporary literature. The "Century Magazine" for October has for frontis- piece an excellent portrait of that new and powerful writer, Mr. Rudyard Kipling. There is a paper on him as a writer by Mr. Edmund Gosse, which it is a matter of course to say is thoughtful,critical, and incisive. The illustrations of the various articles are, as usual, of the highest class, and amongst the papers there should be particularly mentioned My last days in Siberia," by George Kerman; "Aerial Navigation,' "A Water Toura- ment," "Who was Eldorado," and "A tour in Nica- ragua." In addition there are "Tonics of the Time" ; "Open Letters " ; and some very readable bric-a-brac. " Scribner's " for October leads off with "The Corso of Rome," being the fourth illustrated article on the great streets of the world. Other important illustrated papers are "Hunting Ameripn Big game," and " The Biography of the Oyster.' The new story "The Wrecker" is continued; and there are two capital con- cluded stories, besides several miscellaneous papers of interest, including one on " Carlyle's Politics" by Mr. E.

C. Martin. The "Strand Magazine" may now be said to be thoroughly established as a popular monthly. It kas made a decided hit with "Portraits of Celebrities at different times of their lives." The latest issue illustrates in this way Professor Owen, Mrs. W. H. Kendall, Mr. W. H. Kendall, the Duke of Connaught, Dr. Robson Roose, Mr. Michael Maybrick, and Mr. Henry Russell. The short stories and sketches are all good, and the illustrations are numerous, and in most cases excel- lent. Following on his Sea-side Library series at id. each, Mr. John Heywood has issued detective stories at the same price, from the pen of Mr. W. Henderson, Chief Constable of Edinburgh. As the writer has had a large experience in various parts of the kingdom, it is a mat- ter of course to say that he has something good to tell, and he tells it in a style which is interesting without being sensational. " Watches, Clocks, Jewellery, and Plate."—This is the title of s pamphlet just published by Mr. Benson,

which contains over 200 pages of illustrations, Soc.; it is by far the largest and most complete work of its kind issued, and it will be sent post free to any part of the world by J. W. Benson, of the Steam Factory, 62, and 64, Ludgate Hill, EX., or from his West End house, 25, Old Bond-st., W., London.

div.head: UNIVERSITY REVOLT IN RUSSIA.
div.p: UNIVERSITY REVOLT IN RUSSIA.

A St. Petersburg correspondent says a conspiracy against the life of the Czar has been discovered at Kieff. In the same city a printing press used for the publica- tion of seditious ilocuments was seized by the authori- ties on Saturday last. There has been also a serious outbreak of aisturbance,s among the students at the university, and some vehement speeches have been de- livered. 4 number of arrests have been made, but without in any degree moderating the excited tone of the mass of young men. On the contrary, the spirit of revolt, seems to be rising and spreading.

div.head: POSTMASTER-GENERAL'S REPORT.
div.p: POSTMASTER-GENERAL'S REPORT.

HOW £25,000 WENT THROUGH THE POST. The thirty-seventh annual report, issued on Monday, by the General Post Office and prepared by the late Post-Master General, gives the estimated total number of letters, postcards, book packets, circulars, samples, newspapers, and parcels delivered in the United King- dom during the year ended March 31, at 2,623,987,956, showing an increase of 8.2 per cent. on the previous re- turns. The average number of letters,&c., to each per- son of the population of the United Kingdom during the year was 69.6, that of letters, alone being 452. Next on the list is the class including book packets, cir-- culars, and samples, the averages per head of the population being 128; postcards averaged 6-1 only, newspapers 4.3, and parcels 1.2. Of 2,577,700,000 letters, &c., delivered, about 65.2 per cent, were deli- vered in England and Wales (29.7 per cent. being in the London postal district alone), 8.9 per cent. in Scotland, , and 5.9 per cent in Ireland. Of letters returned 136,644 were reissued to corrected addresses, 5,750,527 were re- turned to senders, 222,491 returned unopened to foreign post offices, and 458,608 remained which could not be disposed of. The number of registered letters dealt with was 201,267, or 9,433 more than in 1889-90; but 31,168 other letters were found to contain articles which rendered registration necessary. Referring to the partial strike of London postmen, in July, 1890, the late Postmaster-General said :—" I was compelled at once to take stringent measures to restore discipline, and found it my painful duty to dismiss from the public ser- vice in one morning about 450 men." Under the head of " Curious Incidents" the report says the public still frequently seek to avoid payment of registration fees by sending money in all sorts of parcels and at various times during the year sovereigns had been found packed with butter, flowers, dripping, figs, and puddings. The following instance of "reckless economy" is given :—A lady residing in Siam forwarded to London several parcels declared to contain walking sticks and stationery of the value of £7 103., but the vigilant eye of the Customs House officer promptly detected a brilliant collection of diamonds and jewellery worth upwards of £25,000. . . . The postage at the registered letter rate would have amounted to about £30." Some time ago, says the report, a lady adver- tised, asking persons to send 3d. each in aid-of the Bishop of Bedford's Whitechapel Refuge Fund. The advertiser changed her address without notice, and by the time her new address was discovered no fewer than 16,268 letters, containing £l9l, and addressed to her, had accumulated and were awaiting delivery.

div.head: HARVEST THANKSGIVINGS.
div.p: HARVEST THANKSGIVINGS.

ST. PETER'S, WARRINGTON. The harvest thanksgiving services were held at St. Peter's church on Sunday. The Vicar, the Rev. T. Rigby, preached in the morning and the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, in the evening. There was also a children's service in the afternoon. The church was tastefully decorated with oats, dahlias, asters, sunflowers, grapes, apples, &c. The -collections at the three services produced over £7.

ORFORD CHURCH. The annual harvest festival was held in Orford Church on Sunday, four services being held in the course of the day. The morning preacher was the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., Rector of Warrington. In the evening the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, M.A., Rector of Winwick, occupied the pulpit. The church had been tastefully decorated for the occasion with wheat, oats; lilies, dahlias, asters, sunflowers, and other blossoms, all contributing to give the building a bright and cheerful appearance.

div.head: PADGrATE CHURCH.
div.p: PADGrATE CHURCH.

The annual service of thanksgiving for the ingather- ing of the harvest was held in Christ Church, Padgate, on Sunday. The day's services commenced with a cele- bration of the Holy Communion at eight o'clock. At the usual morning service the preacher was the Rev. M. F. 0. Bridgman' curate of Christ Church, Bootle, and son of the Rev. A. A. Bridgeman, a former vicar of Padgate, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. H. Siddall, vicar of St. Thomas's, Ashton-in-Makerfield. There was a good congregation at each service, particul- ary in the evening, when every seat was occupied. Har- vest hymns were heartily sung, and an anthem was given at each service by the choir in a creditable man- ner. Mr. A. Harding was at the organ. With regard to the decoration of the church,the work had been most successfully carried out by the ladies of the congrega- tion,especial assistance being rendered by Mrs. Langham Miss Sanders, of Castle Eden, and Miss Appleton. The offertories amounted to £l3 Os. id.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY CHURCH,
div.p: GREAT SANKEY CHURCH,

The harvest festival in connection with St. Mary's Church was held on Sunday. The day's services were commenced by Holy Communion at 8.15 a.m. The sacrament was administered by the Rev. T. E. Winder, and there was a large number of communicants. The church had been most tastefully decorated by the follow- ing ladies :—Misses Tinsley, Jeans, Fraser, Grange, Thorpe, Forster, Ellison, Bolton, Bennett, and Mrs. Ait- ken and Mrs. Spinks. The decorations are generally considered to have been far better done than before. The ornamentation of the rood screen, the pulpit, and the altar were worthy of•special mention. The morning preacher was the Rev. Morley Stevenson, M.A., princi- pal of the Warrington Training College. He selected as his text the words, "Man shall n'ot live by bread alone," and preached an excellent sermon, to an attentive con- gregation. Holy Communion was celebrated after the morning service, by the Rev. T. E. Winder, assisted by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, M.A. The number of com- municants was again large. In the afternoon, at three o'clock, a children's service was conducted by the Rev. T. E. Winder, who took his text from Proverbs x. 5. The service was a most successful one, the singing being very hearty. All the scholars attending the Sankey and Penketh schools were present, numbering over 650. The preacher fn the evening was the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton. He took for his text the words "Were there not ten cleansed, but where are the nine ?" The sermon was a most earnest and impressive one. During the whole of the day the congregations were very good. At each service the church was crowded, but in the even- ing, large numbers had to go away disappointed, there being no room in the church. Collections were, taken after each service in aid of the church expenses. The amount realised was over £22. During the day special harvest hymns were sung by the congregation. As al- ready announced, the services will be continued at St. Mary's Mission, Penketh, this (Wednesday) evening. Tne preacher will be the Rev. M. F. B. Rinney, M.A., of Sutton, St. Helens.

WESLEY CHAPEL, WARRINGTON. On Sunday, harvest thanksgiving services were held at Bevvsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, Wanington. The usual decorations had been carried out in a very tasteful manner. At the morning service the preacher was the Rev. Alf. Freeman, who preached a sermon most appro- priate to the occasion. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. John Gunnell, who selected for his text Matthew vi., 11. Special hymns and anthems, with full orchestral accompaniment, were rendered at each service. The anthems in the morning were "0 Lord, how manifold are Thy works" (Barnby), and "Sing a song of Praise" (Stainer) ; and in the evening "fle shall feed His flock" (with solo by Mrs. Dobson), " Sing to the Lord of harvest" (Barnby), and Jackson's service in F. Mr. J. M. Muir, A.C.0., presided at the organ On Monday evening a full choral service was held, Mr. W. Barlow presiding. The programme included sacred songs, anthems, &c., and was well rendered by the choir, who were aided by a number of other local vocalists. The choruses were excellently dealt with by the choir, and Miss Dobson, who sang the principal song, "What tho' I" trace each herb and flower,' was also very successful. Votes of thanks to the Chairman and performers brought the concert to a close.—On Tuesday evening a fruit banquet and social gathering was held in the large vestry, adjoining the chapel. There was a large attendance. The Rev. A. Freeman presided,and, in the course of his opening remarks, took occasion to explain the objects and plan of the Christian Workers' Association, which has recently been established in connection with the chapel. He said that amongst other things they had in view during the coming winter were the holding of cottage services, distribution of tracts, and district visitation. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. A. H. Dunn, J. W. Hayward, Hickman, H. Y. Jones, and others. The choir gave a selection of music. The proceeds of the meeting were devoted to the fund for the poor of the society.

• DUTTON. The harvest thanksgiving service was held in Dutton Iron Church on Sunday, when the sacred edifice was crowded to overflowing. The .desorations showed that great taste and skill had been bestowed upon them. Amongst those who helped in this work were Mrs. Hervey Talbot, Dutton Lodge (who undertook the altar and chancel), Miss Best (Aston Lodge), Mrs. John Priestner. Misses Bean, Mr. irayler, and others. The Vicar, the Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett, was assisted in the service by the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar of Frodsham (who preached the sermon). The offertory, which was in aid of church expenses, amonnted to £5 9s. 50.
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. 'Mr. F. H. Gossage presided and there were present Messrs. Brown, Wright, Midwood, Neil, Tilley, Heyes, Taylor, S. Sadler, Cook, Dr. O'Keefe, Oppenheim (clerk), Hoyle (accountant), Sinclair (surveyor), Carr (engineer), Lowe (nuisance inspector.)
GAS AND WATER COMSIITTRE.-THE NEW BORINGS.

The minutes of this Committee stated that the gas was tested on the 28t1 ult„ when the illuminating power was 17.20 candles, free from sulphuretted hydrogen. The engineer reported as follows :—Netherley Boring Con- tract—The first borehole has been sunk to the required depth, i.e., 400 feet. On plumbing this hole at a depth of 200 feet, at which point the pump suction will be fixed, the amount of deviation from the perpendicular proved to be 7.4 inches. The contractor's workmen are now en- gaged moving the boring machine to its position over the second hole. The whole of the cast-iron _tubes in connection with the latter hole are already in position. The concreting in the space at the back of the tubes has also been completed. Yield of water from New Borehole. —There has been an increase of about 20 feet in the working level of the water in the oval well, much of which is, of course, due to the recent heavy rainfall, as alluded to in Inv last month's report. It may be reasonably supposed, however, that about one-half of the foregoing increase is due to the extra water rising in the new borehole. The water level in the new borehole is from four to five feet above that in the existing well when pumping is in operation; but when pumping is suspended the water quickly attains the same level in both wells. The water is flowing freely from the new to the old well, through the fissures in the rock, has been clearly proved during the latter stages of the boring operations. Each time the boring bar has been sent down the water in the oval well has almost immediately become discoloured with sand, which has as quickly cleared off again after the withdrawal of the bar. The increase in the yield of water, however, has not been so great as I had anticipated. It will be seen from the samples of the strata passed through that the rock at the bottom of the borehole is of a harder and less coarse nature than the average of that previously passed through. From this it is reasonable to assume that if this hard bed is penetrated, coarse water-bearing rock will be again met with beneath. I therefore recom- mend that the second boring be continued to a. depth not exceeding 600 feet or 200 feet below the contract depth, which could be stopped at any intermediate point in the event af the rock proving less favourable or faulty. This work, with the boring machine and gear all in position, could be done at comparatively small extra cost. A certificate for £l5O on account of this contract is submitted.—Burst Water Mains.—On Sun- day morning, the 28th ult.,the 12inch water main under Marsh road bridge gave way. The necessary repairs were made and the water turned on about 7-30, when the main gave way a second time, a few yards away from the first burst, which delayed the turning on of the water. until 4 a.m. on the Monday morning. The acci- dent was due to the decomposition of the pipes. The mean rainfall for the month was 3'197 inches. The water in stock was 7,341,083. gallons. It was recom- mended that the firemen whilst occupying the Fire station Cottages be allowed an additional renumeration of one shilling per week for their services. That the engineers engage a store keeper at a salary of 245. per week.—Mr. Brown in proposing the adoption of the minutes said they were allowing the firemen who lived at the cottages an additional is. per week because the rents were higher than they had been accustomed to pay and because the men were always ready in an emergency.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which was carnet

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT tiItDAX, OCTOBER 17, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT tiItDAX, OCTOBER 17, 1891.

They had been told that there was an immense amount of property at stake, and that the Board ought to be very cautious how they interfered with the rights and privileges of property, but to poison people wholesale was not one of the rights and privileges of property. It was the duty of the Health Committee to take up this matter in real earnest and find out what were their powers in law and eaforce them. He was sure that the United Alkali Company would not do anything to abate the nuisance unless absolutely compelled.—The Chairman said he believed that it was the feeling of the Board that the Health Committee should deal with this matter.— Mr. Wright: We will take it into consideration. He had been told that the gas was now being turned up the chimneys and it was consequently carried further away arid the outlying districts received more than they did in the centre of the town. He had recently a conversation with one of the Government inspectors, who said he felt confident that the greatest smell arose from the waste heaps, which were not laid exactly as they ought to be.—Mr. Heyes said he hid had a con- versation with the Alkali Inspector, who gave him the same information,but he begged to differ from him. He did not believe the smell came from the waste heaps.— Mr. Sadler said during last week the nuisance was intolerable in Ann-street.—Mr. Brown said there was no doubt a fegrful escape of some kind or another .—The Chairman kid the Committee would consider the matter, and the subject dropped.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing :-Improvement Loans, £5,100-The Clerk reported that, subject to the approval of the Committee, he had arranged with the St. Helens Corporation for a loan of £2,100 at 3i per cent. interest, the principal repayable in 20 and 10 equal annual payments, the Board to pay 10s. per cent. commission. Recommended that the Clerk's action be approved and confirmed, and that the loan be accepted upon the terms named. Recommended that the offer of Mr. John Hamrnill, now submitted, for a loan of £3,000 at 31- per cent., the principal repayable by 30 equal annual payments, at 10s. per cent. commis- sion, be accepted. The Accountant's report for Septem- ber stated :-Treasurer's balances: Credits General account £5,414 2s. id. Gas Sinking Fund account £669 Ts. 2d. Water Sinking Fund account £1,141 19s. Main Sewerage account £1,183 17s. 3d. Private Improvement receipts account £941 14s. 11d. Charity account £57 9s. sd. Science and Art account £3 Us. Total £9,412 3s. 10d. Debits Fire Station and Cottages account £2,530. Public Improvements account £250. Infecti- ous Diseases Hospital account £143 N. 2d. Stables, kc., account £ll2 us. 4d. Private Improvements account £240. Total £3,276, showing a net balance in the bank of £6,138 3s. 4d. Collections-The collections during the at oath have been-on General District Rate account £2.315 2s. Water account £59 16s. 4d. Gas account £79 Os. 2d. Gas Products account £214 14s. 6d. Pri- vate Improvements £3Ol 13s. lid. Other sources £ll4 19s. 3d. Deposits £l4. Total £3,099 6s. 2d. Loans- The sum of £5OO has been borrowed during the month for a term of seven years at 3i per cent. interest, and offers to lend various sums at the same rate of interest repayable by annual instalments, subject to the payment of a fee of per cent.' are submitted. The advortise- ment for loans wanted has been withdrawn. Arrears of Gas and Water accounts-Proceedings have been taken for the recovery of various accounts as recommended by the Committee last month; the proceedings for the re- covery of minimum charges are receiving the attention of the Clerk.-Letters,3rd September,from the Liverpool Silver and Copper Co. Ld., and 11th September, from the United Alkali Co. Ld. (Gaskell-Deacon's Works and Hall and Shaw's Works), are submitted, stating that they have appealed against the assessment of their works. Accounts amounting to £4,152 18s. Bd. were passed for payment.-The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Mr. Midwood.

div.head: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE,
div.p: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE,

The Highways Committee recommended that the por- tion of Violet-st., not already adopted having been sewered, levelled, paved, flagged, metalled, channelled, and made good, and provided with proper means of lighting, to the satisfaction of the Urban Authority, be declared a highway, and that the clerk give the neces- sary notice. The plans were approved of a house in Henry-st., for Joseph Newall ; plans of a house in Birch- field-road, for Robert Hurst, were disapproved, as also plln of alteration to Central Hotel, for Greenall, Whitley and Co. Ld.—Mr. Sadler moved the adoption of the minutes, and in reply to Mr. Brown, said the automatic disinfectors were Axed as a twelve months' experiment to cost ss. a year, exclusive of the apparatus. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the follow- ing recommendations :—That the Clerk be instructed to issue the necessary advertisement in compliance with the General Order of the Local Government Board, 23rd of March, 1891, of the intention of the Local Board to formally appoint Walter Lowe an Inspector of Nuisan- ces for this District for a period of one year at a salary of £ll4 per annum. In order to meet the requirements of the Local Government Board, that the salary of the Medical Officer of Health be apportioned as follows, viz: —For his services as Medical Officer of Health £llO per annum, for his services as Superintendent of the Hospi- tals £lO per annum. Upon the application of Cowburn and Sons, that they be allowed the use of the market weighing machine for the purpose of weighing slag,stone, &c., in connection with their street contracts at the re- duced charge of one penny per load. The Medical Officer's report for September, submitted and read :—Births, 82, 3174 per 1,000 ; deaths (total). 54, 20-90 per 1.000; in children under 1 year, 17, 8-58 per 1,000; bet- ween 1 and 5 years, 19, 73 per 1,000 ; zymotic diseases, 10, 387 per 1,000 ; inquests, 3. Notifications of infec- tious diseases as follows were received :—Measles, 415 ; croup, 3 ; enteric or typhoid fever, 11; puerperal fever, 1 ; scarlatina, 3; diptheria, 1 ; erysipelas, 4. Total, 438. Infectious Diseases Notification Act,lBB9—Recommended that the orders of the Local Board passed on the 14th , January and 9th December, 1890, be revoked, and that the Local Board do order that, from and after the Ist day of November next, measles be no longer an infec- tious disease within the meaning of the Act, and that the approval of the Local Government Board be obtained to such order, also that the question of the revocation of the orders of the 14th January and 9th December be decided to be one of emergency.—There are six inmates in the Accident Hospital and nine in the Infectious Diseases Hospital. The Surveyor reported that the heating apparatus at the laundry of the Infectious Hos- pital had been fitted up, and was working in a satisfac- tory manner, but, owing to a broken pipe, it was not yet complete. The flushing tank and automatic syphon had been fixed, but had not yet been tested.—Mr. Wright moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said twelve months ago they were told that it was impor- tant that measles should be declared an infectious disease under the Notification Act •, now the medical men said it was useless keeping measles on the list as it did not aid medical men ln preventing the spread of the disease. In August and September 540 cases of measles were notified, and if they went on at this rate the Board would soon have to provide a special rate for notification fees. div.p: THE StILPHURETTED HYDROGEN NUISANCE.
Mr. Heyes called the attention of the Health Com- mittee to the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen during the past month. IL had been far worse than ever before.

div.head: LORD TENNYSON AND THE CZAR.
div.p: LORD TENNYSON AND THE CZAR.

Lord Tennyson has addressed the following letter to a member of the Russo-Jewish Committee :—" October Ist, 1891.—Sir,—I have read what is reported of the Russian persecutions by your paper and by the Press generally, and if that be true, I can only say that Russia has dis- graced her church and her nationality. I once met the Czar. He seemed a kind and good-natured man. I can scarcely believe that he is fully aware of the barbarities perpetrated with his apparent sanction.—TENNYSON."

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE HON. ALGERNON
div.p: WILL OF THE LATE HON. ALGERNON
EGERTON, M.P.

Probate of the will, dated 2nd September, 1890, of Col. the Hon Algernon Egerton, of Worsley Old Hall, Woes- ley, Secretary of the Admiralty 1874-80, M.P. for South Lancashire 1859-68, for South-east Lancashire 1868-80, and for Wigan 1882-5, who died at 3, Belgrave-place, on the 14th July last, aged 65 years, and was a son of the first Earl of Ellesmere, has been granted to the executors, his wife' the Hon. Alice Louisa Egerton (daughter of the late Lord George Cavendish), and his brother-in-law Mr. James Charles Cavendish. The testator bequeaths to his wife £l,OOO and his plate, pictures, books, horses, and carriages ; and to his son,George Algernon, £16,000. He devises and bequeaths his residuary estate, the value of the personalty being £19,752 153. 3d. in trust to pay the income thereof to his wife, during her life, and sub- ject to her life interest, to hold the residuary estate in trust in equal shares for all his children.
THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION AT SOUTHPORT.

On Tuesday morning the business proper of the autumn session of the Congregational Union of England and Wales commenced in the Cambridge Hall, South- port. The large hall was crowded in every part. The Presidental address was delivered by the Rev. John Brown, of Bedford, on" The Historic Christian people; a reassertion of their duties and rights." A resolution was adopted expressing profound gratitude at the signal success which marked the gathering of the first interna- tional conference. The council sympathise with Dr. Dale in his illness •, thank the Rev. Dr. E. Mackennal for the manner in which he had represented the union in the secretarial work of the council,and request that the com- mittee would take into consideration the several points of interest to which council called attention, with a view to the presentation of a report and suggestions for action to the earliest possible meeting of the assembly. Another resolution ',was to the effect that the cultivation of closer relationship was required between the various free evan- gelical churches of the country, and that opportunity should be afforded for the development and manifesta- tion of this essential unity. The meetings were resumed on Wednesday, when papers were read on the necessity for sending out more missionaries and on the importance of quickening Con- gregationalism in villages and towns. A telegram of greeting was read from the Congregational Union of California. A resolution was carried in favour of minis- ters in large cburches in towns and cities visiting with- out fees the weaker churches of rural districts, so as to bring rich and poor into closer sympathy. On Thursday Mr. Albert Spicer and the Rev. Fleming Williams made a statement en behalf of the Social Ques- tions Committee, and suggested that district committees should be formed to co-operate with the London breth- ren upon any questions having the special regeneration and uplifting of the people for their objects. In Eng- land there were 10,000 parishes with Church schools only,and the committee were determined to try to bring about a juster arrangement.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Foulkes. TEE CAUSE LIST comprised 220 original plaint sum- monses, 10 adjourned plaint summonses, 2 default sum- monses, 47 original judgment summonses.

TRESPASS Er Cows.—Peter Cliffe, Whitley Inferior, market gardener, claimed against Robert Wilkinson, Whitley Inferior, farmer, the sum of £1 12s. for damage done to some oats and garden produce.—From the evi- dence of the plaintiff is appeared that on September 4th, two cows belonging to the defendant got through a fence belonging to him into the highway, and strayed along until they obtained access to plaintiff's field through a fence that was not in good condi- tion, and went amongst the oats, and did damage to the extent claimed. On September 28th plaintiff saw five cows of the defendant in his field. The plaintiff had the damage estimated, but he had not his valuer present at that court.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: Plaintiff admitted that the valuer had refused to come to the court, but denied that the valuer had told him that he had no claim because his fence was in a bad condition. Plaintiff, in answer to further questions, admitted that there was an opening in his own fence which ran along the highway, and it was in conse- quence of that opening' that the cattle had obtained access.—Mr.Browne, for.the defendant, submitted that on September 28th the cattle were going along the highway in an ordinary way, and for a legal pur- pose. The defendant was not responsible for the damage done to the plaintiff's property, as his hedge was out of repair. He argued that the damage claimed for was exorbitant, and further none was proved.— His Honour, in giving judgment, said that he felt a difficulty in deciding this case, inasmuch as it was clear defendant was not liable for the damage done on Sep- tember 28, because the cattle were going along the high- way for a legal purpose, but with regard to September 4 defendant was at fault, inasmuch as his hedge must have been neglected, or otherwise the cows would not have got out; and if cows strayed on the highway plain- tiff was not bound to fence against them. He had great difficulty in deciding as to the amount of the damage done, but inasmuch as no person had been called to prove it, he would therefore non-suit the plaintiff.

CLAIM AGAINST MESSRS. H. EVANS AND CO.—James Leech, an elderly man, who resides at Parr, St. Helens, claimed £2 6s. Bd. from Messrs. R. Evans and Co., col- liery proprietors, of Havdock, in lieu of a fortnight's notice ot dismissal.—Mr. Wilson, of Wigan, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Stuart for the defendants. The claim was for damages in consequence of the defendants having dismissed the plaintiff without the usual fort- night's notice. It was said that plaintiff had been em- ployed by the defendants for nearly 30 years.—For the plaintiff it was stated, that on the 18th July he was un- able to go• to his work in consequence of illness, and he had to remain at home for two or three days from the same cause. When he went back to work he was, how- ever, peremptorily dismissed.—For the defendants it was alleged that plaintiff had not attenaed his work in conse- quence of his drinking habits.—A verdict was given for the defendants.

CLAD( AGAINST A CONFECTIONER .—The trustees of the late W. N. Sharp, printers, &c., of Bradford, sued Jona- than Finch, confectioner, of Warrington, for £l5 2s.,for goods sold and delivered. The plaintiff's solicitors,Messrs. Wright and Trewdods, of Bradford, were represented by Mr. E. A. White,of Warrington ; and Mr. Horridge, bar- rister, of Liverpool, instructed by Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth, of Warrington, defended. It was stated on behalf of the plaintiffs that their agent,Mr. W. R. Verity, of Manchester, called upon the defenchnt on the 20th August,and obtained an order from him for one hundred gross packets of coloured football cards, which specta- tors at football matches frequently place in their hats. This order was transmitted to the plaintiffs, and the cards, which were in stock, were putup in a parcel and delivered to the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co. Very soon after giving the order the defendant, however, appeared to have repented of the bargain and at once wrote to the plaintiffs cancelling the Order, but the plaintiffs would not agree to this, and defendant having refused delivery of the goods the present action was brought. For the defence it was denied that any order had been properly given. Defendant's daughter had signed the order form, and according to the plaintiffs this was done at the request of her father, but for the defence it was said that Miss Finch signed the form at the request of Verity, she thinking that the latter only wanted her father's address. Mr. Horridge also took objection to the line of action taken by the plaintiffs as it should have been one for non-acceptance of goods. His Honour concurred with this, and also considered that there had really been no proper contract entered into. He therefore gave judgment for the defendant with costs.

COLLISION OF BicycLas.—A young man named Walter Beswick sued Jesse Norcock for two guineas, damage done to a bicycle. There was a counter-claim made by Norcock, for £2 ss. ed. also for damage to a bicycle. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Beswick, and Mr. Forshaw for Norcock. The plaintiff's evidence was that on the 11th June last be was riding a bicycle along the road at Crowley, near Northwich, when he saw the defendant and a young man riding, both on bicycles, in the oppo- site direction to him. They were on the wrong side of the road. Defendant,although he saw the plaintiff,never attempted to get out of the road. He came along with his arms stretched up, his legs guiding the machine. When the defendant was close upon him the plaintiff turned aside, and, the defendant turning in the same direction,a collision occurred. The plaintiff and a farmer named James Earle gave evidence in corroboration of this statement.—On the other hand it was stated that the plaintiff crcssed over from one side of the road to the other and rushed into the defendant. A verdict was given for the plaintiff for 305., and also on the counter- claim.

COOlO3 are often called upon to provide sweet dishes of cus- tards and blanc-manges at short notice, and at times when It is not convenient to obtain eggs. As a useful guide to the preparation of many choice dishes and delicious custards without eggs and half the trouble our readers should write to ALFRED BIRD AND SONS, BIRMINGHAM, for a free copy of their little book entitled "Pastry and Sweets." There is nothing to pay; a post card will bring it by return free.--..ddvt. An appeal has been raised against the refusal of the Westmoreland justices to renew the licence of the Coach and Horses, near Appleby. The point raised in the appeal is whether the justices exercised their discretion judicially or arbitrarily. Immense sensation has been created in Berlin by the disclosures made during the trial of Imperial Councillor Manche, who has been sentenced to nine months' imprisonment for corruption in the disposal of titles and distinctions. It transpired that during many years Herr-Manche received large sums as commissions from the recipients of titles or distinctive rank.
THE GALE. SHIPPING DISASTERS, &c.
The Press Association says telegrams received from different parts of the country on Thursday indicate that the gale has not abated. A fearful storm still rages in the Irish Channel. _ _
An unknown schooner, observed in distress at Holy- head on Wednesday, is reported to have gone ashore at Cemlva. Papers picked up show she was on a voyage for Cardiff. Nothing is known of the crew. _

A later telegram from Holyhead says that the vessel reported ashore at Cemlyn was the schooner Ocean Maid. It appears that the crew were landed by the lifeboat for safety, and hope to go on board again when the weather moderates. The vessel which was in distress is now supposed to have foundered off Carmel Point. She belonged to Newhaven and had sailed from Cardiff with ooals. She was a vessel of 280 tons burthen. Stormy weather is reported from East Herts, West Essex, South Bedfordshire, and North Notts. Lloyd's states that the schooner Alice Eleanor, of Wexford,stranded in Milford Haven, on Wednesday. The steamerCastlemaine is reported ashore at Fleetwood The violence of the gale has made breaches in the sea wall at Newhaven. The steamer Arfieur has arrived at Newhaven, and reported sighting in the Channel the Duch steamer Prince Phillippe disabled through the Ir;ss of her rudder. Great fears are entertained concerning the vessel's safety. A Folkestone correspondent says the continental traffic thence is still suspended. The Deal Hovel!er has put off at great risk to a barque in distress. Manchester travellers are waiting to cross the Channel. At Leicester, on Wednesday, the storm dismantled the whole of Wombwell's Menagerie, and a bison and seve- ral monkeys, birds,and serpents perished from exposure, while the celebrated lion Wallace is said to be dying...

A pathetic incident occured on Stanimo're Kirkby Stephen, when two brothers engaged in gather- ing sheep lost their way in the darkness and crept into a hollow for shelter. One lay on top of the other to keep him warm, and next morning was found dead from cold, the other being only just alive. A Newhaven schooner of 280 tons is believed to have foundered off Holyhead, but nothing is known of the crew.

The storm continued on Thursday, and was very severe on the south and west coasts. Many shipping disasters were reported, and the Channel steamers were much impeded by the high seas. Inland the storm was accom- panied by thunder and lightning, and much damage was done to property. The vicarage of Woodville, near Burton-on-Trent, was struck by lightening, and its occu- pants had a narrow escape. Owing to the heavy rains several rivers overflowed, and in Wales and some of the Southern counties tracts of land were flooded. A sad accident occurred in the Rhondda Valley. A man attempting to drive across the swollen river was swept away, and another man tried to rescue him, but they were both drowned. In the Dee Valley a number of sheep were drowned, and in other parts of the country great damage was done to live stock and agricultural produce by the floods. The storm was very fierce in London, and at Knightsbridge, a heavy hoarding was blown to the ground, injuring several persons.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.

The funeral of John Kirk, engine driver, of Leinster- st., Runcorn, took place on Sunday, at Runcorn Ceme- tery. His mortal remains were followed to the grave by about a hundred Ship Canal employes. it will be remembered that Kirk was killed on the previous Mon- day near Moore, by his engine overturning and crushing him beneath its great weight.

div.head: FIRE AT NORTON.
div.p: FIRE AT NORTON.

About half-past ten o'clock on Monday evening, a watchman, named Wm. Walker, in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal, discovered that the engine shed at Big-field, Norton, was on fire. He raised an alarm, and P.C. Boyle, being in the vicinity at the time, des- patched a Messenger for the Runcorn Fire Brigade, .but happily, before their arrival, the flames had been ex- tinguished by the workmen with the company's fire ex- tinguishing apparatus. The fire is supposed to have orignated from a spark from, an engine. The damage, which is estimated at £150,i6 fully covered in the Lan- don Fire Assurance Company.

div.head: PONTOONS AND DRY DOCKS.
div.p: PONTOONS AND DRY DOCKS.

The Manchester Ship Canal Pontoons and Dry Docks Company, Limited, has been registered, with a capital of £300,000, in 30,000 shares of £lO each, 100 of which are founders' shares. The Directors are Mr. George Renwick, J.P. (Fisher. Renwick, and Co.) ; Mr. Thomas Bell,J.P. (Messrs. Pyman, Bell, and Co.) ; Mr. Joseph T. Eltringham,J.P.,and Mr. Alexander Taylor, all of whom are intimately connected with the shipping interest and are resident at Newcastle-upon-Tyne and North Shields, and they have themselves described the memorandum of association of the Company for upwards of £42,000 of the first issue of the capital-121,000,—leaving only £78,000 available for public subscription. The Man- chester Ship Canal Company will nominate two of its Directors to the Board after allotment. A plot of land containing close upon 17 acres,and situate above the Mode Wheel locks which constitute the en- trance to the Manchester and Salford docks, has been secured for the Company from the Ship Canal Company on advantageous terms in perpetuity, the plot having a frontage to the canal of 1,389 feet. The Company has also had conceded to it the right to construct dry docks, shipbuilding berths, and workshops, and also jetties in the canal alongside their land, and to moor pontoons there for repairing ; and also the right to moor other pontoons in the lower portions of the canal, at places to be hereafter arranged,so that repairs can be done to ships and vessels which have not occasion to come up as far as Manchester and Salford. A railway siding is to be constructed by the Ship Canal Company to the Com- pany's premises, which will put them in communication with all parts of the country. The plot of land is the only one now available for the purposes nrthe Company above the Mode Wheel locks and this appears to be a most important factor, inasmuch as ships will be able, in consequence of the inequality of the water level, to float direct from the Manchester and Salford Docks into the repairing docks without having to descend to the lower reaches of the canal and then to return for the purpose of taking in cargo. The canal will be 13ft.lower in level below the Mode Wheel locks than it is above them, so that this fall will enable the dry docks to be partially emptied without the necessity and expense of pumping an immense mass of water out. The Company proposes to proceed at once with the construction of one large dry deck, which will be fitted with powerful pumps to ensure its being rapidly emptied, and also to forthwith provide one or more pontoon floating docks, which will each be about 250 ft. to 350 ft. long, and 60ft. to 70ft. wide, and capable of docking vessels up to from 2,500 to 3,500 tons burden. It is estimated by the direc- tors that an expenditure of not more than £lOO,OOO will be required during the next two years, but suffi- cient margin has been left in the amount of capital to provide for ample accommodation, and so as to keep pace with any increase of trade. Owing to the numerous casualties and heavy wear and tear inseparable from the navigation of ships, and to the fact of bottoms of iron and steel vessels rapidly fouling, it is absolutely necessary that they be ,periodically placed in dry docks, or upon pon- toons, for the purpose of examination ,cleaning,painting, and repairing. It appears that such facilities as are proposed to be provided by the Company are a necessary adjunct to the Ship Canal. Ship repairing, it is well known, is a most profitable business, and very remunera- tive dividends are paid by various concerns engaged in the trade. The number of directors of the Company is I not to exceed nine or be less than four, and the qualific- tion of a director is (except in the case of directors , nominated by the Ship Canal Company) the holding of shares of the nominal value of £2,000. No promotion money has been or is to be paid. It is' evident that the gentlemen who have founded the Company, all of whom hail from distant places, have great faith,not only in the success of their own scheme, in which they have a very large pecuniary stake, but also in the prosperity of the Manchester Ship Canal. The services of Mr. E. Leader Williams have been retained as engineer, and the Com- pany has been registered by Messrs. Payne, Galloway, and Payne, solicitors of this city.

div.head: FIRST FOREIGN STEAMER.
div.p: FIRST FOREIGN STEAMER.

We are informed that the cargo of the Norwegian steamer Hertha, the first steamer unctex a foreign flag entering the Ship Canal, consisted of 590 tons of flint stones, not sugar as stated, and that she arrived from St. Valery-en-Caux.

div.head: WIDNES FERRY APPROACH
div.p: THE WIDNES FERRY APPROACH

By a clause in their act, the Manchester Ship Canal Company were compelled to excavate the rock on the Widnes foreshore to a depth to give as good passage for vessels as had previously existed on the Runcorn side of the river,and in order that the approach to Widnes Docks should be kept unobstructed. This rock has been exca- vated and there is now a sheer fall of about 8 feet along the side of the promenade and the bottom of Mersey-st., constituting a danger to pedestrians in the night time and to the numerous children who are in the habit of making this neighbourhood their playground. A deputa- tion from the Local 809. rd have had an interview with the executive committee of the Ship Canal and suggested that they should construct a suitable wall along the fore- shore, but this suggestion they could not see their way to carry out. They, however, offered to contribute a sum of £2oo,leaving it to the Local Board to carry out such a scheme as they thought proper. The Board have con- sidered the subject in private,and have resolved to accept the offer of the Ship Canal Company and to defer for further consideration the method by which the approaches to the river shall be made safe.

The memorandum prepared by the Labour corres- pondent of the Board of Trade states that while the condition of the labour market is not yet seriously bad, it la nevertheless in a declining condition,being best des- cribed, perhaps by the word "moderate." Mr. J. F. Lambiton, a Liberal member of the Canadian House of Commons, has assured his constitutents that the disclosures of corruption during the past session are but it tithe of what will be forthcoming next session, when disclosures more startling and more_damaging to the party in power will be made.

SATURDAY. OCTOBER 17, 181.

"What Ttz.; Salford Working-men's Should he Social and Sanitary Association , Done was aisefully eMployed,en Monday night, with the. Bishop. of Salford in the chair, in, considering .what aetion should be taken in view of, the impending. Municipal electioes. What an. advantageit wouldibe if there was a similar organ- isation in every, town,with the clergyand ministers, of all denominations ready to lend so helping hand in making. tke homes-of the poorer classes healthirtr, and therefore happier t But in these matters the clergyman is, as &rule, like the usher who "sat remetefr alb"- a. solitary if not a melancholy man. All honour to the Bishop, of Salford :F-or coming on the scene,. and assistin,g,in formulathag a wise policy. It is stated that, in, concluding his speech, he "read a.list of eleven qirstions which it is proposed to submit to municipal cendidateeeat the coming elections, dealing among other sub*ts with the compulsory closure of ineanitary dwelling houses, the supervision of sanitary undertakings by the Medical:Officer of Healthethe provision by the TbWD Council of amusements and recreations for the.peepleeandl an increased number of open spaces,. the. reduetion of licensed housere and increased stringency in the supervision of the lower grades .of licensed houses." Why should not the electors of every-town in the,kingdom arrange a similar series oil questions, altering them arcourse to coves their special requirements? Except when a nuisance becomes intolerable,as in the case of the Intercepting Depots at Warrington, they show thems,elves. indifferent in, matters of sanitation; hut that is because they clo not sufficiently realise how tout drains, narrow courts, and unpaved yards, and passages are destructive of health and of lithe Now and again spasmodic threats are made to close insanitary. dwellings,, but they usually end in tempovary and wholly inadequate repairs,and the mischief7goe3 on as befOre. There would soon boa change in all this if the working- class. electors insisted; upon candidates beinei; pledged in these , matters before returning them to the Council' Chamber. Health is every- thing 'to the worleing.-eraan, for -when that fails , everything fails ; and yet it is a matter of common !observation that. in, certain localities health is be- ing risked hour by hour in housesso badly drained, that fever-breeding gases are always in the, air. More power ought to be put in the hands of Medical Officers, of Health. In Glasgow' the Medical o,fficer has under Mini a drain-besting staff, who have found that an enormous majority of drains tested. in the city„ many of them new, are in an insanitary condition. Why shenld there not be a. like staff in every town? it would cost something, to be sure; but better spend a small Sum in keeping disease out of the house than a large sum in expelling it after it has oh- tallied possession. Then there is the smoke nuisance; it is simply ignored in most Lancashire and Cheshire towns. Vested interests, which are not always working- men's interests, are so strongly represented on Corporation Committees that offenders are allowed to do pretty much as they like, even when they are breakirg the bye-laws every day. In War- rington tha Sanitary Committee, instead of doing their duty in an open and regular manner, have an illegal and bad system of permitting offenders to ply a nominal fine, rather than submit to the

_ exposure and cost which would result from lie Prosecutions. What would be thought of the Watch Committee if it brought before itoffenders against the licensing laws, and let them off With a small fine instead of leaving them to be dealt with in the ordinary course of law? It would be regarded as a parody on the principles ef justice; and so it ic with the Sanitary Committee. As to the Watch. Committee of Warrington its weakness is of another kind; it suffers through having upOn it twci members who are interested in the drink trade—one of them actually a publican and brewer The town has attained an unenviable notoriety as a place where drumkennevs is tolerated and there- fore rife, and where prosecutions of drink-sellers, which are remarkably few, have of late become ridiculous by proving abortitre. There is no dis- guising the fact that things aTe going from bad to worse. The policeman's wordiis accepted as gos- pel when it is a case of dealing with an offender who is found drun*;; but the same officer would seem to, be looked upon. as incapaNe of telling the truth when it is a matter of- dealing with a publicaa, who is accused of an infra.o- - of the law. The way to arrest this, down- grade tendency is to place men upon the Watch Committee who we above suspicion, who can be trusted to act without fear and without Favour— who will not seek tor serve publicans r but to serve the public. In saying this -we hold;that -we are speaking in the bestinteresto, of "the trad's:;'-' for it is this toleration of law-breakers which makes it all the harder for the law-abiding7nublican • to. get a living. It will be seen from this outline 0g work to be done that thera is plenty fortho. electors, to think about, and act upon (I.'4lring the, present Municipal Campaign. Let then 4 be wise,' and wise in time: Noleinber w:141 soon be-here.

He laws been holding forth. in Wales, and trying to frighten Nonconformists with a picture of what may happen to the Protes- tants of inland if Herne iile thould be panted. He states that, in 1884, "There was no Liberal of any eminence—there was.no I,lberal of the slight- est influence or importance—either in vales or Englawl who er motioned Home Rule oxs:ept uI te'rrns of repudiation and of disapproYal." More than that, until the county fra,nchise was extended ie Ireland as in Englafld, it could not be said 0310 the voice of Ireland had been clearly heard. Mr' GLAIisTONs had always shows himself ar.Mialls to listen to that voice, and when, as • the result' of the elections of 1885, he found that the poolli° of Ireh.nd, by a vary large- majority, domande', self-government, he went to work, like a souna statesman and true democrat, and prepared 3, Home Rule measure. Home Rule. The wise man of Birmingham would have people believe that h 0 at any rate has never changed his mind, and that he is still right whilst everybody who differs from him is wrong. He is bitter at the prospect of Ireland having the opportunity of managing her own affairs in her own way; and seems to have quite forgotten that, when Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill was under discussion, he expressed himself as in favour of the principle of Home Rile, but not of the proposed method of carrying it out. Indeed, he has had sundry -schemes of his own; and there is no doubt they had some good points; but they have never held the field. As he has not been able to induce either Englishmen or Irishmen to give a serious ear to his disposals, he appears to have given up the task in despair, and figures now in the character of" The Bogie Man." Welsh- men he insinuates, will never see the Church dis- established, if they allow Home Rule to take pre- cedence. Their only hope,we suppose, is to trust to Mr. t.IIIAMBERLAIN, who will persuade the Tory 'Government to put Disestablishment in the front of their next programme. The sky of course may fall, and then we shall catch all the larks. Welsh- men, however, know what they are about. They .are in favour of Home Rule because they believe in civil liberty; they are in favour of Disestablishment because they believe in religious equality; and they are in favour of 'Mr. GLADSTONE because they know that, having once put his hand to the plough, he has never yet looked back.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The Parnellities are in the thick of preparations to bring out two new papers—a morning and an evening. One would be quite sufficient to cripple their ;lender resources ; two will be "Sudden death," after a brief spasm. The late Trades Congress is bearing fruit. The Parliamentary Committee, after a prolonged dis- cussion, have decided to frame a Bill on the lines of the Local Trade Option, which requires the assent of a two-thirds majority of those concerned to secure the enforcement of the law. From this stage the eight hours question may be said to have become a question of practical politics.

There hasibeen an uneasy feeling as to the mass- ing and moving Of troops in Russia; but the Czar has gone out of his way to assure Italy that he is anxious to preserve the peace, and that all that he is aiming at is keeping order within his own dominions. This may not mean much, but it is better than an ominous silence. There is certainly nothing to fight about; but then that doesn't mean much as wars go.

Further developments n the Ship Canal: last week witnessed a trial trip of the Syndicate steamer, St. Mawe's Castle, from the 'George's Landing Stage, Liverpool, for Northwich,via East- ham and the River Weaver. This week it is an- nounced• that an important Company is being formed, mainly by men from the Tyne side for starting a Ship Canal Pontoons and Dry Docks Company, with a very influential backing. There's water in the canal now, and before long there will be "money in it."

The Liberals of Warrington set themselves the task of raising £l,OOO by a Bazaar, and they have raised £1,220. That is one good thing, and another good thing is that the Bazaar has brought workers of all classes of Liberals together in a way which is stimulating and hopeful for the future. Socially, as well as financially, the enterprise has been a great success. The women have done their part in a manner which is beyond all praise; and it remains now far the men to complete the task by working to win in November and at the General Election.

Captain Shaw has got the worst of it in his little duel, on paper, with the London Fire Brigade Com- mittee. He expressed himself as holding a strong opinion that "existing arrangements •' were not such as to conduce to the success of the brigade, and yet, when pressed on the point, he declined to say what were the "existing arrangements" to which he takes exception. Captain Shaw may be said to have, performed a similar feat to that of Lord John Russell who, metaphorically speaking, chalked up " No Popery" and then ran away.

Lord Salisbury had to return from France for the purpose of fixing upon a leader in the House of Commons in place of the late Mr. Smith. Three candidates were in the .field--Goschen, Balfour, and Hicks-Beach • and it is understood that Lord Salisbury for a while kept humming:— How happy could I be with either, Where t'other 'dear charmers away, But whilst they all teaze me together To neither a word will I say. And yet he was 'compelled to choose; and that choice has fallen upon his nephew, Mr. Balfour, the present Secretary for Ireland.

A London correspondent says :—" The choice of the leadership of the Parnellite party rests between Mr. John Redmond and Mr. Pierce Mahony. It will probably be Mr. Redmond, as a man of action is required. Mr.Mahony would be a cultured figure- head like Mr. M'Carthy. Mr. Mahony is a scholar and a gentleman, a small landed proprietor, has been a laud commissioner, is a pier and harbour commissioner, and is noted as a successful breeder of the celebrated Kerry cattle." As a matter of fact Mr. Mahony has been informally placed in the position of leaden He is well-known in War- rington, as he has twice addressed large audi- ences with considerable effect.

Lecturing on Palestine at Penketh, on Tuesday, the Rev. Dr. Leach said :—" One very sad feature about the Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem,was that Turkish soldiers had to be kept in the build- ing continually to keep peace amongst the members of the different churches, because the spirit of fanaticism was so very bitter between them that if left to themselves they fought like Turks." What a curious commentary on 1,800 years of preaching of the gospel of "Peace on earth and goodwill to men !" Whipping the offending Adam out of man is certainly a very slow process.

The smaller Authorities have a difficulty in mak- ing good use of the money granted to them for the purposes of promoting technical instruction. At the Ashton Local Board, on Monday, it was resolved on the motion of Mr. Valiant, seconded by Mr. Mitchell," that the Board be recommended to make grants of £l5O rto the Wigan Mining School and £2O to the Haydock Mining School, and that the balance of £6O be reserve for ex- penses in connection with local classes for cookery and dressmaking, and for travelling expenses.' This is "a more excellent way" than attempting to form a purely local institute with but little prospect of success.

There seems no reason to doubt the version of -the story given by Mr. Edmund Yates, as to the late Mr. W. H. Smith being once proposed as a member of the Reform Club and rejected. It is stated that he was described as a publisher, and that, as he was not referred to as a newsvender' it was held that he was not properly described. It would seem that there was snobbishness on both sides ; snobbishness on the part of the proposers in "keeping dark" as to his being a newsvendor ; and snobbishness on the part of black-ballers who thought a newsvendor " was'nt good enough." It is to be hoped the Reform Club is beyond this sort of thing now-a-days ; if not, it certainly needs reforming.

Next week we shall publish another letter re- ceived from Mr. W. Unsworth, in which he con- tinues his record of incidents in the voyage, with his family, to Australia. He encloses a note from a Mr. J. W. Greaves, written in reply to an in- quiry about a workshop, in which that gentleman, on finding Mr. Unsworth was from Warrington, says :—" I will have a talk with you about War- rington and Manchester, and gas, when next I see you. I was five years at Penketh School, and have been nine years in connection with gas works."
Sc , tball d thlo eSthlt jotle
Mr. Unsworth, who is now in Melbourne, adds : "I have met with a number of.people who know all about Liverpool, Warriugtou, and Man- chester."

It is stated that the proposal to request Sir Gilbert Greenall to allow himself to be again nom- inated for Warrington was coldly received at the Conservative Club,on Monday evening. There was not so much as a "hear, hear "—to say nothing of a cheer. The rank and file cannot understand the move seeing that Sir Gilbert is so old and feeble as to 'be unable to attend to his duties in Parlia- ment. Rumonr has it that the strings are being pulled to get him a peerage; but Lord Salisbury will probably think enough has been done in con- verting the brewer into the baronet. It is stated that Sir Gilbert will give his reply to the deputa- tion in three or four weeks; but it is absurd to suppose that he will consent to enter upon another election campaign.

ACcidents will happen ;but are' they not alto- gether too frequent at St. Helens? It is pretty plain from the evidence given in the case of the two men who lost their lives at Sutton Glassworks that the curve at which the trolly was tilted is a dangerous one. It is described by the engineer of the works as " a sharp curve " ; and another wit- ness said it wits common for the men to exclaim " Look out at the points." The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the death of the two men was accidental, but suggested that the company- should devise some means to prevent the glass fall- ing off in case a waggon again left the road during the transport. This is good as far as it goes ; but then the jury might have gone further, and urged the necessity of special means being taken to ease the curve, or, at any rate, minimise its dangers.

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN. Services of thanksgiving for the ingathering of tk e harvest were commenced on Friday night last week, when the Rev. Canon Robssn preached an appropriate sermon. On Sunday the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Canon Poaler, of Downpatrick Cathedral, Ireland, who preached twO eloquent discourses to large congre- gations. The decorations were of a charming character. The collections were in aid of the Curates' Fund. AN UNMANAGEABLE BOY AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. Thomas and Major Ilazlehurst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, a boy named Wm. Hougton, aged 11 years, was charged with wandering abroad, and not being under proper guardianship. It appeared that the boy habitually slept away from home, and on Sun- day night was found by P.C. Thompson sleeping in a fire hole at Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele's works. The father said he was quite unmanageable. The Bench committed him to an industrial school until he is 16 years of age. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—Gsmtawn, Warrington, —Advt.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCH. Atthe fortnightly meeting of the above order an essay was given by Mr. Janus Bisbrown on "The drinkinir customs of society." The writer very forcibly des- cribed the Various ramifications ,of our drinking system, and spoke of the fearful havoc drink had wrought in our midst. He said it was powerfully entrenched in custom and appetite, and was a fruitful source of misery and wretchedness. He strongly condemned grocers licenses and referred to the fact that the drink crave was heredi- tary and that the only absolute safeguard was total abstinence. There was a discussion after the reading of the paper in which the following officers and members took part :—Messrs. Edward Kay, Thomas Holt, Thomas Heesom, Samuel M. Temperlev,W. Bisbrown, and Thos. Cooke. 1. vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Bisbrown for his interesting paper. Mr. Wesley Cooke occupied the chair.

ROBBEEY OF L 3 AT WIDNES. John Gannon and Joseph Waters, of Oxford-st., were brought before the Widnes magistrates' on Monday, charged with stealing £3 belonging to John McKew. The men lodged at No. 4, Oxford-st., Waters sleeping in the same room as McKew, and Gannon in another room. On Saturday night McKew placed his money under his pillow, and next morning he discovered that it had been taken. At midnight, the landlord, Peter , Cain heard a noise downstairs, and on proceeding be- low, 'he found Gannon sittingon a bench in the kitchen, and the door was open. Gannon said it was "through a drop of drink," and then went to bed. When'the rob- bery was iliscovered next morning, Gannon acted in a very excita le manner, and asked if they thought he had taken the money. P.C. Murray found £2 10s. in the closet, and Gannon was taken into custody. Waters was apprehended at his work, and said he found the purse between the bed and the window. Both prisoners denied the charge, and were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

------- --- - WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD FINANCES. A special meeting of Widnes School Board was held yesterday week, for the purpose of passing the balance sheet for the half year ending September 29th last. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided,and there were present Major Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. B, Brown, C. E. Barlow, S. Quin, and G. H. Danby, (clerk). The statement showed an income of £5,363 6s. 6d., including a balance of £466 14s. 4d., grant from education department, £127; from rates, £3,900; school fees, £825 is. 7d.— The expenditure amounted to £5,216 Us. 7d ; the chief ' items being salaries of officers of Board £313 16s. 6d. ; legal and other expenses of administration £B4 10s. 4d.; salaries of teachers, £2,900 4s. 2d.; books, apparatus, and stationery, £l6l us. 10d. ; fuel, lighting, cleaning, repairs to building and furniture, £564 19s. 9d. ; rents, rates and taxes, £23 85.,: contrioution to industrial Ischools £56 6s. 10d. ; repayment of loans, £344 Os. 6d. ; interest on loans, £727 19s. id. The outstanding liabil- ities of the Board amount to £32,963 13s. 10d.

RUNCORN. The anniversary meeting of the Runcorn Branch of this Society was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Tues- day evening, under the presidency of Mr. Jas. Pritchard. The Rev. J. Symons, F.G.S.,delivered a lecture on" The Bible in India," illustrated by magic lantern slides. There was a large attendance and a collection was made in aid of the funds of the Society. SUDDEN DEATH AT:WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at Widnes Police Court, on the body of Edward McGeever, aged eight years, son of a labourer who lives in Cromwell-St. The deceased became sick in the early hoursof Monday morning, and afterwards was unconscious and died before the doctor who was called In had arrived. He had been healthy ...boy and had eaten heartily on Sunday. After hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of accidentaCdeath.

ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES. Harvest thanksgiving services were held in this church on Sunday, the edifice having been beautifully decorated with flowers and fruits for the occasion. The preacher was the Rey. J. Connell,B.A., curate of Belfast (formerly of Widnes), who delivered two eloquent discourses to crowded congregations. The services were continued on Monday evening when the Rev. J. T. Madden vicar of St. Lukes, Liverpool occupied the pulpit. The amount realised by the collections will be devoted to the fund for restoring- the flooring of the church. LAWN MovrEßS.—Garland, 51. Bridge-it., WarringtAm. and at Earleatown.—Adz,t. LIGHT WEIGHTS AND LIGHT BREAD.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Walter Hough- ton, farmer, Lunt's Heath, was fined 53. and costs, for having in his possession two 561 b. weights which were 5 or. and 10 drachms and 3 oz. and 14 drachms light re- spectively. For being in possession of scales whin were 8 drachms light, Richard Bridge, grocer, Cronton, was fines ss. and costs.—James Travis, grocer, Church-st.; Farnworth, was charged with having sold three 41b. loaves which were altogether 10 or. n drachms light. The defendant excused himself on the ground that the bread was stalg, but the Bench considered it a bad case and imposed a line of 10s. and costs.

. TUE SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN; In aid of the building fund of this new institute, a football match between Runcorn and St. flaleas was played on the ground of the former, on Wednesday afternoon. Owing to the wet and boisterous weath-r, the attendance of spectators was not numerous, and the fund will not benefit as much as anticipated. The-gamc was well contested. - In the first half the visitors played with the wind, and Cross scored a try. In the second half Massey and T. Davies scored for Runcorn, Hough- ton landing a goal 'from one of the places. The final score was—Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try ; St. Helens, 1 try.
LICENSED VICTUALLERS AND BENEVOLENT ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN,

On Thursday evening a meeting of the licensed victuallers of Runcorn district was held in Wilson's Hotel for the purpose of considering the desirability of forming an association with the above title. There was a good attendance and Mr. J. W. Lightburn presided. It was admitted on all hands that such an association would be an advantage to the trade, and Mr. Lightburn proposed and Mr. Thomas Jones seconded a motion forming the Runcorn Licensed Victuallers and Benevol- ent Association, and it was carried unanimously.—Mr. Arther Hough,of the Riflemen's Arms was then appointed secretary and he was instructed to draw up a code of rules and submit it at the next meetings. AU the persons present joined the association. A VIOLENT MOTHER AND SON AT WIDNES. - •

At Widnes Petty Sessions cn Thursday, Bridget Hughes and Michael Hughes, ef Barn-st., mother and son, were brought up on remand charged with unlaw- fully wounding Martin Hughes. The prosecutor is hus- band of the female prisoner and father of Michael, but for some time he had been separated from his wife. On the Bth inst he was sent for to see Michael who is a soldier on furlough and he went as requested. Some drink was brought in and afterwards his son butted him in the face.. awl he returned to his lodging.—The two prisoner's followed him there and Michael struck him several times in the face, and in self-defence he caught hold of him, when his wife struck him three times on the head with some weapon he could not see.—Dr. Hudson who attended the man at the hospital, said he had two wounds on the back of the head penetrating to the bone; his face was contused, his eyes blackened,and blood was flowing from his ears. A poker would cause such wounds. He had lost a large quantity. of blood and was very weak. Evidence was given showing that the woman had the poker in her hands.—The prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial and the woman was granted bail. .
