The collection realised £ll4 3s. Bd. • THE PROPOSED FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.

A meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Frod- sham was held in the Public Hall, on Thursday night. There were about 50 persons present. Mr. H. E. Hey- wood presided. The minutes of the previous meeting were read and passed, and then Mr. Jpseph Edwards described the various steps that had been taken by the Parochial Committee and Rural Sanitary Authority, and again alleged that the scheme was thrust upon the town- ship by the lordship. He proposed "That this meeting of the ratepayers'of the township of Frodsham entirely repudiates and condems the present scheme for the supply of water to Frodsham, and recommended for adoption by the Parochial Committee, and requests the Centre Sanitary Authority of the Runaorn Union to reject the same."—Mr. Youd seconded.—Mr. J. Corker said he would guarantee to drown Frodsham for £5OO if they would not stop him. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said had he not been in the chair, he would have proposed an amendment.—Mr. Shore proposed that we do not reject the scheme.—Mr. Proud seconded. He regretted that the Local Government Board would not sanction the formation of a water district, but the township wanted water, and they should have the best scheme that could be devised. It would help them if Mr. Edwards would give them an alternative scheme.—Mr. A. Dawson se- conded the amendment. For 20 years he said the water question had been before the ratepayers,and nearly £2OOO had been spent on different schemes without anything being done. In his opinion the lordship did not want water, and he was in favour of the present scheme if a better one could not be proposed—Mr. Riley stated that Runcorn was supplied with water from the same bed as that from which it was proposed to supply Frodsham. After further discussion, the amendment was put to the meeting, and twelve voted for it. There were 21 votes for the original motion, which was declared carried.

In the Preston Comity Police Court o n Wednesday, a weaver., named Margaret Brogden, was awarded £BO damages against the Preston Spinning and Manufacturing Company, for thc.loss of an eye, which had been strucl, by a shuttle.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A GIRL AT WIDNES. On Thursday afternoon- Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes Police Court on the body of Ellen Roberts, aged 15, daugh- ' ter of a furnaceman who lives at 54, Albert-road. On the first September, during a storm of wind a shed was blown aown:iaear Bradley Hotel, and the deceased was struck by some of the falling timber. She, however, recovered from her inluries suffici- ently to go about the house; but afterwards became very ill and though every medical aid was rendered 1 by Drs. McLennan and McCambridge, she died on Tuesday last. -A verdict of "Accidental death "was
returned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Waxrington.—Airt.

DEATH OF MB.. THOMAS CAWLEY The death is recorded of Mr. Thomas Cawley,which took place on Tuesday night, at his residence Birch- field. Garston. The deceased, who was 53 years of age, was managing director for Messrs. Arthur Wareing and Co., tanners and size merchants, Win- wick-st., Warringtcn. He was at one time treasurer of.the Warrington Conservative Club, and was at the time of his death a member of the Conservative A.ssociation. The cause of death was typhoid fever,' from which Mr. Cawley had been suffering for three or four weeks. He leaves a widow and three sons and two daughters to mourn his loss. Mr. Cawley was also well-known at Newton-le-Willows, where he lived prior to his removal to Garston. .EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Causola, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rtes) at the "Examiner ": Office, by Cunard, anion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental; and other Lincs.—John Walker, agent. "Examiner ' Office, Bewsey-st.. Warrington.--Advt. COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT PEASLEY-CROSS. About ten o'clock,on Thursday, a serious accident took place in the Whitecross Colliery, Peasley-cross. A fireman named James Davies, of Islands Brow,, and a. day wageman named Peter Maddocks, of Peasley-cross-lane, were with the underlooker. George Twist, examining a portion of the roof. The roof sounded all right, and the men considered it safe, but while they were talking the roof fell in With a crash, and buried Davies and Maddocks. Davies was seriously injured, his legs being broken, and Maddocks is also badly hurt. The men were removed to their homes and medical assistance secured. Mr. Kennedy, the Liberal candidate for St. Helens, came up to the colliery shortly after the accident with a party of gentlemen, and was shown through the colliery by Mr. Biram, jun., and Mr. Turner. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.---J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE COLLISION AT CREWE RAILWAY STATION. On Thursday evening, Major Marindin, one of the Government inspectors, conducted an inquiry at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, into the circum- stances attending the collision at Crewe Station on Saturday, when the second portion of the Scotch express, due in Crewe at 3.25 p.m. ran into two stationary engines at the extreme en, of thestation, Several officials of the railway company attended the inquiry, including Mr. Shaw, district superin-. tendent, of Liverpool, Mr. Linaker, Mr. H. Turnbull, and Mr. G. Whale, assistant superintendent of the locomotive department. Evidence was given by the driver of the train, the signalman, Wilkinson, conductor Owen, and other persons concerned, and it was shown that the driver passed the danger signal before entering the station. Mrs. Pollard,the lady who sustained such serious injuries, is still making favourable progress. THE CLUB BAKERS OF WARRINGTON.

The following letter has been addressed to a con- temporary :—" Sir,—Permit" me a little space in your valued and esteemed paper to make reference to the late case of Strange v. the Club Bakers of Warrington. It is untrue as regards Mr. Strange causing his bakers to resume their work so early on Sunday nights. lam alone to blame for causing those premises to be open on Sunday nights at the aforesaid time; and it seems I studied the men's happiness and camfort before the laws of the coun- try and the by-laws of the society. Formerly it took the men fifteen and sixteen hours to complete their day's work, and under my way of working they can do the same amount in ten or eleven hours; and if I have violated the laws, I am very sorry. But I would venture as far again with my new scheme if it would benefit my fellow-workmen in health, happiness, and comfort.—Yours, Sze., W. FORSHAW, Foreman of the Works." UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.--J. and W. Burro's, Saukey-st., Warrington.—Adv EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT BOLD.

James Spencer, 31 years of age, a labourer of 45, Pecker's Hill-road, Sutton, was killed at Bold Col- liery, under extraordinary circumstances on Satur- day night. Spencer was engaged unloading bricks from a waggon in a siding at the colliery. Another waggon ot bricks stood afe g feet away, and after the deceased had emptied the first waggon he was expected to deal with the second load. He was working at the spot alone, and about seven o'clock he was heard to scrcam. Several men working in the vicinity ran toward him and found that he had been crushed to death between the buffers of the two waggons. How deceased got into that position is a mystery, as no shunting operations were going on at the time. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Vulcan Inn, St. Helens Junction, on Tuesday. Mr. A. Jackson, certificated manager, appeared for the firm.—The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death." THE PROPOSED COMPENSATION DISTRICT. On Monday afternoon, at the Town Hall, Middle- wich, a mw,ing ef salt manufacturers and property owners was held. The subject for consideration was as to their action with regard to the proposal made by the Northwich Local Board to make the district under the Brine Pumping (Compensation for Subsidence) Bill to embrace the whole of the county of Chester. It was discussed in all its bearings, and it was pointed out that if the sugges- tion was carried into effect, those belonging to Middlewich and neighbourhood would be called upon to pay for the damages taking place in North- wich and other sinking localities. Whilst perfectly willing t o contribute to the damage caused by brine pumping created by them, .they strongly ob- jected to be made responsible for the doings of others. It was decided to oppose the proposition of Northwich, and, if necessary, to engage a legal gentleman to represent them at the local inquiry to be held by the Local Government Inspector.. Tit NON-COUNTY BOROUGHS ASSOCIATION..

A meeting of the Non-County Boroughs Associa- tion was held at the Westminster Palace Hotel on : Wednesday, Mr. Oldroyd„ M.P., being in the chair. Among those present were Mr, J. Rowntree, MX., , and representatives for the corporations of Batley, Dewsbury, Dover, Workington, Crewe, Luton, Dar- wen, Southport, Stalybridge, Folkestone, East- bourne, Wakefield, Ossett, Warrington, and Ripon. The meeting was called to consider the position of non-county boroughs 'with regard to recent legis- lation and also in view of the probability of further measures being introduced into. Parliament at an early date seriously affecting their interests." The following resolutions were adopted unanimously : "That in order to remove the injustice caused to non-county boroughs by recent legislation this Association is of opinion that such boroughs should .be put in the same DOSition as county boroughs?' "That a committee consisting of the president,vice- president, and treasurer and the town clerks of Morley, Dover, Lmigton, Darwen, Dewsbury, and Stamford be appointed with full powers to take all such steps as to them may seem to be the best for , giving practical effect to the foregoing resolution, i and that all expenses thereby incurred be paid by a ' levy upon the members of the Association. BASSINETTES.—J. S. Garlan,d, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.— Advt.

FAILtrRE OF ON tARLESTOWN CONTRACTOR. On Monday Mt.' Unsworth, builder and con- tractor, Of Earle'stown, suspended-- businciss with liabilities estimated at son:fettling like £l,OOO. A meeting of the creditor's was held at Warrington on Wednesday afternoon, but no offer being made,it was decided to take bankruptcy proceedings.

THE PAYMENT OF JURORS AT WIDNES. At the conclusion Of an inquest. held at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, a juror asked Mr. W, T. Husband, the deputy coroner, if he were going to pay the jury fOr their,attendance.—Mr. Husband : No, but I hope to do so next time. The hall of the Conservative Club had been engaged for a mee.ting to discuss the question,and he sincerely hoped that at the next inquest he should be able to pay the' jurymen half-a-crown each.

- WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT. At this Court yesterday morning, before Mr. Registrar Nicholson the case of Wm. Hill, lately carryinglcn business as a contractor at Doctor's Bridge, Runcorn. Questioned by Mr. Potter, assist- ant official receiver, the debtor stated that a, receiv- ing order was made against him on a creditor's petition. He attributed his failure to the hard winter and overbuying and losses on cnntracts. The liabilities scheduled were £1.331 9s. 5d., and the net assets were put down at 2,:',388 7s. 7d., leaving a de'ficiency of £946 is. 10d. The debtor said he was ' a draughtsman by trade. In the spring ot 1889 he commenced business as a brickmaker in Irwell- lane, Runcorn, his capital consisting of four houses and one house and a.shop at Latchford, worth then about £7OO and on which the bank made advances. In July 1890,. he commenced building arid gave up the brickmaking business two months ago. The official receiver questioned him closely as to his business transactions and as to the time at which he became aware of his insolvency; and after fur- ther questions had been put by Mr. Forshaw on be- half of creditors, and Mr. Linaker, of Runcorn, himself a creditor, the inquiry was adjourned.
RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The first concert of the season in connection with Runcorn Musical Society took place in the Public Hall on Monday evening. A crowded audience as- sembled and were well recompensed for their patronage by a rich musical treat. The principals engaged were Miss Dews and Signor Foli, voca- lists; Senor Albeniz, solo pianist to H.M. the Queen of Spain; and Senor Arbos, solo violinist to Her Majesty of Spain; an array of talent vocal and instru- mental seldom if ever brought together on a platform in Runcorn. Miss Dews was in capital voice, and she took the auditory by storm in her first song "Entreat me not to leave thee" and she was rapturously encored. She was also encored for her expressive rendering of "The flight of ages," and responded with a charming inter- pretation of "She wore a wreath of roses." In the socond part she sang "The Mission of a Rose," and was again recalled. Signor Foil is a name known the wide world over and he fully sustained his great reputatien, his vocalisation being characterised by great power, verve and expression, and he raised the audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm. Each of his efforts was vocifer- ously encored, and he graciously responded on each occasion. His contributions were "Pm a Roamer," "The Golden Guineas," and "Blow, blow thou wintry wind." The performances of Senor Arbos on the violin were quite a revelation to local concert goers. His manipulation of the instrument was brilliant in the extreme, and the music he brought forth was e.xceed- ingly charming. Senor Albeniz was equally successful on the piano. He is gifted with delicate touch and the wonderful execution of his performances delighted the crowded company. Both gentlemen were encored on each appearance. The piano used was Steinway Con- cert Grand. The chorus was scarcely so large and powerful as usual, numbering only about 70 voices and of the four pieces they essayed in the course of the even- ing, the "Lullaby of Life " was the most successful. Their ether items were " Praise the Lord," "When the winds breathe soft," and "Beware." Mr. E. W. Hum- phreys was the conductor, and Mrs. W. B. Kay, the accompanist, of the choir.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT WIDNES.
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT WIDNES.

A few days ago Mr. Oppenheim, Clerk to the Widnes (Jambi Board and Mr. Hoyle, secretary to the Widnes Technical Instruction Committee, had an in- terview'with Mr. J. P. Muspratt, deputy clerk to the COUnt-,; Con nail of Lancashire, and Mr. Lloyd Evans the aAviSer of the Technical Instruction Committee. Mr. Oppenheim has since made -a report to the local Technical Instruction Committee which is now in the hands of the printer, but we have been priti- leged to make a few extracts. In the first place Mr. Oppenheim pointed out the funds available for distribution by the County Council arose and went on to observe that the permanent nature of the grant depended upon three things—(l) the non repeal of the Customs and Inland Revenue Act, 18u0; (2) Parliament refraining from otherwise determining, as to thc applica- tion of ;,:te duties within the ineantng of the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Act, 1890 ; (3) An entire change of policy on the part of the County Coun- cil or a practical alteration by administering the funds' themselves instead of through the local authorities. With respect to the first and second of the above observations, no positive assurance could of Course, be given : but it was the gener.dly accepted opinion that seeing that the funds provided had been so generally applied to pur- poses of technical instruction Parliament was not at all likely to make iny alterations' with regard either to the source of the funds or their mode of application, without making other financial provisions for enabling local authorities to carry on the work undertaken on the faith of receiving the grants. And with regard to the third observation, Mr. Oppenheim.was assured that there was no likelihood of the C.C. making any alteration in ' the mode of distribution of the funds so long as the lOcal authorities apply the same efficiently and well for the .purposes of the Act. There was every reason, therefore, for assuming that an annual grant in aid of technical education may be relied upon. A 2 to the amount of such grant, it would, of course, depend upon circum- stances ; but he was informed that it was not likely at any time to be . much less than the amount at present proposed to be awarded' (£480). The only condition attaching to the grant at present was that the County Council would require to be satisfied that the money was being properly expended, and with that object an account pf the expenditure would have to be furnished to and audited by the auditor under the Local Govern- ment Act, 1888. It should be observed, however, that the County Council do .not rep,:ard favourably the ex- penditure of any pare of the present grant in buildings, but prefer that it should be principally expended in teaching. With regard to the acquisition of land and the erection of buildings he (the clerk) did not find any express power under the technical Instruc- tion Act to local authorities (as in the Libraries Act) to hold land and erect buildings, although powers to borrow, are contained in the Act and under other circumstances this might have given rise to a little complication, in the event of the Committee recommending the erection of schools and the Board determining to adopt such recom- mendation ; but any such difficulties would, he thought be remOved when the district received a grant of a chaxter of incorporation. The Department of Science and Art had powers to make grants towards buildings for Science and Art schools, but there was reason to fear that such grants would shortly be suspended. As an application under this head would have to be made before November Ist, it would be seen, in the event of any serious determination to build b.ling entertained that some provisional communication upon the subject should be entered into with the department. The County Council are also prepared to make grants in aid of acquiring suitable premises for the purposes of technical instruction. Whether they would consider the case of Widnes Local Board a proper one or not is not clear, but inasmuch as the County Council are about to deal with a further fund of £17,000, portion of the " local taxation duties" for the financial year ending 31st March, 1891, he recommended that an application be made for a grant towards a building and this applica- tion should be in the hands of the Council before Mon- day next. Of course it was a condition precedent to sanction be given that this Committee first decide as to whether the erection of schools should be recom- mended or not. In the event of the erection of schools the money required for interest and sinking fund would in the first place have to be provided out of the local rates, the County Council grant being reserved for teaching and other cognate purposes. He was informed by Mr. Lloyd Jones that the only question open with regard to the grant to Widnes district was the matter of an appli cation by the governors of Farnworth Grammar School, for a grant of £BO., out of the total sum sum awarded to Widnes. The proposal of the governors was to establish classes in theoretical chemistry, practical chemistry, magnetism and electricity, and mathematics. It cer- tainly seemed undesirable to have two sets of classes in Widnes, and he had reason to believe that whatever view the Local Board took upon the subject, the same would receive the support of the County Council. A suggestion was made by Mr. Lloyd Evans that the Wid- nes Technical Instruction Committes should undertake to establish such of the above classes as are non-existent, and that the masters of the Farnworth Grammer School or one of them might he employed as teachers of such classes and this suggestion is a valuable one. He should also like to add that many of the pupils attending the Farnworth Grammar School, are now resident in Wid- nes, their claims would therefore appear to be on the rural sanitary authorities within whose jurisdiction they live and not on this authority. In conclusion he pointed out that all applications to the Science and Art Department for grants towards apparatus, Sm., would be suspended at the end of this year. If buildings- were erected considerable fittings would be required and it might be desirable to endeavour to obtain a provisional grant before the time expired al-

though it was not at all certain that an application for a grant of such a character would be entertained.—After considering this report the Conimittee have passed a reso- lution with respect to the claim-of the Farnworth Gram- mar School, in which they declare that it is undesirable that two authorities for providing technical education should be established in the district or that any funds allotted to the district should.be directed from the Local Board, but that the claim of the governors to special arrangements for teaching shouicrbe fully recognised by the Local Board in any complete Scheme they may adopt. This decision has been communicated to the County Council, together with a formal request for a special grant towards building technical schools. In the meantime Messrs, Gossage, Deacon, Carey, Midvi7ood, and .Dr. O'Keeffe have • been appointed to formulate a scheme of technical education for the distric:, to visit ex- isting technical schools, with a view to ascertaining what was being done by other authorities, and also to select a' suitable site or sites for the erection of Technical Schools for the consideration committee. Steps are being at once taken for teaching the subjects not already arranged for and the sub-committee are empowered te hire for-the purpose the necessary temporary rooms.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The Runcorn Volunteer Baud are making a strenuous effort to raise funds to purchase a set of now instruments which I need hardly state are not up to the present requirements. The large sum of .£3OO is necessary to carry out their intention. An appeal is being made to the public for help, and in return the band promise to place their services at the disposal of the townspeople on occasions when music is wanted. In the past the band have afforded much pleasure to thousands,and I hope their appeal ' will meet with a ready response. Mr. Jas. Woods, the bandmaster, will be glad to receive donations, however great or small.

After eleven years of faithful service to the rate- payers of Widnes,Dr. O'Keeffe has resigned his seat on the Local Board with the avowed purpose of be- coming a candidate for the vacant post of Medical Officer of Health. His voice was full of tears as he avowed his intention, and he quite broke down as he handed his written resignation to the Chairman. The severing of so long and so pleasant a connec- tion was without doubt a severe wrench to the worthy doctor's feelings, and Mr. Gossage remarked that, but for the purpose of the resignation, the Board would unanimously have asked him as an old and useful and valuable member to reconsider his decision. The thanks of the Board were due to him for industry and through efficiency he had dis- played' as a member of the Board. Dr. O'Keeffe, after expressing his thanks for their kind expres- sions, left the arena in which he had played a Con- spicuous and successful part for so long a period.

Speakman, of Runcorn, has invented a new cartridge, to which has been given the name of " Speakman's Safety Cartridge." It is claimed that when this cartridge is tired there is absolutel no claim, and on Saturday last a series of exhaus- tive experiments were made at the Bedford Leigh Collieries of Messrs. John Speakman and Sons. In, every instance the result was highly satisfactory, , and the cartridge proved everything that was claimed for it. A large number of gentlemen in- terested in mining were present, and expressed un- animous approval.

Now that the local authorities of Widnes and Runcorn have combined with the object of securing a Vehicular Bridge across the Mersey there are more hopes of the scheme being carried out. That the bridge would be an immense boon to the two towns and to the surrounding neighbourhood is self evident, but the expense of the undertaking will oause the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire to pause before they embark upon the Scheme. Eloquent and skilful advocacy may, how- ' ever, do much and I hope that success will be achieved.

The Committee of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners appointed to consider the question of deep docks, have had the matter under discussion, and tbe outcome is that a deputation will shortly wait upon the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and urge upon thorn to provide the required acco- modation for sips ot large tonnage. The subject is of extreme importance to the town,rind Mr.Light- born is deserving of the thanks of tlle. ratepayer:: for his action in the matter,*

Although nothing has been heard Of the Techni- cal Education Scheme of the Commissioners for some time, the tsubject has not been lost.sight of. A few days ago a deputation visited Stockport, Hyde, and Stalybridge to ascertain the experience of the p;overithng. bldies of these towns in carrying out technical cAucation. The deputation obtained much Taluable infitmation, and it is probable that the outcome will be a practical scheme for providing a technical school.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., is announced to address his Runcorn constituents in the Public Hall on Tuesday evening next. Speeches will also be made by Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., and Mr. T. E. Ellis, kLP. Mr. W. Ockleston will preside.

At Runcorn Free Library Reading-room the other day, the current number of the" Magazine of Art" mtilated by the principal engraving being cut out. The despicable thief, whoever he may be, has laid himself open to a heavy penalty, and Mr. Jones, the librarian, asks for the co-operation of the frequen- ters of the reading-room in bringing the present offender to justice and in preventing such an occurrence in future.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday. Rev. Dr. Gastaldi presided and there were present Messrs. W. Whittaker, W. Mel- lor, W. Little, T. Handley, S. Taylor, and W. P. S. alkeld (cleric). The Secretary reported that the Interments for six months to September 25th were 236, corresponding period last year 234 ; increase 2. The fees received during the same period amounted to £209 is.; last year to £207 2s. Bd. ; increase £llBs. 4d. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £5 25. 4d.. and also interest falling due amounting to £23 Bs. The Secretary also reported that the roof of the chapel had been darAaged by the storm and permitted water to come through. The notice board had also been blown down, and would be of no further use. It had however been fixed for 30 years. He was instructed to have the necessary re- pairs executed.
THE DITTON WOUNDING CASE

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Murray, a young woman of Ditton Wood, was charged on remand with doing grievous bodily harm to Michael Murray, her cousin, on the 3rd inst., by striking him on the head with a poker.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the defendant, and said the whole affair was a family quttrrel, and plaintiff did not STih to prosecute, as they were all as bad asbne anotner. Defendant's mother was willing to compensate plaintiff for the loss of his week' g wages.—Michael Murray, the plaintiff, was called and stated that he did not wish to press the case as it was simply a family row. —The Bench : Is the plaintiff out of danger now '1 —Dr. O'Keeffe : Yes, he. is now. There were three wounds on the head, two of which penetrated to the bone, and were of a serious nature, but tie considered that there was no danger at present.—Mr. Knowles :It has evidently been a family brawl.—Mr. Holbrook: How many brawls end in murder P—Mr. Knowles : It has not done so in this case.—Superintendent Noblett said he was willing to leave the case in their Worships' hands.—The Chairman said they would let it pass this time, but still they had no right to use pokers in a family brawl.—Prisoner was then discharged.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOA.RD.

A special meeting of the Runcorn School Board was held in the Boardroom, on Tuesday evening. The members present were Dr. McDougall (in the chair), Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, and the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. The accounts and balance sheet for the year ending September 29th, were submitted. The year i began With a balance of £275 55., in the treasurer's hands, and the receipts were as follows :—Government grants £576 17s. 2d.- from overseers, £950; school fees, £331 7s. Bd. ; books, &c., sold to children, £l9 10s. 83. ; and sundries, £5 4s. 63. ; payments, administrative ex- penses,.£3s7 is. 11d. ; maintenance of schools, £1,092 ss. 9d. ; loan account, £322 35. 83. ; and industrial schools, £l3 7s. 11d. The balance on hand was £373 ss. 93., being £9B more than at the commencement of the year. Deducting the £9B from the amount drawn from rates leaves £852 from that source, equal to not quite 43. in the pound. The amount due to the Public Works Loan Commissioners is r'24,456 15s. 11d. A pre- cept on the overseers was signed for £5OO 'to meet the expenses of the Board for the ensuing half year.—T his waathe whole of the business.
Mr. Frederick Smith, son of the late Mr. W. H. Smith, on Wednesday gave formal intimation to the Strand Central Conservative Association of his intention to stand fotthe divisson.

div.head: WARRINGION LIBERAL BAZAAR.
div.p: WARRINGION LIBERAL BAZAAR.

CONCERT AT THE PUBLIC BALL. On Saturday evening a concert was given before a numerous audience in the Public Hall, in connec- tion with the Liberal bazaar which had just closed in that building. Mr. Thos. Morris, F.G.S.,occupied the chair, and said after the vigorous efforts which had been put forth by the party that week, it would be seen that Liberalism was living, and its oppo- nents might possibly die first. (Hear, hear.) Still, he was bold enough to say that he hoped that so long as Liberalism lived in Warrington, Conserva- tism would live also. It would never do for the politics of the town to be all on one side, because if one side were to die he dared prophesy that in two weeks afterwards the other would tollow suit— (hear, hear, and laughter)—and then, of what use would Warrington be in the political world? None; it would be to all intent and purpose dead, so far as politics were concerned. Ilehoped that the, suc- cess which the Bazaar Committee had experienced. that week augured well for the future of local Liberalism, which would never die so long as War- rington lived. (Applause.)—The Warrington Christy Minstrel Troupe then gave one of their pleasurable entertainments, which was productive of great satisfaction to the audience, who were most fre- quent and enthusiastic in their applause. A few of the jokes were "chestnuts," but all were well received, and a conundrum which was in one sense pre-eminently that of the evening—" What is the difference between the Liberal Club this Satur- day and last Saturday ?" the answer to which was "About £1,200" was mpst acceptable both for its point, and the testimony it furnished ef the favourable financial condition of the Liberal cause. The audience was thus put in all the better humour for the enjoyment of the miscellaneous concert which followed that of the burnt- cork Ethopians. Miss B. Collins obtained a vociferous encore for her singing, her rendering of "The White Squall" being most realistic and happy. Mr. Frank Fallon was a great success in his song in character of "The Dutchman" and his clog dance, receiving a hearty encore for the former. Sergeant Riches was heartily and deservedly encored for a finely executed clarionet solo, Mr. Bruce Scott met with a very good reception, giving much satisfaction by his humourous presentment of imaginary and somewhat free renderings of "The Charge of the Light Brigade" as given by supposititious elocu- tionists of various nationalities, and by an effeminate curate. Mr. Charles Osborne gave a violin solo, and as an encore a "grand imitation of the bagpipes. Messrs. W. Cook and Paton acted as pianists during the even- ing.

THE CONSERVATIVES AND THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON.

A meeting of the Council of the Conservative Association was held on Monday evening, at the Old Club, 11, ..kcademy•street, Mr, Robert Pierpoint, J.P., in the chair, " to consider in accordance with Association Rule 10, the names of candidates to be submitted to the Council by the Ward Committees, anA other important business." The " other import-, ant business,7::_Tliided the consideration of the question of the Parliameniat'Y irerif6:_"26iiftitidn of thct borough. There was a large attendance, whieir included Mr. John White, J.P., Alderman Sutton, ' J.P., Alderman Wright, J.P., Alderman Greenall, J.P., and Councillors Muir, Greening,llepherd, Jas. Fairclough, R. T. Fairclough, William Bolton. and Messrs. John Fairclough, J.P., Alfred Woods, James Smethurst, J. V. Taylor, John Taylor, Geo. Pilling, John Lee, John Hartley, H. W. Cookson, Henry Houghton, A. Brimelow, G. L. Brimelovv, C. R. Ad- amson, and John Hampson (registration agent.) It was decided on the motion of Mr. White,seconded by Mr. Alderman SuttOon, that a deputation be ap- pointed to wait upon Sir Gilbert Greenall, bart., M.P., to ask him to contest the borough again at the next general election. The deputation appointed to wait upon Sir Gilbert consisted of the following gentlemen :—Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Major Nichol- son, Mr. James Smethurst, Alderman. Sutton, Alder- man Wright, Mr. John Roberts, Mr. Geo. Jolley, Mr. Alfred Woods and Mr. Robert Heaton. On Wednesday afternoon the deputation waited upon Sir Gilbert Greenall, at Walton Hall, to ask him on behalf of the party to again- contest the borough at the next general election. Mr. Pierpoint assured the baronet that the expressions of feeling towards him were not only friendly. but affectioß- ate. He was still held in great esteem by the party, who would give him their support if his health en- abled him to again become their candidate. Each member of the deputation spoke in a similar strain, and Sir Gilbert said he would take time to consider his decision and commnnicate with the deputation.

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.

At the Griffin Inn, Peasley Cross, St. Helens, on Thursday,Mr.Brighouse held an inquest on the body of George Tucker, aged 29 years, a sheet glass blower at Messrs. Pilkington's Glass Works, who committed suicide on Tuesday night by drinking a quantity of carbolic acid. Chief Constable Wood watched the proceedings on behalf of the police.—Mar- gery Tucker, the widow, stated that she and deceased had lived separately for two years, but three weeks since he came back to her at her mother's. He had been drinking since Sunday. He had some drink, and was very strange and ill all day on Tuesday. He said queer things and walked up and down the house with a knife in one pocket and a fork in the other. He asked for threepence for a glass of whisky, and she found afterwards that instead of sending for the whisky he had sent her little brother for carbolic acid. As soon as the boy told her she hurried upstairs, and asked her husband if he had got the whisky, and he said" Yes." She said to him If you don't give me that bottle I will fetch Pcilice-constable Littler." He refused to give her the bottle, and she went half way downstairs for the purpose of sending for the officer. On returning to the bedroom she found he had drunk the contents. He was snoring very heavily, and there was a stain of acid on his shirt breast. Dr. Jackson was sent for, but deceased died shortly afterwards. In answer to the coroner, witness said her husband made good wages, but he had been stopped a sovereign for losing two days' work, and that seemed to upset him. On Monday he said he had been told by his mate that he had been "sacked" for neglect of work. Further evidence in corroboration was given, and the jury returned a verdict that the deceased committed suicide while tempoiarily insane, and expressed the opinion that the fines at Messrs. Pilkington's works were too haevy. The coroner soid it was very seldom he disagreed with the finding of a jury, but he did not see how they could add such an expression of opinion. If a man did not like his service he could leave. Messrs. Pilkington had a large amount of capitaF involved in their works, and he (the coroner) did not see what the jury had to do with the regulations.
The body of a woman has been found in a brook at Swinton, bearing shocking marks of violence. The police are making inquiries on the assumption that she has been murdered. _

Reports from Shanghai via Singapore, are to the effect that foreign ministers have broken off negotiations in connection with the recent outrages, and have announ- ced that their Governments must act.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

CHARGE OF AGGRAVATED ASSAULT ON A CHILD. James Toft, married man, aged 59, provision dealer, Naylor-st., was charged before the Warrington borough magistrates on Tuesday morniu„,c,' with committing on °Monday night, an aggravated assault on Harriet Carney, aged 7 years, daughter of John Carney, of Naylor-st. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the defence.—The child and her mother gave evidence,and P.C. 31 deposed to apprehending him and to his denying the charge.— Inspector Spinks also gave evidence ,—Dr. Peacocke hav- ing given testimony, which was favourable to the de- fendant the Bench considered the case in private for a short time, and then fined the defendant £5 and costs.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST I BUTCHER. On Monday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named Watts, a labourer,made application to the magistrates for a warrant for the apprehension of a Warrington butcher, whom he named, under the follow- ing circumstances. He stated that he and a man named John Laing went to the butcher's on Saturday night for some meat, and they had some words about the weight, when suddenly the butcher knocked him down, and stabbed him in the head with a knife, and he had to be taken to the Infirmary or somewhere, to have his head dressed. Witness exhibited a wound in his head to the magistrates. He said he was perfectly sober, P.S. Monaghan said he saw the applicant and his brother shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday night, both drunk, and very excited. He saw the former's.head was bleeding, and asked him the cause, and after some time he said he had been stabbed. P.C. Robinson took him to the Infirmary, and he (Robinson) afterwards saw the butcher, who gave a very different account of the matter from that given by the applicant. He said the man came into tbe shop and would neither pay for meat nor leave it alone, and struck one of his assistants. He knocked his head against a sharp point in the wall, but was not stabbed. The doctor said the wound might have been caused by a fall. Several witnesses could prove that the butcher had noknife in his hand.—Alder- man Sutton said there was a report made by P.C. Hol- lingsworth on the matter, and it was very different from the statement made by the applicant. The Bench declined to accede to his application, but gave him to understand that he would be at liberty to pay for a summons if he chose ; and the case could be heard on Friday.

div.head: RIOT IN EDELESTEN'S YARD.
div.p: A RIOT IN EDELESTEN'S YARD.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning.Thos. Bridge, Mary Bridge (his wife), John Riley, Ann Riley (his wife), and John Barton, were charged with fighting in Edelesten's Yard, off Winwick-st., on Saturday night, the 3rd inst. P.C. Smith, deposed that on that night he was on duty in Winwick-st., when he was informed that there was a general row going on in Edelesten's Yard. Ile went there and found John Riley lying on the ground with his forehead badly cut, and a large crowd around him. Witness assisted him up and got some water and washed his head and sent him to the Infirmary.He after- wards saw the Bridges who seemed to have been knocked about the head, Mrs. Bridge having a cut on the arm. He saw the Rileys also and Barton. Mrs. Riley was marked, and Barton had a cut across the nose—(laughter) and there seemed to have been, a general row. The man Bridge said Riley had been abusing his wife, and he came out with a poker and struck hm on the head,and Mrs. Bridge complained that Riley's wife had stabbed her, and Bridge had kicked the door in. (Renewed laugh- ter:)He and another constable who was with him cameto the conclusion that there were six of one and half a dozen of the other, and reported the lot of them.—P.C. Bar- nett corroborated.—Ann Riley said Mary Bridge charged her with caking a tub of hers, and cited some foul langu- age as used by her.—Thos. Bridge said John Riley was beating Mrs. Bridge and had her on the "floor." He came out of the house "the same as he was wild." Recriminations were exchanged all round amongst the defendants, amidst some laughter from those in court, which was renewed on the Mayor remarking" Like Donnybrook fair, I think."—Alderman Sutton (to the defendants) : Are you satisfied with the damage you have done each other P—John Riley, (whose held was plastered): I have bad too much of it. (Laughter.)— Tide defendants were bound over in their own recognis- ances of £5 each and a surety of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, in default 14 days in jail each.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT,

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair) Councillor Voisey, and Mr. Geddes. DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Catherine Heyes and Ellen Gibbon, charged with disorderly conduct in Bridge- street, on the previous night, were discharged on promising to leave the town. The facts of the case were stated by P.C.'s David Jones and Clough. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb) and Aldermen Sutton, Harrison, and Wright. Daum' AND DISORDERLY .—Ellen Jennion, in Dial-st., on Saturday night, 10s. and costs.—Edward Murphey, in Mersey-st., the same night, ss.—Thomas Jacobs and Mary Ann Sweeney, in Irlam-st.' that night, ss. each.— Ridley Butler was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Fennell-st., on Saturday night, and refusing to quit the Old Crow Inn, 103. and costs.—William Dooley, drunk and disorCerly in Wilderspool-road at 1.30 a.m. on Sunday, had been extraordinarily vio- lent. The' prisoner was bruised considerably, and in reply to the Mayor, said this had been done by "some Oldham chaps." 10s. and.costs.—Mary Turner, who had a black eye, in Knutsford-road at 1.25 a.m. on Sunday, and had been found lying on the footpath.—ln answer to the Mayor she said "I have been teetotal ever since."— The Mayor : Since Saturday! (Laughter.)—P.S. Chant- ler said her husband said it was all women neighbours who drove her to drink. On her promising to remain a teetotaller, she was let off with payment of costs, 3s. 6d. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A CART.—Joseph Lawienson, market gardener, Old Road, Latchford, drunk in charge of a horse and cart, in Bridge-st., on the 3rd inst., was fined ss. ASSAULTING A CONSTABLE .—Thomas Casey was charged with assaulting P.C. Delahaye at a lodging-house in Academy-st. The defendant's thres brothers had come from Oldham and ho had taken them to the lodging- house to fight some men there. Witness found the fight- ing going on, and on his interfering the prisoner struck him in the face, and another man got him by the legs and pulled him down. 10s. and costs. ASSAULTING HIS MornEß.—William Mulligan, aged 21, of 2 Foundry-st., was charged with assaulting his mother, Bridget Mulligan, on the Sth inst. She said he was vexed because there was nothing to eat, and he would not work to earn it. He was sent to jail for a month with card labour. _

KEEPING HORSES AND CARTS STANDING.—Henry greengrocer, Stamford-st., and William Broadhurst, greengrocer, 122, Winwick-road, for allowing their horses and carts to stand longer than necessary in the Market-place on the 3rd inst., were each fined ss. UNSEEMLY LANGUAGE.—Elizabeth Harper, wife of William Harper, 67 Mersey-st., was charged with using unseemly language in that street, on the 3rd inst. Her defence was that her husband told a woman who came to his house she could stop all night. Witness then left the house saying if the woman stopped she herself would not, and went out; and she afterwards used the langu- age complained of because of the conduct of the woman and her husband in her absence. 2s. 6d. and costs. DISCHARGING FIREWORKS—Thomas Holcroft, a boy, on of John Holcroft, 30 Pinner's Brow, was charged

with discharging fireworks in Pinner's Brow' on the 3rd inst.—The Mayor pointed out the danger of frightening horses and causing loss of life through the explosion of fireworks in the streets. The defendant was fined Is. TIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), Alderman
Greenall and Mr. E. J. Guest.

DEturac AND DISORDBRLY.—James Bonner. Bridge-st., on Monday night, ss. and costs.—Michael Dow, in St. James's-street, the same night, 10s. and costs.—. Joseph Warburton was charged with not having appeared to a summons for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick- street on the 26th of June, also with assaulting Richard Boscovr. Boscow did not appear to proceed with his charge, but tor being drunk and disorderly the defendant was fined ss. and costs.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF A DAUGHTER.—WiIIiam Mee, was charged with non-maintenance of his daughter, and was ordered to contribute 7s. 6d. per week. SCHOOL PROSECITIONS.—EIizabeth Bate, 1 Cobden- street, had an order made against her for her boy ta be sent to the training ship Clio. John Bennett. forgeman, Pierpoint-street, had a similar order made against him.— Patrick Carey, labourer, at Dallam Forge, of Dolman's- lane, was summoned, and his wife', who appeared said the schoolmaster sent the boy home because he had'nt boots. ss. including costs.—Frederick Cooper, joiner, Orford-Lane, is. and costs.—William Crank, Aikin- street, Es. 6d.—George Dunbobbin, canal man, Crossley-street, ss.—John Fairbrother, wiredrawer, Hamilton-street, is. —William Fitton. forgeman, Catherine-street, was summoned. While his case was being heard the birch rod was produced for the boy's intimidation, and lay on the table during the remainder of the business. The Chief Constable thought the boy had better be taken down and birched.—Fined Is.—John Gorton, labourer, Aikin-street, ss.—Thomas Moody, forgeman, Pierpoint- street, ss.—James Pemberton, forgeman, Bank Quay, Zs. 6d. A STREET NIIISANCE.—WiIIiam Ward was charged by Mr. Norman, sanitary inspector, with allowing on the 7th inst., tan refuse to run from a cart in Fennell-st. and Mersey-st., and John H. Fleming, junior, was charged with being the owner of the cart.—The defendants said there was nothing but lime waterin the cart—Mr.Norman said this was the 4th appearance of Fleming, and the Corporation had supplied Mr. Fleming with an iron cart, which if kept in repair would obviate the nuisance.— Mr. Fleming said the lime water ate through the bottom of an iron cart--A tanner employed by Mr. Fleming said the refuse was merely lime water.—Mr. Fleming said it was nothing but spite that he was brought up for.—Noth• ing could prevent the lime water running out.—Mr. Norman denied this, and said he had repeatedly warned him.—Mr. Fleming: Are'nt you ashamed of yourself to bring such paltry cases as this? How is it you don't bring other people up who let their lime water run our? There are bucketsful in the street and nothing is done.— Mr. Norman: You can report me to the Sanitary Com- mittee, then, if there are such cases.—Mr. Norman said the Corporation had supplied Fleming with the iron cart. —Mr. Fleming said it had cost him £lO to repair it, as the lime water ate through it.—The Chairman said Mr. Fleming was quite wrong in supposing there was any spite in the case.—Ward was dismissed on payment of costs, and Fleming lined 55. and costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman .Holmes (in the chair),

and Mr. J. Fairclough. WIFB ASSAIILT.—Wm. Finch, 21, Stevenson-st. was charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife, Finch, on the 4th of April. He was bound over in two sureties of £lO each and hi, own recognisances of £lO, to keep the peace for six months; in default a month's imprisonment. DRUNIC.—James Joy, drunk in Wilderspool-road that morning, was fined ss. including costs. MllRSDAL—Before_Captain. Ridgway and Councillor

James Fairclough. - DRUNKENNESS.—Margaret McLoughlin for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, the previous evening, was fined ss. and Costs. FIIIDIT.—Before Alderman Harrison, Dr. Gornall, and

Alderman Wright. DRUNICENNIM.—Jane Edmunds, for being drunk and disorderly,in Winwick-st., on the previous day,was fined 2s. 6d. CIiIIBLTY TO Hossas.—Thomas Wilson was charged with ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, in Buttermarket-street, and fined 10s. in- cluding costs.—Peter Frith, of Lower Whitley, was similarly charged, and was fined 103. and costs.—John Prescot, was charged with working a horse In an unfit state, and James Watson, of Ashton, was charged with having allowed the same to be worked and each was ordered to pay costs.—Jos. Rig by, of Sot- ton,St. Helens,for a like offence was fined ss. and costs. —Thos. Rowley, cab proprietor, linutsford-road, was fined £1 and costs, 16s. 6d., for working a horse which was in an unfit condition.

MownAT.—Becore Mr. A. Thomas and Major nazis- hurst.

MISCELLANEOUS.—EIizabeth Barker, Annie Collins, and Margaret Hancock were each convicted of obstructing the footpath in Church-st., on Sunday the 27th Septem- ber, and a fine of 53. including costs was inflicted. Hancock was also fined 103. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—John Burke (39th appearance) was frned 10s. and costs for a like offence.—Reuben Wilson was summoned for riding through Sutton on a cart with- out reins and he was fined ss. and costs 16s. For having his dog at large, Wilson was fined 6d. and costs 9s. 6d.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
THIIRSDAY.-11e-fo-ie-ir. _H. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. T. S.
Timmins.

DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Thos. Devine, Ellen Lowe, Patrick Redmond, Nora Redmond, and John Byrne. Mary Tar- pey was fined 7s. 6d. and costs. BREACHES OP THB PEACE.—Matilda Shaw, Elizabeth- st., and Patrick Behar,Margaret-st., were bound over to keep the peace for three months, for creating a distur- bance in the street.

REFUSING TO QUIT.—A fine of 103. and costs was im- posed upon Jas. Duffey, of Mary-st., for refusing to quit the Runcorn Vaults,when requested by the landlord. The defendant was creating a disturbance in the bar. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION.—Thos. Murphy, of Gossage- st., was fined 2s. ed. and costs for obstructing the foot- path in Widnes-road, on the 7th inst. ROBBING A PAWNBROKER.—Catherine Hughes, of Pitt- st., pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of boots from H. Lyred's pawnshop, Waterloo-road, on Tuesday. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed. CHIMNEY ON FlR.—John Simpson,Bank-st.,was fined is. and costs.
EDUCATION ACT.—Three persons were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of 6d. and costs was imposed.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. H._Ga.skell jun., and Lieut.-Col.
Gaskell.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon John Bradley, Adlington ; John Higgins, Cock-st. ; Peter Molloy, Cromwell-st. : Wm. Philips, Litherland ; and John Melia Cronton, Joseph Killala, no fixed abode, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs.—Mary Jane Riley of no residence made her 15th appearance and was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. TEE ALLEGED HOUSEBRBAKING.—James Ryan, no fixed abode, was again brought up charged with having on the 2nd inst. burglariously entered the dwelling house of Daniel Crawley; and stolen articles worth 6s. On the application of Superintendent Ik!obblett the prisoner was again remanded in order that his cares: might be traced. Tax WORST OF A BARGAIN.—Wipiam Goulding, 43, Moon-st., was charged with assaulting Michael Carroll, on Sunday morning.—Prosecutor stated that he was coming from his work on Sunday morning, and when passing prisoner's house, he came out, and, without any provocation, caught him by the neck and knocked hiat down, and whilst on the ground kicked him near the eye. When prisoner allowed him to get up, he went home, but returned again and broke prisoner's window and door.—Mr. Poole, who appeared for Goulding, said that the row had evidently been sorted by Carroll, and there seemed to be an old bother between the men, and they were both to blame, but unfortunately Carroll seemed to have got the worst of the bargain.—A fine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days in default, was imposed. CAUGHT RED HANDED.—Catherine Matthews, of Marsh-st., was charged on remand with having on the 7th inst., stolen a shirt worth is. 6d., the property of Bridget Weir, from a clothes line. The prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Wood with the shirt in her posses- sion. She behaved in a very excited and noisy fashion in court, and when committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial she descended below singing and shouting. The prisoner is a character well-known to the police.

div.head: GENERAL BOULANGER'S WILL.
div.p: GENERAL BOULANGER'S WILL.

PARIS TtrESDAY.-It is announced that the daughters of the late General Boulanger intend to contest certain clauses of their deceased father's will. They will make four claims against it. The statement has excited some sensation, and the progress of the suit will be followed hem with great interest.

div.p: THE RUSSIAN FAMINE.
THIRTY-TWO MILLIONS IN DISTRESS.

A Vienna telegram says advices from St. Petersburg state that the number of distressed persons appealing to the Government amounts to 32,000,000. The Gov- ernment require at least 320,000,000 roubles to supply the famished peasants and others with rye.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 17, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 17, 1891.

but the ball was as rapidly sent back to the further end of the field. Hampson, by a dashing bit of play, made matters more even, and although Hamlett twice over re- lieved his lines very finely, the hoinesters would not be denied, and thoroughly tested the defence of the War- ringtonians. The Oldham men certainly had hard lines, but after Daniels had cleverly relieved, Bailey, Davies, Knowles, and Hampson took the ball from the danger- ous proximity to the goal. Directly afterwards Hamlett, when surrounded, grandly punted to midfield, and thn ball being mulled, a foothold was obtained at the home "25," where Lally secured possession, and by one of his inimitable runs got a splendid try under the post. This place, like the others failed, and Warrington, who had shown greatly improved formed, retired winners by 0-4-2 to nil. STOCKTON HEATH V. EARLESTOWN "A" TEAM.—On Saturday Stockton Heath was visited by the Earlestown "A " team. The visitors commenced the game, Lawless returning into touch. After the throw-out,the homesters began to press, Berry scoring at the corner flag. On the drop-out the game was very loose, but the visitors were over-matched at all points, scarcely reaching the half- way flag. At half-time the home team were leading by 2 goals, 2 tries, and one minor to the good. In the second portion of the game the visitors continued to play loose! which made the game pleasant, but owing to the superi- ority of the homosters the game was very one-sided. On the call of time the home team easily ran out victors by 4 goals, 3 tries, 1 minor to mil, Broady being credited with 3 tries, Higham 2, and Berry and Hallows 1 each.

WIDNES v. MossLay.-LPlayed at Widnes, on Saturday, before 8,000 spectators. A lot of rain had fallen during the morning, and consequently the ground was in a very sodden condition. Widnes were without Craig, whose placed was filled by Taylor. Brennan kicked off for Widnes. He also met the return, and the result was that Holmes forced a touch-down. Last Saturday's reverse appeared to have hada beneficial effect on Widnes, their combination being greatly improved. Mossley played a good defence game, and Widnes had to return without scoring. A free kick to.the visitors gained them little ground, the Widnes captain getting in a huge punt. Farmer followed up well,and play ranged dangerously near the Mossley line. Drummond made his mark in a good position, but Taylor's kick was charged down. A free kick was awarded to Widnes opposite the goal, Taylor just missing the desired mark. Mossley afterwards gave Widnes defence a lively time of it, but Hartles proved equal to the occasion, and Drummond .transferred play to the other end, where the Widnes forwards delighted their supporters with their fine passing, but without re- sult. At half-time neither side had scored. Final result —Widnes two points, Mossley two points. The Widnes team was composed of the following :—Full back, J. Taylor; three-quarters, H. Peters, D. Brennan, J. G. Craig ; half-bai,ks, J. Drummond and H. Barber; for- wards, G. Hewitt, E. Gordon, J. Whelan, J. Johnson, E. Emery, J. Holmes, A. Lyons, H. Farmer, and J. Hard- man.
