div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RANGERS V. RED ROCS (WIGAN).—The Rangers journeyed to Wigan to play off the return fix- ture with the above club, and returned home victors by lgoal. 5 minors, to 1 try. C. Holt dropped the goal from full baak, which gave the Rangers the victory. The game was sturdily contested, but the visitors man- aged to hold the upper hand .to the finish, and won as stated above.

ST. HELENS RECREATION A TRAM V. RUNCORN A Taus. —This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday. The home team kicked off, and Sidler received. A scrimm- age ensued. Bolton made a nice run, but was tackled at half flag. Sidler made his mark, but the referee ordered a scrimmage, and from this Runcorn carried the play tothe Recs.' line, a minor being kicked, and another following from the same means. An off-side try was obtained by Runcorn, the referee having previously blown his whistle. Half-time arriving, Runcorn were leading by 1 try to nil. Final result—Recreation A 2 tries, Runcorn A 1 try. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND v. BOWDON RANGERS IST. —Played at Warrington on Saturday. The visitors ar- rived late, and a game of two twenties was played. The home team kicked off, and at once pressed their oppon- ents on the line, where for some time the game was hotly contested, but from some loose play A. Deakin got possession and ran In a good try. Upon the drop-out Savage, Hall, Hinchcliffe, and Bradbury played up pro- minently for the homesters, and from a combined rush the last-named player placed a second try to his side's account, the kick at goal failing. After the usual inter- val, Bowdon played up better, and after several futile attacks upon the Warrington line, Marriott got hold in his own half, and scored, no goal resulting. Fleming scored the third try for the homesters, but the goal kick was again at fault. From this point Bowdon was out- played, and the home team eventually ran out winters by 3 tries, ‘2 minors, to 1 try.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.

More than ordinary interest was centred in the first meeting of the above clubs this season, which took place on Saturday at Wildarspool. The fine form displayed by each organization has been the talk of all enthusiasts In the county, and Oldham's latest victory over Brough- ton Rangers by the large score of six goals and a try served to prove that Warrington would have all their work cut out to maintain their unbeaten certificate. Two special trains were run from the town of Spindledom, and the gate was estimated at between five and six thous- and. Oldham had their full strength, but Boscow and Lawless were absent from the home combination.

Ashton kicked off and the usual exchanges having been witnessed, the visiting forwards had the better of the initial scrimmages, Donohue on one occasion saving in smart style. J. T. Bate got clear, but the slippery state of the oval prevented a good chance, and Nevins responding to a kick by Hurst, play was taken to the Oldham quarters. The Oldham forwards packed the better and changed the venue, wilful offside play allow- ing Turner to demonstrate his kicking powers. The kick at goal was short and McCutcheon with a short zig-zag run at last faced .Tolley, and preferring to kick the Warringtonian charged it down, the homesters almost scoring. Hurst and McCutcheon cleverly ran the oval out, and Webster was applauded for a fine tackle. Bate next showed up with a short run and being aided by short passing by Randles, Holmes, and Berry, Oldham had now to act solely on the defensive. Warrington were now playing much the stronger game of the two, their forwards displaying better combination than at the opening. Gwynn was foiled by Barnes in an effort to clear, but Pennington was on the alert and saved in grand style with a huge kick. Webster promptly responded, and Barnes and Ashton were pro- minent in some loose play, which terminated in Webster kicking and placing his team on side. Jolley ran in only to fine the point over-ruled. This slice of luck for Old- ham evidently encouraged them, and from a scrim- mage formed the oval was worked to Sampson, the ball being returned. A fine display of passing by Warrington forwards found the ball bobbing on the Oldham line,and Hurst in endeavouring to clear infringed the rule and was held under the posts. The two Bates were within an ace of scoring, and although Oldham relieved slightly, Ashton, a moment later had hard lines in not having a major point allowed. Combination by the Oldham men gave them a footing inside the Warrington quarters, but their stay was but short, and rushes by Buckley, Turner, and Jolley were concluded by.Gwynn making his mark. Passing by the home forwards started by Donohue roused the enthusiasm, and another exhi- bition by the two Bates, Barnes, and Evans found the latter dropping at goal, Pennington saying. McCutcheon showed up on the drop out, but Warrington were not to be denied, and a well-meant rush was concluded by J. T. Bate passing to Jolley for the latter to complete an excellent try, Barnes having little difficulty in plac- ing a goal. this reverse was followed by Oldham attacking ma the re-start, and barely had the game been recommenced before Gwynn, with a lucky fly kick, got the oval within easy reach of the home goal, and Gwynn passing across to Hurst, the latter outwitted Webster and Sampson, scoring cleverly. Pennington took the place, and put the sides on a level footing, the latter point bringing half time, each side being credited with a goal. Gwynn re-started, and Turner's reply being seconded by Jolley and Ashton, Warrington invaded for the first few minutes. Hurst, however, got clear, and was only pulled up under the posts, Sampson tackling him well. Barnes cleared his lines only to find Pennington as safe as ever, and although Sampson got the oval away, a mull caused the Warrington goal to be severely harassed. A series of uninteresting scrimmages were hereabouts witnessed, and the monotony was barely relieved by James Bate before another bout of forward play rendered the game a trifle uninteresting. Gwynn ran finely, but Hurst did not accept the pass. McCutcheon was afforded a chance but Evans spoiled the Welshman before he could male headway. Pennington made his mark from a kick by Bate, but the ground was speedily recovered by Jolley, a clever run and pass to Webster bringing about an attack on the railway goal. J. Bate was brought down a few yards from the line, and though Hurst relieved, the offside tactics of the Oldham front rank found play on the visitors' lines. A minor followed to Warrington's credit, but misfortune was in store for Warrington. Sampson was tackled on his line, and from a scrimmage which ensued, a glaring mistake was made by the referee in awarding Oldham a Penalty kick, which Pennington utilized to advantage—a point which won Oldham the match, and brought about Warrington's first downfall. The-decision was hailed with an amount of dissatisfaction, and Warrington failing to score during 'the remaining portion of the game, the final score was Oldham, two goals (eight points), to Warrington, one goal and two minors (We points). Teams :—Warrington : Sampson. back; Evans, Barnes and Webster, three-quarters James Bate and J. T. Bate, half backs; Ashton (captain), Turner, Jolley, Nevins, Randles, Berry, Donohue, Holmes, and Buckley, forwards. Oldham: Pennington, back; McCutcheon, Gwynn, and Hurst, three-quarters; Mills and Thomas, half backs ; Ashworth, Ingham, Holden, Broome, Tuhoy, Andrew, Ingram, Nuttall, and Blomley, forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Beswick, Swinton. WARRINGTON A v. OLDHAM A.—The rain which had fallen incessantly, luckily cleared off when these oppon- ents faced each other at Oldham. Having lost the toss, Warrington started the contest, and the venue of the struggle was taken to the home 25 by Bailey. There was an early demonstration that the players had great difficulty in gathering the leather, and chiefly aided by these means Oldham gained a footing inside their anta- gonists' ground. A wild pass lost the momentary advan- tage, for Lally, seizing the oval, cleverly frustrated his eager foes, but only a minor resulted. Persisting in the attack, Warrington were looking dangerous, until a mistake let in Wolstenholme and Gill, the ball being forced well into the visitors' quarters. Hamblett re- plied to the effort, and being assisted by others of the team, the leather was grandly, taken three parts the length of the -field in the loose, and Heesom scored first blood. Following the drop out, Knowles punted finely, and some splendid passing between Antrobus, Heesom, and Potts, placed another try to the latter's credit. At length Oldham had a look in, taking play to midfield, from whence it was quickly forced to the Warrington line. A stiff few minutes were witnessed, and just as the visitors' citadel was threatened with imminent dan- ger, Teare, Davies, Dillon' and Molyneux rushed away to the 25. A magnificent bit of play ensued, when An- trobus, getting the ball, threw to Potts, who ran finely into the home quarters, and then repassed to Antrobus, ' whn took the ball and chance also, and galloped over, gaining a beautifully-got try. Kershaw and Dronsfield were next prominent with a dashing dribble, but Barnes responding with a grand run along touch, the home team were again sorely pressed. The Warrington for- wards were playing exceedingly well, although the wet state of the ground spoiled the passing of the backs, otherwise the score would have been considerably aug- mented. Still pressing, Rowlands', Davies, and Dillon were conspicuous until a free kick to Oldham relieved theirlinesr- A kick returned the ball, and Teare, by a grand tackle frustrated Beaver's attempt to clear. The backs on both sides gave a display of their kicking abilities, but Knowles charging a return of Arsden, another minor was conceded. Rowlands then showed by a quick follow up ; but, subsequently, Thomas and Wolstenholme headed a rush into the Warrington terri- tory, where Daniels saved finely, and half time arrived with the visitors leading by three tries to nil. Immedia- tely on the resumption of hostilities Antrobus was hurt, and had to retire for a time. It was now that the home forwards showed their pushing abilities, and con- centrated their attentions on the Warrington goal until Molyneux, Dillon, Bailey, and Knowles effected a capital relief. Oldham returned to the attack, and in was at this stage that the forwards got rough, and it the indiscriminate mixing up_ which followed, the de- fence of the visitors was sorely tried, Teare and Davies saving capitally. Eventually Lally got splendidly away,

div.head: TUEBROOK V. RUNCORN.
div.p: TUEBROOK V. RUNCORN.

These teams met at Tuebrook on Saturday. The visitors opened the play and made tracks for the home quarters, when Pearson relieved; but Faulkner initiated a pas- sing movement, and following some close scrimmaging Bayley relieved on the line and punted down the field. Pendlebury relieved, but was attended to by Ellams,and after the forwards had slightly relieved, Davies picked up and ran in an easy try, which Faulkner converted. The home forwards played better after this reverse. Jones and Ellams put thoir side in a good position, but breaking through seemed impossible, and the opposing forwards, led on by Faulkner, dribbled well down the field. Again the home line was reached, and Davies scored a second try, but the place kick failed. After the drop-out, the home backs had a hard time in, stemming the rushes of their opponents. A free kick relieved the pressure, when a further attack resulted in Hollings- worth crossing the Brook line, the kick at goal being a failure. With a lead of a goal and two tries in favour of Runcorn, the teams crossed over. Bleasdale set the ball rolling, but immediately afterwards the services of the home-backs were once again called into requisition. The forwards at length broke away, and Wooton dribbling down, the ball was taken over the Runcorn line, Cooper scoring a try for the home side, but the point remained unimproved. The game proceeded on fairly even lines, each end being in turn visited but as neither side was able to add to the score, Runcorn won a good game by a goal and two tries (9 points) to a try (2 points). BARROW V. ST. HELENS RECREATION. —Played at Caven- dish Park, Barrow, ch Saturday. Nothing was scored In the first half. Tom Dickinson just missed with a drop at goal. Mossdale and Ellison scored tries, Pyke kick- ing a goal. Close on time Pilkington ran half the length of the field and scored. Final results—Recreation 9 points, Barrow nil.

div.head: EMBEZZLEMENT BY A CLERK AT WARRINGTON,
div.p: EMBEZZLEMENT BY A CLERK AT WARRINGTON,

Benjamin James Gregory was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before Alderman Hohnes (in the chair) and Mr. J. Fairclough, with hay- ing on July 30th ,embezzled from the firm of Messrs. Richmond and Co., gas stove manufacturers, Warrington the sum irf £l2 12s. sd. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor for the prosecuting firm, said the prisoner was employed as a clerk in the firm of Richmond, and Company, and whilst in that capacity he received several ac- counts one of which, namely the one mentioned in the warrent, was that of an account with the Warringtnn Gas Committee. There was a difference of the sum of £l2 12s. sd. between the books of the prisoner's firm and the Gas Company,and it was afterwards discovered that the prisoner had received the sum and not ac- counted for it. He had in the meantime departed for America, whence he came back last week. The prose- cuting company had since received a number of letters. One, dated September 20th, was to the following effect: —" Dear Sirs,—Having come to the conclusion that my wisest course would be to return to England, I returned by the Alaska. I take the earliest opportun- ity of acquainting you with the fact, and of my extreme sorrow for the foolish step which I took, and to inform you that I am willing to do all in my power to retrieve it. You will know best how that can be done. I hold myself at your service, knowing that you will deal as leniently as you can for my parents' sake. My parents will refund the sum,which I took for my journey to New York,although their means are extremely limited." • Mr. Browne (con- tinning) said that the prisoner had been apprehended at Dover, and arrived in Warrington the previous night. He, therefore asked for a remand until Friday next. He had been informed by his clients that the defalcations up to the present amounted to £3l, but there might be others, which were as yet undiscovered.—Mr. Unsworth, solicitor for the defence, agreed to the remand, which was fixed for yesterday. Yesterday the prisoner was again brought before the magistrates on the charge. Mr. Brown represented the prosecuting firm, and Mr. Unsworth the prisoner. Mr. Browne said that the amount of the defalcations dis- covered up to that day was £3l 9s. 2d., but his clients could not say whether or not that was the total amount. Prisoner had promised to give all the information he could. His parents had made reparation to Messrs. Richmond aild Co., and they, knowing the respecta- bility of the parents, and also that he had got another situation to which to go, and was greatly penitent for what he had done, would undertake not to make any further charge, and leave it to their worships to deal with the case as they should think fit. Mr. Unsworth said the prisoner's parents were both over 70 years of age, and they had scraped together all the money they could in order to make reparation for his misdeeds. Prisoner had been in the •employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company for over 15 years before going to Messrs. Richmond and Co., and he had been given an excellent character. He added that prisoner said that some of the other sums which he was supposed to have embezzled had really been paid over to the firm but he had neglected to mark them in the books of the firm. He suggested that prisoner should be bound over to appear when called upon, or, if they could not do that, be sentenceed to three days' imprisonment and he could then be discharged, as he had already been in prison three days.—The Bench adopted the latter sug- gestion, and passed a sentence of three days' imprison- ment.—The prisoner thanked the Bench for their kind- ness, not so much for himself as for his parents ; he felt it more on their behalf than on his own. He was certain he should never find himself in a similar position again, and it would be his endeavour to repay to his parents the money which they had sent down to the firm,

div.head: DUEL WITli UMBRELLAS.
div.p: A DUEL WITli UMBRELLAS.
TERINBLE INJURIES.

M. Titard, contributor to the Paris journals, who was discovered insensible in the Place de la Bourse on Satur- day morning, has succumbed to his injuries. Before his death he mentioned a name which gave the police a clue It seems that M. Titard had found a lady friend of his at a tavern in company with one of his rivals. Warm words ensued, and the trio adjourned to the lady's apart- ments; where the two men fought with umbrellas. From he nature of his injuries it appeared that, after one of his eyes was forced out of its socket, his rival stamped upon his face with heaVy boots, breaking the frontal bone and destroying the sight of the other eve. The mur- derer of M. Titard has been arrested.

div.head: MR. HEALY AND THE PARNELLITES.
div.p: MR. HEALY AND THE PARNELLITES.

Mr. T. M. Healy, presiding at a convention of dele- gates of the National Federation at Cavan yesterday, said a great man had gone to his account, and the best tribute they could pay to his memory was to push on the work to which he put his hand before any cloud inter- wened between his vision and the goal of what was best for Ireland. The personal insults flung at his party by Mr. Parnell, the charge of beirg corrupted by English gold, had long since been forgiven. He had hoped that in the grave of Mr. Parnell would be buried all the con- troversies respecting his leadership. He was sorry to And this was not to be so. He hoped Mr. O'Brien would give to the world the story of the famous negotiations, and he promised to publish letters containing such ex- posures as had never before been heard.

div.head: VACANCY OF CORK.
div.p: THE VACANCY OF CORK.

It has been decided by Mr. Parnell's followers to nomi- nate a candidate for the vacancy in Cork, and to give preference to a local Protestant Home Ruler. Mr. Craw- ford Nedley, a prominent merchant, will be invited to stand. It has been decided that the names of the new Parnellite organs shall be the "National Independent" and the" Evening Herald "respectively.

div.head: SIR M. HICKS-BEACH AT STOCKTON.
div.p: SIR M. HICKS-BEACH AT STOCKTON.

On Tuesday -- niglit_Sigiltiabz.el Hicks-Beach addressed a Conservative and Unionist Uernonstratiln at Stockton- on-Tees on the occasion of the annual meeting of the Northern Union of Conservative Associations. Be said his name had been mentioned in connection with the vacant leadership of the house of COMMORS, but he neither expected nor desired that the office should be conferred upon him. Criticizing at great length the Newcastle programme of the Liberal party, he denounced it as sheer humbug. Unionists, he said, were asking and would continue to ask what Mr. Gladstone intended to propose with regard to Ireland.

div.head: MR. GOSCHEN AT CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: MR. GOSCHEN AT CAMBRIDGE.

Mr. Goschen, addressing a crowded meeting of Con- servatives at Cambridge, on Thursday night, paid a tri- bute to the Memory of Mr. Smith, and said that Mr. Bal- four had triumphed over the Irish spectre, and the country acclaimed it. The Unionist party was grateful, and what was more natural than the wish of the Union- ist party that he who had wrung respect even from the Irish members should in the House of Commons lead the Unionist hosts to those further battles on which the cause they all had at heart had still to be fought. Re- ferring to the Newcastle programme, he said it bristled with dissolutions. They talked of shortening Parliament itself. He accused the Gladstonian party of advocating payment of members for the purpose of making them delegates rather than representatives. The aim of the Gladstonians seemed to be solely to please the working- classes. He claimed for the Unionists every desire to improve not only the condition of the working-classes, but of all classes of the community.

div.head: STATUE OF JOHN BRIGHT.
div.p: STATUE OF JOHN BRIGHT.

The Earl of Derby unveiled on Saturday, the marble statue of John Bright which has been placed in Albert Square. Although the weather was very unfavourable, an assembly of several thousand people gathered in the Square. After the unveiling ceremony Lord Derby addressed a crowded meeting held in the Town Hall. He pointed out that Lancashire specially claimed Mr. John Bright, not merely because he was born and bred in the county, but because he embodied in a peculiar degree the qualities which were usually held to be char- acteristic of Lancashire—strong and clear opinions, de- termined purpose, and plain, uncompromising speech. His lordship spoke of Bright in his character as orator, and mentioned his speech in the House of Commons in the early days of the Crimean War as one of the most famous and eloquent he ever heard. Lord Derby pro- ceeded to speak of Bright as a statesman. The four main ideas of Bright he held to be the benefits of demo- cratic government, the folly of war, the wisdom of a Free Trade policy, and the advantage of treating religion as a thing apart and disconnected from the administra- tion of secular affairs. The Mayor (Mr. Aid. Mark), Mr. W. Mather, M.P., Mr. H. J. Roby, M.P., Mr. Henry Dunckley, and other gentlemen took part in the pro- ceedings.
SIR WILFRED LA.WON AND RUNCORN WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.

Inreply.to an invitation to speak at the forthcom- ing meeting in connection with the Runcorn Wesleyan Temperance Society, Sir Wilfred Lawson, Bart., M.P., has written as follows :—" My dear Sir, —Thanks for your kind note; but there are so many things looking through the November fog, that I could not make the engagement for Runcorn, which you suggest, so you must excuse me for the present. Your letter gives.. a very interesting account of matters in your district. I daresay it is.only a type of many other places. What can be done, so long as the people themselves go on voting for publicans ? As Disraeli once said, " Who can contend with the machinations of an uncontrollable stupidity ?" Still, sense seems to be steadily making its way among the electors, at any rate the leaders think so, from what they are saying; and I hope that we shall soon prove to them that they are right ; though I fancy, from what you say, that Runcorn will not be in advance of public opinion.—Yours, &c., W. LAWSON. October 10, 1891, Brayton, Carlisle.

THE WARRINGTON SANITARY CENSOR AND THE DEPOTS AGAIN

At:the close of the magisterial business, on Mon- day, the Mayor (Aid. R. W. Francomb), Harrison, Sutton and Wright being present on the Bench, Mr. William Diggle again presented timself, and com- plained of the smell from Howley Intercepting Depot. He had, he said, smelt it strongly that morning. He had a small property in the neigh- bourhood, and had to live there, and was contin- uously annoyed with this matter. He had paid very great attention to it for some time, to see if he could remedy it. He had been at considerable trouble and expense in doing so, and he had sub- mitted his plans to the Sanitary committee through Mr. Wright. He called to see Mr. Wright, and he advir ed him to submit them to the Sanitary com- mittee. He put them into his hands, and he believed that gentleman let them go to the Borough Sur- veyor. He (Mr. Diggle). did not know whether the Surveyor had attended to them or not, but after waiting a month, he went and got them back. The plans if carried out would prevent any nuisance. The nuisance was caused through getting a lot of material very stale and putrid and agitating it in an Open agitator. Ihe nuisance was not caused in collect- ing it. His plans would cure that, as there would only be new material to deal with and sent away as it was collected. He was told by the Borough Surveyor the other day that the Corporation were going to put a chimney up, but he reminded him that that had been done before without effect.—The Mayor: Mr. Diggle, we have had this up in the Council Chamber last Tues. day.—Mr. Diggle; But if you had called upon me I would have warmed his jacket. (Laughter.)—Alderman Sutton : That is threatening. (Laughter.)—The Mayor: —Mr. Wright informs me they have this stuff removed every day. It is not kept there.—Mr. Diggle : Oh,bet- ter not tell me so. This nuisance is created unnecessarily, I am satisfied.—After some remarks from the Bench, which created much merriment, but which are better unreported, Mr. Diggle, in reply to questions, said the smell was like that of beef or matter that had been kept too long.—The Mayor ultimately announced that the Bench would proceed ta the spot themselves.—Mr. Diggle: Thank you,l will wait about.—Alderman Harri- son: Mr. Diggle will be your escort, Mr. Mayor.—The Mayor , accompanied by Mr. Diggle, subsequently pro- ceeded to Howley dep'ot, when it was found that there was no smell, the works having been temporarily stopped.

WORK AND WAGES.

Sir,—Will you allow me to make a correction? In my letter a fortnight ago I made the following statement. "My wife says it takes 10s. a week for shoes for my ads." I should have said for the family,instead of lads. —Yours truly,
SOCIAL REFORMER.
BISHOP JAYNE AND THE CHURCH CONGRESS.

Sir,—The Bishop has just delivered himself of a speech at Rhyl, in defence of the Church in Wales. Is it true that he pockets out of Welsh tithes the sum of £746 a year? If so he may well cry "wolf." Is it also true that the following get out of Wales from the same source 400 a year :—Bishop of Lincoln ; the Dean and Chapter of Windsor, £1,800; the Bishop of Glouocster, £844 ; the Deans and Chapters of Oxford,Gloucester, Manches- ter, Worcester and other deaneries. £9,000 :a year. At Chester he is just reported as giving his sanction to pro- cessions with a cross. Processions were condemned in the Purchas judgment, in 1871, and the Bishops Jewel, Burnet, and Archbishop Grindal all strongly condemned crosses and crucifix.

The object of most of the speakers at the Rhyl Con- gress is stated in their own paper the "Church Times" of March 24th, 1871, viz :—" We are contending for the extirpation of Protestant opinions and practises through- out all England." If the thirty-nine articles are too tight for theta, why not show their henesty and relin- quish their emolument and not be doing the work of Ro ne with it? John B. Bayshaw. D.D., a Romanist wrote of the Ritualists in 1884—" They do not follow " the teaching of their bishops except in so far as they, "happen to agree with it, and in short they do not ack- " nowledge any authority on earth as being apPointed to "teach them, and to which they consider themselves "bound to submit." The only symbols in the New Tes- tament are water, bread and wine, if you add to these is it not saying that they are insufficient and therefore that Christ's work isincomplete ?—Yours truly, Frodsham, Oct. 13th, le9l.
ROBERT FOULKES
LABOURERS' WAGES IN AMERICA.

Sir,—Mr. Whitham, in MS letter which you published in a recent issue, refers to my friend, Mr. Winstanley, paying his farm labourer • one dollar a day, whilst he (Mr. Winstanley) could earn 31 dollars a day as a skilled artizan. When I gave you the extracts from Mr. Win- stanley's letters which you published, I might have added, what was well known to me, that, in addition to the dollar a day, Mr. Winstanley provided his men with food. In one of his letters to me he spoke in rather a complaining tone of the amount of cooking required through having thege men at work on his farm.- Mrs. Winstanley is far from strong, and the additional work was almost more than she could do. He said that at every meal several courses were served—even at break- fast, beefsteaks, ham and eggs, hot cakes, potatoes, and three or four kinds of pies and tarts being the Usual fare —to say nothing of fresh salmon and other fish, and game which are plentiful in the river and on his own land. Rabbits also figured frequently on his table. Indeed, these were so numerous that at times he laid poisoned wheat on purpose to rid himself of the nuisance of their depredations on his crops. As showing that there was no want of generosity on the part of my friend towards his men, I will give the following passage from a letter I received from him a fortnight ago :—" I went down ,the field to cover the grain that was thrashed, as it was raiuing a little, and there the men lay scattered round amongst the straw with just a blanket over them. I should have liked you to have seen them: you would not easily forget the scene. Poor fellows, they are tired out and nearly burned up with the heat and dust. A little while ago I took them a bucket of apples and a bucket of peaches and they received them very gratefully." It strikes me that my friend is not a bad sort to work for, and I hope this explanation will be satisfactory to my friend Mr. Whitharn. Mr. Winstanley corroborates Mr. Whitham's statement as to the excessive supply of labourers in the far west.—Yours truly, JOHN GANDY.

div.head: PRAYER AS EVINCING WANT or FAITH.
div.p: PRAYER AS EVINCING WANT or FAITH.
" oye orlittle faith...therefore take- no thought, saying what shall we eat, what shall we drink. For your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of these things. Matth. vi. 30-31. '

Sir,—l am glad to make the epistolary acquaintance of" Gnostic)' It is quite refreshing in these,days,when the glare of general enlightenment servos also to shew as the vast extent of our ignorance, to meet with one "who knows." From: 'One, self-styled the "knowing tine," much in the way of information might be expected. But, sir, you know the proverb as to the blessing of non expectancy. "Gnostic " justifies the proverb. I have not time to follow this master of inconsequent state- ments through the mazes of his metaphysical divergences from the point at issue. At present my position is that prayer for the alteration of natural conditions, atmos- pheric or otherwise, is unreasonable, and an evidence of the want of sound faith in that beneficent over-ruling Providence to whom the suppliant is pleading. All prayer is of one of two kinds. The suppliant asks for some- thing he has not already got--or he pleads for the reten- tion of something he is already possessed of. The above quoted words of St. Matthew are condemnatory of prayer in either case. So in the case of prayer for changes of weather. Nothing, I think, ,ea o be more certain than

the intimate inter-relationship of the weather of our planet. To alter the weather in England would neces- sitate a corresponding alteration in the weatker of the continent and consequently of the whole world. How parochial-minded the man must be who expects his own little local interests to be furthered at the general ex- pense. Again, it is very unreasonable to say "Thy will be done," and then pray that that Will be altered to be in conformity with our own desires. Surely if Infinite Wis- dom has decided that such a course or condition of things is best, the selfish pleadings of us poor mortals can but be regarded as an impious and impertinent in- terference with His decrees. What would be thought of the man who would pray in so many words that the Lord should change His mind—reconsider His decisions and generally alter His views in confGrmity with those of His creatures. This may be regarded as the reductio ad absurduns of prayer, but it is essentially what thousands of people do unthinkingly every day of their lives. Let such people ask themselves the question—" Is the view of the subject upon which I am about to pray not likely to be seen by the All Seeing ? Can I present any• reason to the All Wise for a reversal of His judgment?" , The answer, and the only possible answer for a sane per- son, is—none! Then why pray? The only logical and truly reasonable prayer for one who sincerely belieVes in an over-ruling Providence is simply—" Thy will be done." To pray for an alteration of this will is an im- piety only to be condoned by the ignorance of the sup- plicant. I have heard long-winded prayers which were, metaphorically, a familiar tapping of the Deity on the shoulder with the reminder of something He might have forgotten, or a view of the question which might not have occurred to Him! Of course this aspect of the matter did not occur to the supplicants, consistent logical thought being quite out of the range of possibility there. Hence it is their practice to address the Deity as though He was fickle, inconstant, wavering, and forget- ful.

Your knowing correspondent is too diffiise. Let us first settle the point at issue, i.e., thc. logical position of prayer. Then I shall be happy to cross swords with him on the many blunders he has perpetrated in his meandering diversions from the main issue. Notably as to "my anthropomorphism "—as to who it was denied the laws of mind—why the laws of Chemistry are not as universal as "gravitation "—how man has the "power of modifying nature." Perhaps when " Gnostic " has leisure (enough) he will tell us how he " knows " that the laws of combining proportion do not obtain in (say) Jupiter as they do here ? There is one paragraph in my critic's letter which I must examine, as it deals with matter in hand. It is that in which he takes exception to my remark that "No logic with which I am acquainted countenances any connection between prayer and meteorology." He comments upon this—" But whether there is or is not a connection between the two can be decided scientifically only by appealing to the methods of science," that is the methods of deductive or inductive logic. Accordingly, his acquaintEnce with logic is more conspicuous for its ignorance than anything else." Now, I repeat I have failed to find the logic to countenance us in asking the Creator to change His mind or alter His laws for the temporary convenience of a small section of His creatures. I say I have been unable to find any such warranty. Let " Gnostic " inductively or deductively do this for us. As one who arrogates to himself the title of the "Knowing One" this surely is not a difficult task. I know not what other vocation" Gnostic" may have, but here isa job likely to last him for the term of his natural life. May you and I, 812, live to see its com- pletion ! In the meantime many things will happen and "Gnostic "may cease to make assertions without proof. —Yours, &c., Penketh, 11 October, 1891.
JOHN PEERS.
LIFE INSURANCE: ITS USE AND ABUSE.

Sir,—The above very important subject is one which demands the very earnest attention of all right-minded people of our villages, towns and cities and demands every possible effort to extend its usefulness amongst the artisan and labouring classes of this country, for whose benefit it is chiefly intended. At the same time we should denounce in strong terms what are known to be abuses and degrading practises of persons, both in- side and outside of the good institution of life assur-

div.head: Ance.
div.p: Ance.

It is a plain fact that the great majority of contracts made, are made and paid upon and depend upon the hard-working housewives of our labouring and artisan classes. These women are canvassed during the day by agents, and are pressed to make contracts upon the lives of their husbands, their children, and after these, their father and mother, their uncles and aunts, brothers and sisters and other relatives, not knowing anything what- ever only what the agent has to give or what suits his purpose to give, or withhold: They know nothing of serious responsibilities in paying upon these policies; but simply pay on and on in faith believing that all is gospel truth preached by the agent, who may be a man of honour, a local preacher, a man of salvation, a re: formed scamp, or a liar. She takes these policies without even taking the trouble to open them and see for herself if only one name or two is on; whether right name, or wrong age ; if deferred benefits or immediate benefits, so often promised, but so seldom put on or realised by the assurant. Never was a word more fitly spoken than the remark of Judge Coventry, a county court judge, a short time ago at Blackburn when he stated that—" It would he a good thing if letters twenty feet high could be posted in towns, showing people their responsibilities in taking out life assurance policies." If plain direction and instruction were issued to the people with the same earnest zeal that is displayed in pushing business, by the large insurance companies and societies, who do business among the working classes, setting forth in clear language what was the proper uses and advantages of life insurance and at the same time warning the people of the great danger of entering lives outside the family circle, and pc4inting out the penalties of those found guilty of gaming and wagering in the lives of other persons, then, and only then, could the large companies and societies expect to free themselves of so much speculation in human beings;which they so much complain of, where the dividends are seriously lessened by the thousands and thousands paid away to persc.ns they know well are not entitled to receive one-tenth or fractional part of the claims paid out. hind large numbers of people who are entirely un- aware of what the amounts allowed by law upon, children and upon adults, and whether prohibited bklaw ,from'entering the next door neighbour, friend, cousins, or any they desire toanake money upon. Many believe upon entering, that if children are entered in two differ- ent companies or societies they can draw to any amount almost, not knowing that £6 is the full limi on children , 'dying under the age of 5 years and £lO umltthei age of !10 years. Many examples could be given of persons having increased one penny, making two-pence weekly lon the child, say several years ago. They have paid on upon the assurance that they could obtain double amounts, as stated on their policies, when death took place. Then again, how many uncles and aunts are to-day paying upon policies on the lives of nephews and nieces, and also grandfathers and mothers upon their grand- children, when at the same time parents are only allowed to enter, pay, and draw the money at death, of their children! ft cannot be too widely known, in order to prevent trouble and anxieties when paying upon the lives of other persons, that no matter who they are the law speaks plainly upon the question of Assurable Interest. One extract from an Act of Parliament is as follows "No Insurance shall be made on the life of any person, where the person on whose account it shall be made, shall have no interest, or by way of gaining, or wagering ; and that every such Insurance shall be null and void." So that where any policy is issued in the favour of any person who neither supports the assured person nor is liable for his or her interment or cannot prove a legal debt, that policy can be declared null and 'void by the next of kin ; or any interested person could set aside the policy and prevent the Company or Society from paying the claim, or could prosecute such claimants. Another extract says Where the assured has an interest in such life, no greater sum shall be received from the in- surer than the amount of the interest of the insured in such life." This was intended to guide the Assurance Offices as well as the insurer; that no greater sunr was to be received in premium nor policies issued for more money, than was requisite to cover the loss sustained by the in- surer. But alas ! how often this is evaded as well as the conditions of previous extract. When in every locality we hear of such large sums of monPy being handed over to persons who pocket from 80 per cent. downwards and who are great gainers in the death, thus bringing dis- credit and curse rather than the blessings intended by the founder of Life Assurance. With your permission, I will continue thf) subject in another letter.—l am, yours faithfully, JOHN MOORFIELD. 44, Parker-st., Warrington, October sth, 1891.

div.head: LIQUOR TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC.

Sir,—ln her able and comprehensive address to the Liberal Bazaar meeting last week, the Countess of Carlisle expressed a hope that the time would come i7rben the liquor traffic would be rooted out of the land aito,gether. In this truly patriotic wish all true citizens must-join, and I pen this letter as a contribution, however small, towards its accomplishment.

Is the liquor traffic a necessity a good or an/ evil thing? Twill endeavour to answer this threefold ques- tion as briefly as the importance of the subject will per- mit. That men requireArink, cannot be questioned .for a moment. It is absolutely essential to their being, and they can no more exist without it than they can live without food or clothing. But the nature and quality of the beverage must be thoroughly suitable to bodies which, in the language of Scripture, are fearfully and wonder- fully made. :Drinks that are abnormal, impure, and not adapted to the wants of the human system, when hi- dulged in, will be sure to produce disease, and even death. Now He who knoweth our frame, infinitely better than we do ourselves, has provided richly for His crea- tures in the matter of drink as well and as wisely as in

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 17, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 17, 1891.

all other matters pertaining to them. In the pure streams and fountains of water which adorn and fertilize the earth ' • in the cattle on a thousand hills, and in orange and other groves He has bountifully given us beverages that meet the wants of our nature. These good creatures of God are salutary in the highest degree, and serve the purpose for which they were intended in a manner which affords a striking proof of the Divine wisdom in adopting means to ends. These , beverages cool the parched tongue, allay thirst, refresh and invigorate the exhausted frame, and impart clear- ness and serenity to the mental faculties. They are most agreeable and welcome to the taste, and their daily, hourly use in households and elsewhere never leads to excess of any kind. No headaches, no inflamed paSsions, no injury to mind or body result from their consumption, and the world has never yet seen paupers, lunatics, or criminals that were made by their use. And then they are so widely diffused and so inenensive that a cup of water, or of milk, is at all times within the easy reach of the poorest person. Moreover, these beverages need no Acts of Parliament to regulate and control them, and no policemen, magistrates and judges to punish their consumers for disorderly conduct, for these men are at least sober, and peaceable citizens. Now if milk, water, and the juice of fruit are the divinely appointed beverages for the human race, it follows, of course, that alcoholic drinks are not required at all. , But I go a loll!, step beyond this and declare, without fear of contradiction, that they are not only unnecessary but are absolutely unnatural in themselves and fraught with the direst consequenee tojrnankind In this case, as well as in others, tike character of the tree is known by the fruit which it produces. The first operations of the Liquor traffic involve the total loss of enormous quantities of nutritous and wholesome grain, and we can imagine the satisfaction with which Satan, the great destroyer of the works of God, will view the nefarious operations of the Brewery and Distillery. In those huge fountains of drunkenness, he will see poor and miserably paid men toiling seven days a week in destroying the food of the people, and evolving from , its ruin a poisonous fluid to be attractively bottled up and exposed for sale in in palaces and beerhouses all , over the country. And this infernal work is the source , of a large revenue to the paternal government which employs an army of ecclesiastics with salaries ranging from £15,000 a year downward for preaching the Gos- pel of Rim who said "Gather up the fragments that no- thing be lost," and enjoys the distinguished patronage and support of the "gentry and clergy" of all denomi- nations of religionists! All this may be so, and the Greenalls and Walkers of society may erect Art Galleries and Churches, and endow priests, but neither patronage nor pious sops will remove the brand which attaches to them as co-operators with Satan in destroying the works of God and debauching their fellow-creatures. The liquors thus manufactured and vended are, of course, utterly unnatural, and have not one redeeming , feature to set against the black catalogue of crime and misery of whinh they are the instigators. Indeed, so re- piignant are the beer, whisky, gin, &c., of the publican to the unvitiated taste of human beings, that I believe men would not touch them at all but for the false spirit or drunkenness which they inspire. Instead of allaying natural thirst, they create ark unnatural one, which in- creases with their consumption until at last the poor toper loses all sense of thirst or anything else. Their use, even in moderate quantities, is always accompanied with a kind of insane and unhealthy excitement, and when the drinking is heavy and prolonged ,this excite- ment frequently developes into a wild ferocity under the iniuence of which men often commit crimes of the most revolting and diabolical nature. Would it not be highly absurd to suppose that bever- ages which produce such terrible results as these could be otherwise than unhealthy and dangerous to human life? The trade mark which they set upon their votaries is a convincing proof of their deleterious nature. Blood- shot. eyes, bloated faces, foul breath, and coarseness of voice and manner, are signs which invariably dis- tinguish habitual tipplers from the happier and wiper men who shun the public-house as they would shun the plague. And these symptons of disease and death are awfully emphasised by the numerous graves of drunk- ards to be seen in every cemetery and burying place in the land. _ _ .

Lastly, let us think for a moment of the terrible cost of this diabolical traffic. The value of the millions of tons of grain which it absorbs and destroys every year is only a trifle when compared with the expenditure which it involves in other ways. The loss in money alone, to say nothing of health and reputation, which the publicans inflict upon the wage-earning classes is beyond calculation. The sober and industrious of all classes are heavily taxed to maintain "the finished arti- cles" of the trade in the shape of loafers, paupers, and madmen; while vast sums are needed for policemen, magistrates, and judges to protect our streets from being totally overwhelmed with its disorders, and to punish its criminals. Well now, what is our plain and imperative duty in regard to this unnatural health and wealth destroying traffic? Should we go on tinkering and patching it as we have hitherto done in the hope of minimising its ravages and bringing abouts its ultimate extermination ! Nay verily, past and bitter experience has taught us the absolute futility of such a course. For centuries we have tried to grapple with this Christian Moloch" by repressive Acts of Parliament, and other remedial measures With the damning result that to-day we stand before the world as the most drunken nation upon the face of thevarth, our workhouses and asylums full of paupers and lunatics, and our prisons with criminals through the work of the publican ! Tile only way to reform the Liquor Traffic is to reform it out of existence altogether, and in a future letter I will endeavour to show that this is by no means an impossible task. Yours faithfully, lONA.
THE PROPOSED VEHICULAR BRIDGE
ACROSS THE MERSEY.

The proposal to construct a vehicular bridge across the Mersey, to join Runcorn and Widnes, has been carried a step further. The idea origin- ated with the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, who sought the co-operation of the Widnes Local Board, and the latter body on Tuesday resolved in conjunction with the Commissioners to memorialise the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire in favour of the construction of such a bridge.

"We are glad to see that Dr. Tomkins " advice to parents" is in it 999th edition; no house is com- plete without it."—Quarterly Review. Oh, listen little children to a fellow little child. Who by its parent's cruelty is being driven wild; I'll tell you what I've suffered, and I'll tell you what

to do, And if you'll only do it it will be the best for you. 1 was a happy little boy, as happy as could be, For many, many years—at least till I was nearly 3; I romped about from morn till night, I laughed and
so grew fat, But what I'm going to tell you very quickly altered that.
Twas on a bitter day in March, a memorable day, When pa came in from business and unto ma did
say; "Here is that 'Advice to parents' and I saw his face expand— It has only cost me ninepence as I got it second-
hand." Oh ! I wish that Dr. Tomkins was my pa for just a week, There's me an several more would make it hot for
him, the sneak ! . We'd daub his clothes with treacle ; put some salt
into his bed, And most carefully put in his chair a tack stood on

its head. _ The evening of that same day is the well-remem- bered date, When Mr. Dr. Tomkins won my everlasting bate ; I was reading the barometer whin stood at ten degrees, And the stuff was under zero, so it meant that it
would freeze. Twas when I had ray evening bath I heard about this QUACK, For ma she poured a gallon of. cold water down my
back; And she sweetly smiled and murmured as she froze my little blood ; "Dr. Thompson recommends it, and it will do the darling good."
How I gasped for breath, and hollered! for it took me unawares; It was something like an earthquake,'or a tumble down the stairs.
I will leave YO-ti---t-o imagine the condition of my nerves, For you cannot take cold water like you do pills—in preserves.

CADISHEAD.

SIIIP CANAL MISSION HALL.—On Monday evening an entertainment of a varied character was held in the above hall by the famous "Tiniest" from the Orphan Homes, Manchester. The boys to the number of thirteen, rendered songs and glees, and also gave an amusing dialogue. Musical drill and exercises were also part of the grogramme. The newly appointed missionary, Mr. F. Foster was in the chair.

WESLBYAN CHAPEL.—The harvest thanksgiving services of this place of worship were held en Sunday. The chapel was tastefully decorated for the occasion, and presented a pretty appearance. The services were con- ducted by the Rev. B. Yates, both morning and evening. At the evening service there was a large gathering, and the choir assisted by the Cadishead Orchestral Band, rendered "All Thy works praise Thee," and "0 Lord, how Manifold." Collections were made in aid of the Circuit Fund. On Monday evening, the Rev. J. Crewe, pastor of the Congregational Chapel, preached, taking as his subject, " The capacity of the earth for producing." There was a fair congregation present. On 'Kuesday the fruit and vegetables were disposed of.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN IN WALES.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN IN WALES.

Mr. Chamberlain on Tuesday night addressed a meet- in.. near Llanybyther, a remote village in Cardiganshire, and, referring to the death of Mr., Smith, said he was a great loss, not only to his party btit to his country. The difference which had arisen in the Liberal party,were due to Mr. Gladstone having thrown aside the pro- gramme upon which all Liberals were agreed, and accepted from the hands of Mr. Parnell a new policy upon which they differed, and which Mr. Gladstone had himself donounced as dangerous. The result of that had been to delay indefinitely the carrying out of what was dear to the Welsh people—viz., Disestablishment of the Church. He contended that Mr. Gladstode had never said a word in faVoiii ofthe piineiple `of disestablishment, and that he only accepted it, not because it was right, but because it was expedient for himself. Mr. Chamber- lain went on to say that he would have made disestab- lishment the first item in the unauthorised programme during the agitation of 1885, and was only withheld from doing so out of consideration for Mr. Gladstone's wishes. He described the Newcastle programme as ab- surd, and held that the House of Lords had nothing to fear if it insisted apon the opinion of the country being once more taken respecting Home Rule.

div.head: COMMONS LEADERSHIP.
div.p: THE COMMONS LEADERSHIP.
MR. BALFO UR'S APPOINTMENT.

. The Press Association learns that Lord Salisbury immediately upon his arrival !n England communicated with Mr. Akers-Douglas, chief Conservative Whip. Mr. Akers-Douglas went on Wednesday to Hatfield, where he remained with the Premier during the afternoon, and on his,return to London in the evening he made inquiries for Mr. Goschen.. It is understood that Lord 'Salisbury his been in communication with Lord Hartington, but the leader of the Liberal Unionists remains at New- market. Mr. Goschen arrived at the Treasury early on Thursday, and was joined shortly afterwards by Mr. Akers-Douglas. The Chancellor of the Exchequer sub- sequently walked to Arlington-st., where Lord ;Salisbury had arrived shortly after noon. Mr. Goscchen shortly after this interview with the Premier left for Cambridge to address a political meeting. The" St. Stephen's Review "says it .has the best autherity for stating that Lord Salisbury has deCided to offer the leadership of the House of Commons to Mr. Balfotir, and that Mr. Balfour will accept the honour. The Standard " says it is in a position to state that Mr. Balfour will succeed the: late Mr. W. H. Smith as leader of the House of Commons. The "Daily News" says :—We understand that Lord Salisbury has ,definitely offered the leadership of the House of Commons to *-14Ir. Balfour, together with the First Lordship of the Treasury. In case of M.r.Balfour's aebeptance of the leadership, Mr. Jackson, now Finan- cial Secretary to the Treasury, will be Chief Secretary to the Lord-Lieutenant in Mr. Balfour's place. The appoint- ment of Mr. Balfour to be First Lord of the Treasury does not vacate his seat for East Manchester, as he al- ready held an office under the Crown, and transference from one such office to another has not necessitated re- election since th 4 Reform Act of 1887. But the Secre- tary to the Trearury, being formally; appointed by the Lords of the Treasury, does not hold an office under the Crown ; so that if Mr. Jackson succeeds Mr. Balfour as Chief Secretary for Ireland, he will cease to be member for North Leeds, and must present himself again to the constituency. Mr. Jackson's majority in 1836 was 619, 'and in 1885, 257.

An attempt has been made to assassinate Dr. Sacaza, the President o f Nicaragua, by a corporal of the Palace Guard. The miscreant was caught near the President's bedroom, and beaten almost senseless by the soldiers.

div.head: F RODSHAM.
div.p: F RODSHAM.

UNION CHURCH .—The harvest thanksgiving services at this church were held on Sunday, when the Rev. Charles Craddock preached. The church, as on previous occasions, had been tastefully decorated with corn;fruits, and flowers. PRIMITIVE METHOD/ ST CHAPEL. Harvest thanks- giving services were held in the above chapel, Frodsham Bridge, op Sunday morning and evening, the preacher being the Rev. H. Davenport, of Frodsham. The chapel Was tastefully decorated with flowers kc. . _ _ _ _

BIBLE SOJIETY'S MEETING.—The fifty-ninth annual meeting of the Frodsham branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held on Monday night, in the Town Hall, Frodsham, under tke presidency of the Vicar of Frodsham, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A. From the report read by the Hon. Treasurer (Dr. F. P. Weaver), it appeared that the receipts of the past year amounted to £6l, the payments were £1 55., which left a bilance of £59 155., which had been handed over to the treasurer of the society in Chester. The report was received and adopted, on the motion of the Rev. E. P. Alexander,M.A. (Alvanley), and seconded by the Rev. J. E. Symonds,the deputation, who gave a full account of the society's work in Russia. The resolution of the adoption of the Treasurer's report having been put to the meeting and carried, the Rey. E. Mari-den (Aston) proposed, and the Rev. P. Pizey (Wesleyan) seconded, the re-election of .the officers of the branch, which also was carried unanim- ously.

PRESTON BROOK.—On Sunday the annual harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Wesleyan Chapel, which had been neatly decorated with fruit, vegetables, flowers, &c. The afternoon service commenced' at 2.30 when the Rev. William Arrowsmith, of Runcorn, preached to a good congregttion from the words "0 that man would praise the Lord for His goodness." Psalm evil 8. The evening service commenced at 6.30, and the preacher for this occasion was Mr. Gurst, of Helsby, who took for his text Mal. iii. 10," Bring ye all the tithes into the storekouse," &c. During the after- noon service, the choir sang the anthem, "Make a joyful noise" (Simper), and in the evening "Praise the Lord," ,by the same composer. At the close of each service a collection was made in aid of the organ fund. On Mon- day evening at seven, the services were continued in the chapel, and the Rev. J. Hanby, of Halton, preached, after which a collection was again made for the same abject, and the fruit, vegetables, &c., were disposed of.

TEICHNICAL INSTRITCTION.—The first of a 'series of lectures previded by the Cheshire County Council on the principles of agriculture was delivered in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday, by Mr. Lincoln Hardy; the lecturer appointed by the Council for No. 3 district. There were but a few persons in attendance, some dozen of whom, however, have joined the class which is being formed. As the lectures are free to all, this fact cannot be too widely published.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meet- ing of this society was held on Monday evening in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Mr. Thorpe being in the chair. A paper was read, entitled " Books, and how to read them." Mr. Brown, Mr. Brereton, Mr. E. Moston, Mr. Taylor, and Mr. A. Robinson took part in the discussion which followed. WESLEY CHAPEL.—The annual sermons in connection with this chapel were preached on Sunday. There were two services, morning and evening, the preacher being the Rev. J. E. Rattenbury. The preacher took for his text in the morning St. John i. 1 and 2. and in the even- in the third and fourth verses. The chapel had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, and presented a very pretty appearance. Anthems were sung, and a collection taken at each service.

FIREWORKS LICENCES.—At the Altrincham Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, the magistrates renewed the licenses of'the following among other persons, enabling. them to. sell fireworks :—Warburton, William West; Lymm, J. B. Taylor and Elizabeth Gibbons. Notice ha i been given of an intended application by Seth Walters, Thelwall., Superintendent Walker said he had given notice of an objection to the appliarronT—The applicant lid at the huts at Thelwall, and as there was a powder maga- zine, he entirely objected to the license. The applicant did not come forward, and no license was granted. Low., BOARD.—An extraordinary meeting of this Board was held on Monday evening, all the members of the Board being present. The business of the meeting was to consider the appointment of teachers for filo technical instruction classes. After a long discussion, Mr. Brown, of Warrington, was appointed shorthand teacher ; Mr. R. Oddy, teacher of drawing ; and the Rev. J. Edwardes-Evans, teacher of French. The appointment of a teacher of cookery acd dressmaking; was left in the hands of a sub-committee, which con- sists of Messrs. R. Dutton, F. Swallow, J. Holt, and R. Whitelegge. The Committee have instructions to com- mence the daises as soon as practicable.

CONGRHOATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—An admirable en- tertainment was given by the Band of Hope of the Con- gregational Sunday Schools on Monday night, to a large, appreciative, and enthusiastic audience. The piece performed was "Little Red Riding Hood," the vari- ous impersonations were well sustained, and the singing throughout gave great satisfaction. The following were the characters :—Miss Moston, the mother; Miss Mary Drinkwater' Red Riding Hood; Miss Jane Appleton' rose; Miss Florrie Brearley, buttercup; Misses Dinah Daniels, Eliza Daniels, Eliza Appleton, E. Hinton, Fanny Thorneycroft, and Maggie Leah represented bluebells; the wolf was well rendered by Mr. Jas. Hewitt; Master Arthur Astley was the woodman, and Master J. R. Bar- ton was Robin.

-THU RECTOR OF LYMM.—The Rector of Lymm, the Rev. G. ,W. Guest, is at preseut staying at the Hotel Metropole, Brighton. LYMM C.E.T.S.—The first meeting of the above society took place in the Parochial School, on Tuesday evening. The children were divided into bands of ten,who elected a captain, who was to be responsible for the mainten- ance of order by that ten at public meetings. AGRICULTVRAL LECTURE.—The first lecture under the County Council was held in the Grammar School on Thursday night, at which Mr. Hardy gave a lecture ex- planatory of the course of lectures or classes which are to be held free to all, and weekly,at the Grammar School. The Rev. J. Edwardes-Evans introduced the lecturer in a few appropriate remarks.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. YEsTERDAy.--:Belore Mr. William . Long (in the chair), . .
Dr. Brabazon, and Mr. John Dewhurst.

Does AT LARGE.-15ercy Ratcliffe, whose wife ap- peared in his stead, was fined 3s. 6d. for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled at Lymm, on the 27th of Sep- tember.—George Henry Brereton, was also fined 3s. 6d. for a similar offence at Thelwall Heath, on the 23rd of Cctober.—lsaac Pollard, of Partington, was mulcted in the sum of ss. for keeping a dog without a license on the 10th of October.

AN UNLICENSED GUN.—William Glover, a young man, of Warrington, was summoned for using.a gun at Thel- wall on the 16th August, without having a license. The Bench fined the defendant 10s. and costs. CHILDREN'S SQUABBLES.—Robert Kirke and James Robinsm were summoned for assaulting George Elliott, a boy aged 11 years at Lymm on the 18th September. The charges were dismissed.

Worrall, labourer, a middle-aged man, was charged with assaulting Arthur James Hoult, Ship Canal employe, at 4trhelwall, on the 20th Sentem- ber.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs. CHARGE AGAINST A CADISHEAD YoUTM—George Cassells, aged 15, of Lerd-street, Cadishead, was charged with indecently assaulting Harriet Knight, aged 13, at Partington, on the previous Wednesday. The defendant appeared to be a dull, unintellectual youth,his father and mother defending him.—The case was dismissed.

A telegram published in Belfast on Thursday from Boulogne states that Mr. De Cobain is in very feeble health. A fortnight ago he was in such a critical state that some of his friends were summoned from England. The Postmaster General has decided to make strict in- quiry into the allegations that certain letters passing between Mr. De Cobain M.P., and his solicitor has been tampered with in transit, and at his request all docu- ments bearing upon tbe subject have been forwarded to London.

HARVEST FESTIVAL.—On Sunday the Wesleyans of Golborne, held their harvest festival in the Wesleyan Chapel, which had been tastefully decorated for the occa- sion with fruit, flowers, vegetables, &c., by the members of the congregation. Both mornine, and evening the Rev. John Dugdale, of Wigan, occupied the pulpit, when ap- propriate discourses were given to good congregations. The choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Wm. Mather, sang suitable hymns, and Mr. A. Hayes was at the organ. A collection was made at each service in aid of the school fund, which realised a very satisfactory sum.—On Tues- day evening, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, the Rev. J. T. Wardle-Stafford, of Prescot, gave one of his popular‘ lectures on "Robert Molfat,the apostle of the Africans." The lecturer clearly denoted the character of Moffat,an4l from beginning to end was of a most interesting character. Mr. Robert Openshaw presided.

div.head: AN OLD WOMAN BURNT TO DEATH.
div.p: AN OLD WOMAN BURNT TO DEATH.
An old woman named Gorton was burnt to death in her cottage at Chorley yesterday morning. The cottage also was destroyed. r FERRY STATION BURNT.
The passenger station at Strome Ferry was destroyed by fire yesterday, together with the telegraph system and a quantity of luggage.
STEAMERS IN COLLISION.
The Glasgow steamer Ben Nevis and the Belfast steamer Brill collided off Greenock ,on, Thursday night. The former 'sank, but the crew were saved.
ALLEGED MISAPPROPRIATION OF .£7,184,

_ Arthur Edward Bmithers (52), bank director, was re- manded on bail at the Mansion House, London, yesterday, :charged with converting to his own use £7,184 belonging to the English Bank of the River Plate.

div.head: FACTION FIGH I' AT NEWRY.
div.p: FACTION FIGH I' AT NEWRY.

During a faction fight at Newry, on Thursday night, between the McCarthyites and the Parnellites over a municipal election, Head Constable Williams and several other police officers were injured. Two arrests were made. RESIGNATION OF THE GOVERNMENT OF VICTORIA.
A " Times " second edition Melbourne telegram says: —The Cabinet met after having been defeated in the division concerning the Government Mines Regulatio n Bill, and decided to resign.

div.head: THROWING A YOUNG LADY FROM A TRAIN.
div.p: THROWING A YOUNG LADY FROM A TRAIN.

A Birmingham telegram to the Exchange Telegraph Companyeays a clerk'employed by the Birmingham Canal Company, named A. Silvester, was arrested yesterday afternoon on a charge of throwing Miss Smith,a teacher, out of a train on the Great Western Railway on the Bth Inst.

div.head: FIRE IN LONDON.-5 LIVES LOST.
div.p: FIRE IN LONDON.-5 LIVES LOST.

By a fire which broke out early yesterday morning in West Ferry-road, Millwall, London, five persons lost their lives. The flames were discovered in a back room on the ground floor, and on the arrival of the firemen with manual and escape gallant efforts were made to effect an entrance, but the men were driven back by the excessive heat. Subsequently, Phcebe Walker (70), Annie Missen (27), Violent Missen (4), Phcebe Missen (2), and Charles Missen (1 year) were found suffocated. THE EIGHT HOURS QIUESTION IN AUSTRALIA.

SYDNEY, FRIDAT.—The bovernment has met with a severe rebuff in the Legislative Assembly. A motion was brought forward that the Government Bill to regu- late coal mining and amend the mining law should be referred back to Committee in order that the eight hours provision should be eliminated. The Government pro- posed that the debate should be postponed, but this was rejected by 49 against 44. votes.

div.head: STRAND VACANCY.
div.p: THE STRAND VACANCY.

With the issue of the addresses of both candidates for the vacancy in the Strand Division, the contest may be said to have commenced. Both parties are making active preparations for the coming fight, and canvassing has already commenced. Mr. F. Smith, the Conserva- tive candidate, in his address, says it will be his highest ambition if elected to follow as closely as possible in his father's footsteps in all that pertains to imperial and local affairs. Dr. Gutteridge the Liberal candidate, in his address says he takes his stand on the advanced Liberal and Radical platform, advocating the rights of the people as against class and privilege.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLISION AT SEA.
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLISION AT SEA.
21 LIVES LOST.

Full particulars have just be received of the collision in Port Philip Bay between the screw steamers Gambier , and Easby, which resulted in the sinking of the former and the loss of 21 lives. The -Gambier was inward bound from Sydney, and the Easby was outward bound for Newcastle. The collision occurred a few minutEs after one o'clock on the morning of the 28th of August, when all the passengers were in bed. The Gambier was struck amidships, and the water came pouring into her. Most of the passengers rushed on deck just as they were— in- their night clothing—and the scene was one of intense ex- citement. The poor people were really panic-stricken, and their cries and shrieks were most heartrending. The Gambier was run into shoal water and sank in about seven minutes after the collision. Two boats were lowered from the Gambier, but one got capsized. The captain did his best to obtain order, but it was a most tryiiag time. The Eastby also lowered two boats, and suc- ceeded in picking up a number of the people. There were many women and children amongst the passengers, and some of them had a most terrible experience. Most of the people were unable to get into the boats, and as they were on the deck of tho Gambier, they were washed out to sea as the vessel settled down. A portion of the steamer's two funnels remained above water, but the suction as she sank drew many of the passengers and crew down with her. The most heartrending scenes were witnessed as the survivors were landed. Some mothers then found they had lost their children, others their husbands. One boat was picked up the next morning containing the lifeless bodies of three of the passengers—two men and one little girl. Captain Bell,of the Gambier, wat also carried under by the vortex, and had a hard battle to extricate himself. He was picked up by a boat which had six others in it, and just after his rescue the second engineer was caught as he was being swept past the boat. The Easby took the survivors into Melbourne, and before arrival the passengers presented Captain Bell, of the Gambier, with a testimonial on account of his brave con- duct in doing all he could to save their lives.
FOUND DROWNED IN THE MERSEY.

On Thursday morning about six o'clock, the dead body of a man—was found floating in the Mersey at the en`zance of the Prince's Half-tide Dock, Liverpool, and from documents in the pockets of the clothing it is believed that the re- mains are those of Thomas Shallcross, master of the flat Willie, of Runcorn, and who was washed off his vessel some days ago opposite the Toxteth Dock. The deceased, who appeared to be about forty-five years of age, and was about sft. 3in, in height, had dark brown hair and moustache, and was dressed as follows :—Dark blue pilot jacket, dark striped tweed vest, black tweed trousers, blue striped cotton shirt, grey worsted singlet, bine woollen stockings, and Blucher boots. In his pockets were found £3 2s. 11d., five keys, and some printed receipts made out to captain Thomas Shall.. cross, and signed George Bushell and J. Rees. The remains were deposited in the mortuary at the Prince's Dock.

tiThree passengers have been killed and thirteen injured near Defiance, Ohio, owing to a train leaving the rails while running at the rate of 50 miles an hour. At the Mansion House, London, on Thursday, Freder kit Fryer, proprietor of the "British Building Journal," was committed for trial, charged with obtaining a loan froill a solicitor by falseipretences.

div.head: PEIiKETH.
div.p: PEIiKETH.
HARVEST FESTIVAL.

On Wednesday evening the harvest festival in connection with St. Mary's Mission, Penketh, took place. The Mission Church had been most tastefully decorated for the occassion by the lady members of the congregation and presented a most pleasing ap- pearance. The preacher was the Rev. M. B. F. Binney, M.A.,of Sutton, St. Helens. He selected his text from St. John, chapter xii., verse 24, and preached an excellent sermon thereftim to an attentive congregation. During the evening the anthem by Barnby, "We shall go out with Joy " was sung in a most praiseworthy manner by the choir. At the close of the service, a collection in aid of the church expenses was taken which realized the satisfactory sum of £9 9s. 7d. A large congre- gation assembled for the occasion the church being crowded.
LECTURE ON PALESTINE

On Tuesday evening, a lecture, entitled "'Pales- tine, as I saw it," was delivered in the Wesleyan Schoolroom by the Rev. C. Leach, D.D. (of London.) There was a large attendance, the room being crowded. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., presided. The lec- ture was illustrated by a number of oriental cos- tumes, brought from the East by Dr. Leach, and which were worn by twelve persons. These Dr. Leach exhibited at various stages of the lecture. The proceeds are to be devoted to defraying the cost of the new gas fittings for the school and class rooms. Mr. Garnett briefly introduced Dr. Leach to the audience. In his opening remarks, Dr. Leach I gave a history of the voyage out, and of his meeting with Mr. Garnett. Ile did not think there was any country so attractive as Palestine, or one which pre- , sented so great a variety of climate and vegetable life. Although only about the size of Wales, all degrees of climate were to be found there, from the mountain tops covered with perpetual snow, to the hottest weatiler which could be experienced. fhere was no Government, except that of the Turk, whose chief work seemed to be that of extract- ing with the aid of the sword and bayonet, the taxes due from the poo- peasantry, which they were only too often too unwillirg and unable to pay Speaking of Jewish women, Dr. Leael said that wo- men in England ought to be very thankful for their position, for in the East, women, who were the sole property of their husbands, were very badly treated, and often usedas beasts of burden. At Jerusalem,the visitors went in a towec at the Church of Asceision, and were shown a piece of marble on which is a footprint said to have been made by the Saviour when he ascended into Heaven. Dr. Lc 9,ch said he was sorry to enter Jerusalem after the grand v.iew he got of it from the Mount of Oliyes. The pleasant illusions which they had formed were dispelled as they went along the dirty, narrow, foul-smelling streets, lined with shops. The meeting separated after according a hearty vote of thanks to the lec- turer on the motion of the Rev. T. Ross, seconded by Dr. Lomas.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE BURGESSES OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEN EN,-My term Of Office as one of your representatives in the Town Council having expired, I beg to offer myself for re-election. During the time I have had the honour of representing you, it has been my endeavour to serve you to the best of my ability, and, by constant attendance at the various Commit- tees, I have watched your interests very carefully. • With reference to the Intercepting Depots I have, as a property owner in the ward, a great desire to see removed aivy nuisance which arises from these works, and will gladly lend my assistance to any movement having this object in view. lam strongly of opinion that the rates of the Borough ara excessive, and shall in the future, as in the past, oppose all unnecessary expenditure. Being one of the oldest residents in the neighbourhood, ,am personally known to most of you, and shall esteem it a pleasure to serve you to the best of my ability; and, if I am honoured by a renewal of your confidence, I shall do what I can to merit the tiust reposed in me. I um, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH GARNER. Marshhouse-lane, Warrington, October 15, 1891.

IVOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next IN GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY. OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 19th day of October next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury,will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 19th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester, on THURSDAY, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon' when another Grand Jury will be empannellecl. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 29th September, 1891.

ROROUGH OF WARRING TON. THE ELEMENTARY EDUCATION ACT, 1891. ' TO PARENTS, GUARDIANS, AND IOTHERS. NOTICE IS HEREBY GWEN, that the Fee Grant pro- vided by the above Act has been accepted by the Managers of all the Public Elementary Schools within the Borough, and that the School Fees in certain schools have been abolished, while in others they have been considerably reduced. , The School Attendance Committee, are, therefore, deter- mined to enforce strict compliance with the Bye-laws in the attendance at school of children of school age. Children wilt be required to attend school during the whole time for which the school selected shall be open (i.e.. ten attendances in each week), and'no excuse other than those specified in the bye-laws will be allowed. Dated this Ninth day of October. 1891. J. LYON WHITTLE. Clerk to the School Attendance Committee.

I learn the whereabouts of the stuff taken from tffeir place 7" asked the deeply interested Reybold. "Why you must put the detectives on the track of the plunder. You don't expect me to get into a scrape, do you 2" "Certainly not. You have done your part well. I know a lot of the detectives—always keep on good terms with the force—" "Alit I only wish I could," interrupted Mingo. "I'll give them a hint. I can work that to perfection. Lee often visited you at the store, I believer "Oh! often." " And he inquired about the exits and entrances, end the valuables, and so on and so forth 7" "Never knew a man to ask so many question& Bat, I say, Farley." "What is that, Mingo r I don't want to be no witness." "Nor shall you be. Leave that to me. Before pour plan begins to work Lee will be in another big scrape,•and that will fasten suspicion on him," said Reybold, rising, and turning up his coat collar, and pulling down his hat. "What is that 7" asked Mingo, with his hand on the door. "An old trick of his." "Forgery 2" "Guessed it first time. Now good night. Keep mum, and the scheme will work itself." Reybold shook hands with his creature, and de- scended to the street. And he returned to his quarters that night he actually hummed a popnlar air, so rejoiced was he at his ability to sweep forever from his path the only man—as he imagined—who stood in the way of his success, and whose freedom endangered his nwn liberty.
